questions.stem: In Nepal's road classification, a NATIONAL HIGHWAY (NH) is distinguished from a FEEDER ROAD (FR) chiefly in that the national highway:
options: Is always a bituminous-surfaced road while feeder roads are gravel
Carries only freight traffic and no passenger vehicles
Is maintained by the local municipality rather than the central government
Forms the principal ARTERIAL network connecting major regions and international borders, carrying long-distance traffic
questions.solution:
**It forms the principal ARTERIAL network connecting major regions and international borders, carrying long-distance traffic** — while a feeder road links a district headquarters or an important centre TO that arterial network.

**The classification as it stands in Nepal:**

| Class | Function |
|---|---|
| **NATIONAL HIGHWAY (NH)** ← | **The arterial backbone — inter-regional and international connections. Mahendra Highway, Prithvi Highway, Araniko Highway and the rest** ← |
| **FEEDER ROAD (FR)** ← | **Links district headquarters, major towns and economic centres to the national highway network** ← |
| **DISTRICT ROAD (DR)** ← | **Serves traffic within a district, connecting villages to the feeder network** ← |
| **URBAN / MUNICIPAL ROAD** ← | **Within municipal areas, serving local access** ← |

> **THE CLASSIFICATION IS BY FUNCTION AND NOT BY SURFACE OR CONDITION, WHICH IS THE POINT OPTION (a) MISSES: a national highway may be earthen in a remote stretch and a feeder road may be blacktopped where traffic justifies it.**

> **The class describes the road's ROLE in the network, and the standard to which it should eventually be built follows from that role.**

> **So an unsealed national highway is a national highway that has not yet been built to its proper standard, not a road of lower class.**

> **The distinction matters administratively because the class determines who is responsible: the Department of Roads maintains national highways and feeder roads, while district and urban roads fall to local government — so misclassifying a road misdirects its maintenance funding for years.**

**THE FUNCTIONAL HIERARCHY BEHIND THE CLASSIFICATION IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING SINCE IT APPLIES UNIVERSALLY:**

| Function | Characteristic |
|---|---|
| **MOBILITY — moving traffic long distances quickly** ← | **Few access points, higher speed, controlled junctions** ← |
| **ACCESS — reaching individual properties** ← | **Many access points, low speed, frequent junctions** ← |
| **The two are in direct CONFLICT** ← | **Every access point interrupts the through movement** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CENTRAL IDEA OF ROAD HIERARCHY AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THE CLASSES EXIST AT ALL: a road cannot serve both functions well.**

> **A highway with a shop entrance every fifty metres carries through traffic badly and dangerously.**

> **A residential street designed for through movement is unpleasant and unsafe for the people living on it.**

> **So the network separates the functions by class — arterials for mobility with access controlled, local roads for access with through movement discouraged, and collectors mediating between them — and a network in which that separation has broken down performs badly at both jobs regardless of how well any individual road is built.**

> **RIBBON DEVELOPMENT ALONG NEPAL'S HIGHWAYS IS EXACTLY THIS BREAKDOWN AND IT IS WORTH NAMING AS A PLANNING FAILURE RATHER THAN A NUISANCE: buildings, shops and bus stops line the Mahendra Highway for long stretches, each generating turning movements, pedestrians and parked vehicles.**

> **The road was built for mobility and has acquired an access function it was not designed for, and the result is the accident concentration and the speed collapse that those stretches show.**

> **The remedies — service roads parallel to the highway, controlled access, bypasses around settlements — all work by RESTORING the separation of functions.**

> **And they are far more expensive applied afterwards than the land-use control that would have prevented the development, which is a planning lesson rather than an engineering one and is the reason highway alignment and land-use planning must be done together.**

examTip.trick: **NH is the arterial backbone; FR connects district centres TO it** — classification is by FUNCTION, not by surface type.
examTip.trap: **An unsealed national highway is still a national highway** — the class sets who maintains it and what standard it should reach.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mobility and access are in direct conflict** — ribbon development destroys a highway by giving it an access function it was never designed for.

questions.stem: In highway location surveys, the correct sequence of stages is:
options: Detailed survey, then reconnaissance, then map study, then preliminary survey
Preliminary survey, then map study, then detailed survey, then reconnaissance
MAP (desk) STUDY, then RECONNAISSANCE, then PRELIMINARY survey, then DETAILED (final location) survey
Map study and detailed survey only, the intermediate stages being unnecessary
questions.solution:
**MAP (desk) STUDY, then RECONNAISSANCE, then PRELIMINARY survey, then DETAILED (final location) survey** — each stage narrowing the corridor and increasing the precision.

**What each stage does:**

| Stage | Method | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **MAP STUDY** ← | **Topographic maps, satellite imagery, geological and land-use maps — no fieldwork** ← | **Several possible corridors identified** ← |
| **RECONNAISSANCE** ← | **Rapid field inspection of each corridor, on foot or by vehicle; abney level and GPS** ← | **Corridors reduced to two or three; obviously bad ones eliminated** ← |
| **PRELIMINARY survey** ← | **Instrument traverse along each surviving corridor, with approximate levels and soil observations** ← | **Comparative estimates; ONE alignment selected** ← |
| **DETAILED (final location) survey** ← | **Precise traverse, full levelling, cross-sections, soil and material investigation, drainage survey** ← | **Data for the final design and the tender drawings** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE RUNNING THROUGH THE SEQUENCE IS THAT EFFORT INCREASES AS THE AREA NARROWS, AND IT IS THE SAME LOGIC AS THE HYDROPOWER STUDY SEQUENCE: it would be absurd to survey every possible corridor in detail.**

> **So each stage spends a little effort over a wide area to eliminate most of it, and the next stage spends more effort over what remains.**

> **By the final stage the effort per kilometre is very high and it is applied to one alignment only.**

> **Skipping stages inverts this — going from a map study straight to a detailed survey means surveying one corridor precisely without having established that it is the best one, and the precision is then spent on possibly the wrong alignment.**

**WHAT THE RECONNAISSANCE STAGE SPECIFICALLY LOOKS FOR IS WORTH LISTING, SINCE IT IS THE STAGE THAT ELIMINATES MOST OPTIONS:**

| Feature | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Obligatory POINTS the road must pass through or avoid** ← | **A bridge site, a pass, a settlement to be served; a shrine or forest to be avoided** ← |
| **Landslide and unstable slopes** ← | **The dominant constraint in Nepal's hills** ← |
| **Stream crossings and their difficulty** ← | ← |
| **Available construction MATERIALS along the route** ← | **Haul distance for aggregate dominates cost in remote areas** ← |
| **Gradients achievable, and the ridge or valley the route should follow** ← | ← |
| **Existing tracks and access for construction** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHAT MOST OFTEN DECIDES A HILL ALIGNMENT IN NEPAL AND IT DESERVES PRIMACY: a route through unstable ground is a route that will require expensive stabilisation and will fail repeatedly regardless.**

> **Old landslide scars, hummocky ground, tilted trees, seepage lines, and the local name of a place are all readable during reconnaissance by someone who knows what to look for.**

> **That reading costs a few days and can eliminate a corridor that would have cost years of recurrent failure.**

> **So a geologist should walk the reconnaissance with the engineer, and a reconnaissance conducted from a vehicle on an existing road, which is the temptation, sees very little of what matters.**

> **THE FIRST ROW'S 'OBLIGATORY POINTS' CONCEPT IS A USEFUL PLANNING DEVICE AND IT SIMPLIFIES THE PROBLEM CONSIDERABLY: the alignment problem becomes one of connecting a set of fixed points by the best available route between each consecutive pair.**

> **The obligatory points are settled first — the bridge site where the river can be crossed, the pass where the ridge can be surmounted, the town that must be served.**

> **Then each link between consecutive obligatory points is optimised separately, which converts one large problem into several small independent ones.**

> **And identifying an obligatory point wrongly — assuming a river must be crossed at the existing ferry, for instance — constrains everything downstream of that assumption, which is why the obligatory points themselves deserve to be questioned at the reconnaissance stage rather than inherited.**

examTip.trick: **Map study → reconnaissance → preliminary → detailed** — each narrowing the corridor and raising the precision.
examTip.trap: **Skipping to a detailed survey spends precision on an unverified alignment** — the same error as skipping pre-feasibility on a hydropower scheme.
examTip.mnemonic: **Walk the reconnaissance with a geologist** — old scars, tilted trees and seepage lines eliminate corridors that would fail for decades.

questions.stem: The RULING GRADIENT (design gradient) on a hill road is:
options: The maximum gradient that may be used anywhere on the road under any circumstances
The gradient adopted for the NORMAL design of the road's vertical alignment
The average gradient of the whole road from end to end
The gradient below which no drainage is required
questions.solution:
**The gradient adopted for the NORMAL design of the road's vertical alignment** — which the designer aims to keep to, with steeper LIMITING and EXCEPTIONAL gradients permitted only over short stretches where topography makes the ruling gradient unattainable.

**The four gradients defined:**

| Gradient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **RULING (design) gradient** ← | **The normal maximum used in design — the standard the alignment is set to** ← |
| **LIMITING gradient** ← | **Steeper, used where the ruling gradient would greatly increase cost or length; used over limited stretches** ← |
| **EXCEPTIONAL gradient** ← | **Steeper still, used only in the most difficult short stretches and sparingly** ← |
| **MINIMUM gradient** ← | **The flattest gradient that still drains — typically 1 in 200 on a kerbed road, 1 in 100 preferred** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE PEOPLE FORGET EXISTS AND IT MATTERS ON FLAT TERRAIN: a road can be too FLAT.**

> **Water standing on the carriageway is a safety hazard through aquaplaning, and water standing in side drains is a pavement hazard because it saturates the subgrade.**

> **So a longitudinal gradient of at least about 0.5 per cent is required wherever the drainage runs along the road, and a perfectly level road in the Terai is a drainage problem rather than an ideal.**

> **The remedy where the terrain gives no fall is to introduce an artificial saw-tooth profile in the drain invert while keeping the carriageway level, which maintains the drainage gradient without imposing gradients on the traffic.**

**TYPICAL VALUES FOR NEPAL'S HILL AND MOUNTAIN ROADS:**

| Terrain | Ruling | Limiting | Exceptional |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling** ← | **About 3.3% (1 in 30)** ← | **5%** ← | **6.7%** ← |
| **Mountainous, and steep with elevation above 3000 m** ← | **5% (1 in 20)** ← | **6%** ← | **7%** ← |
| **Steep terrain above 3000 m** ← | **6%** ← | **7%** ← | **8%** ← |

> **THE VALUES ARE MODEST COMPARED WITH WHAT VEHICLES CAN PHYSICALLY CLIMB AND THE REASON IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: a loaded truck can ascend 10 per cent, and the limits above are set well below that.**

> **The binding consideration is not whether a vehicle can climb but at what SPEED, and what that does to the road's capacity and to overtaking behaviour.**

> **A heavy vehicle slowed to 15 km/h on a long climb creates a queue, and the queue produces dangerous overtaking on a road with limited sight distance.**

> **So the gradient limits protect capacity and safety rather than tractive capability, and where a steep gradient is unavoidable the proper response is a CLIMBING LANE that lets the queue pass rather than a further reduction in gradient.**

> **A FURTHER CONSIDERATION SPECIFIC TO HILL ROADS DESERVES MENTION: gradient and length trade directly against each other, since a fixed height must be gained.**

> **A gentler ruling gradient means a longer road, more earthwork, more structures and more slopes to stabilise.**

> **In Himalayan terrain that trade is severe — halving the gradient doubles the length — so the ruling gradient is chosen with the total cost in view, and hill roads accept steeper standards than plains roads for exactly this reason.**

> **The compensation on curves is a related refinement: on a sharp curve the effective resistance is greater, so the gradient is REDUCED — grade compensation of about 30/R to 75/R per cent, subject to not reducing below 4 per cent — which prevents the combination of a steep grade and a sharp curve from defeating a heavy vehicle entirely.**
tags: gradient limits protect speed not tractive effort

examTip.trick: **The normal design gradient** — with limiting and exceptional gradients allowed only over short difficult stretches.
examTip.trap: **A MINIMUM gradient also exists** — about 0.5% for drainage. A perfectly level Terai road is a drainage problem, not an ideal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gradient limits protect SPEED, not climbing ability** — a truck can do 10%, but at 15 km/h it creates queues and dangerous overtaking. Add a climbing lane.

questions.stem: In hill road alignment, a HAIRPIN BEND is introduced principally to:
options: Provide a place for vehicles to park and rest
Improve the view for travellers
Reduce the road's construction cost by shortening it
GAIN HEIGHT within a limited horizontal distance
questions.solution:
**To GAIN HEIGHT within a limited horizontal distance** — turning the alignment back on itself so the ruling gradient can be maintained where the hillside is too steep to climb directly.

**Why a hairpin is sometimes unavoidable:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A road must gain height at no more than the ruling gradient** ← | ← |
| **So gaining 100 m at 5 per cent requires 2,000 m of road length** ← | ← |
| **On a spur or a narrow valley, there may be no 2,000 m of hillside available in one direction** ← | ← |
| **So the alignment must double back to find the length** ← | ← |
| **Each hairpin adds height at the cost of a very sharp curve** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE ARITHMETIC THAT GOVERNS HILL ALIGNMENT AND IT IS WORTH INTERNALISING: at 5 per cent, every metre of height costs twenty metres of road.**

> **A 600 m climb therefore requires 12 km of road, however direct the route looks on a map.**

> **That is why hill roads are so much longer than the straight-line distance, and why a village visible across a valley may be an hour's drive away.**

> **And it is why reducing the ruling gradient is so costly in hill terrain — the length, and therefore the earthwork, the structures and the slope stabilisation, all scale inversely with it.**

**THE DESIGN REQUIREMENTS FOR A HAIRPIN ARE SPECIFIC AND THEY EXIST BECAUSE THE BEND IS INHERENTLY DIFFICULT:**

| Requirement | Typical provision |
|---|---|
| **Locate it on the most STABLE and gently sloping ground available** ← | **A spur nose or a bench, never a gully or a slide zone** ← |
| **A generous minimum RADIUS at the inner edge** ← | **Commonly 14 to 20 m for a hill road, set by the design vehicle's turning circle** ← |
| **WIDENING of the carriageway through the bend** ← | **A long vehicle's rear wheels track inside the front wheels — the off-tracking allowance** ← |
| **A FLAT or very gentle gradient through the bend itself** ← | **Commonly limited to 2.5% — a steep grade on a sharp curve is the worst combination** ← |
| **Full SUPERELEVATION, applied through the bend** ← | ← |
| **Adequate spacing between successive hairpins** ← | **So that drivers and vehicles recover between them** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW COMBINES WITH THE GRADE COMPENSATION PRINCIPLE AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT GEOMETRIC RULE FOR A HAIRPIN: the bend must be nearly LEVEL.**

> **A long vehicle negotiating a 15 m radius turn is already using most of its tractive effort against curve resistance and most of its steering lock.**

> **Adding a 6 per cent grade may exceed what it can manage, and a vehicle that stalls on a hairpin blocks the road completely — there being no width to pass and no alternative route.**

> **So the height gain is made on the STRAIGHTS between the hairpins and not through the bends themselves, which means the straights carry a steeper gradient than the average and the bends carry almost none.**

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WHERE HILL ROAD ALIGNMENT IS MOST OFTEN COMPROMISED AND THE CONSEQUENCE IS LONG-LASTING: a hairpin requires a wide, level platform, which means a large cut on the hillside or a large fill.**

> **The tempting places to put one are the gullies, where the topography already forms a re-entrant of about the right shape.**

> **Those are precisely the worst places — a gully concentrates water and is often the head of an existing or potential slide, and a wide bench cut there destabilises it further.**

> **The right place is a SPUR, where the ground is convex, the drainage divides rather than concentrates, and a bench can be cut into stable material — and the difference between a hairpin on a spur and one in a gully is often the difference between a road that needs occasional maintenance and one that fails every monsoon.**
tags: 20 m of road per metre of height
site hairpins on spurs not gullies

examTip.trick: **To gain height where the hillside is too steep to climb directly** — doubling back to find the length the gradient requires.
examTip.trap: **At 5%, every metre of height costs 20 m of road** — a 600 m climb needs 12 km whatever the map distance suggests.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hairpins on SPURS, never in gullies** — convex ground sheds water and is stable; a gully concentrates it and is a slide waiting to happen.

questions.stem: Comparing a VALLEY (river) alignment with a RIDGE alignment for a hill road, the valley route generally offers:
options: Easier gradients and shorter length, but greater exposure to FLOODING, landslides from the valley sides, and numerous tributary crossings
Greater stability and fewer stream crossings
Better access to settlements, which are concentrated on valley floors in Nepal's hills
Lower construction cost in every respect
questions.solution:
**Easier gradients and shorter length, but greater exposure to FLOODING, landslides from the valley sides, and numerous tributary crossings** — while a ridge route is drier and more stable but longer with steeper access.

**The two alignments compared:**

| Aspect | VALLEY alignment | RIDGE alignment |
|---|---|---|
| **Gradient** | **Gentle — follows the river's own grade** ← | **Undulating, with steep climbs to reach and leave the ridge** ← |
| **Length** | **Shorter, following the natural line** ← | **Longer, following the ridge's meanders** ← |
| **Stability** | **POOR — valley sides are the steepest and most active slopes** ← | **GOOD — ridges are the stable remnants** ← |
| **Drainage** | **Difficult — the road is at the bottom, receiving everything** ← | **Excellent — water drains away on both sides** ← |
| **Stream crossings** | **MANY — every tributary must be crossed** ← | **Very few — a ridge crosses no watercourses** ← |
| **Flooding** | **A real hazard, and increasing** ← | **None** ← |
| **Settlements served** | **Some, though Nepal's hill settlements are often on slopes and ridges** ← | **Often good — many hill villages sit on ridges and saddles** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE WHY THE RIDGE ROUTE IS SO OFTEN THE BETTER ENGINEERING CHOICE IN NEPAL DESPITE ITS GREATER LENGTH: a ridge road sheds water and crosses nothing.**

> **A valley road receives the drainage of the entire catchment above it and must cross every tributary, each crossing being a structure that can be washed out.**

> **In a country whose roads fail overwhelmingly through water — slides, washouts, scour at crossings — that difference dominates the whole-life cost.**

> **The Prithvi Highway's difficulties along the Trishuli and the recurrent losses on valley-bottom roads in the monsoon illustrate the point, and the older hill trails, which run along ridges, illustrate the alternative that generations of foot travel arrived at empirically.**

**THE PRACTICAL RESOLUTION IS USUALLY NEITHER EXTREME AND IT IS WORTH STATING:**

| Approach | Note |
|---|---|
| **A route on the valley side, well ABOVE the flood level but below the ridge** ← | **The common compromise for a hill road** ← |
| **Kept above the active slope toe and below the steepest upper slopes** ← | ← |
| **Crossing tributaries high up where they are small** ← | **A crossing near a tributary's confluence is wide and deep; the same stream 200 m upslope may be a culvert** ← |
| **And using spurs to change level** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A GENUINELY USEFUL ALIGNMENT TECHNIQUE AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED: the cost of crossing a tributary falls steeply as one moves upstream.**

> **A road that dips into each side valley to cross the stream where it is narrow trades a little extra length and some gradient for a culvert instead of a bridge.**

> **Over a route with twenty tributaries that trade can be worth a great deal, and it is why hill roads wind into and out of every side valley rather than running straight across their mouths.**

> **The limit is that each such excursion adds length and two curves, so the optimum is a matter of comparing the structure saved against the road added — which is a calculation that can be done for each tributary individually and often is not.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON WHY VALLEY ROUTES ARE CHOSEN ANYWAY, SINCE THEY FREQUENTLY ARE: the gradient advantage is decisive where the road must carry heavy freight, and the shorter length reduces the initial cost, which is what tends to be compared.**

> **The stability and maintenance disadvantages fall on a later budget and on a different organisation.**

> **So the institutional structure favours the valley route even where the whole-life analysis favours the ridge, which is the same misalignment of incentives seen throughout this material — and naming it is the first step to correcting it, by requiring alignment comparisons to be made on a whole-life basis with maintenance costs included.**
tags: ridges shed water and cross nothing

examTip.trick: **Valley: easier grades, shorter, but unstable, flood-prone and full of crossings. Ridge: longer and steeper to reach, but dry and stable.**
examTip.trap: **A ridge crosses NO watercourses and sheds water both ways** — decisive in a country whose roads fail through water.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cross tributaries high up** — a bridge at the confluence is a culvert 200 m upslope. Winding into side valleys buys structures cheaply.

questions.stem: The SATURATION SYSTEM of road planning, used in the Nagpur and subsequent road plans, allocates road length on the basis of:
options: MAXIMUM UTILITY
The revenue each district generates
The length of road already existing in each district
The political importance of each region
questions.solution:
**MAXIMUM UTILITY** — road length being allocated so as to serve the greatest number of villages and the largest population and productive area per unit length, with utility units assigned and the network developed to 'saturate' the area.

**How the method works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Assign UTILITY UNITS for the population served** ← | **So many units per thousand people within a defined distance of the road** ← |
| **Assign units for the PRODUCTIVE AREA served** ← | **Agricultural and industrial output within the influence zone** ← |
| **Add units for other benefits** ← | **Access to markets, administrative centres, education, health** ← |
| **Compute the total utility of each candidate road** ← | ← |
| **Rank the candidates by UTILITY PER UNIT LENGTH or per unit cost** ← | ← |
| **Build in that order until the area is 'saturated'** ← | **Saturation being the point at which further road adds little utility** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE METHOD'S ESSENTIAL IDEA AND IT IS A SOUND ONE: rank by utility per unit of resource, not by total utility.**

> **A long road serving many people may have a high total utility and a poor ratio; a short link serving a moderate number may have an excellent one.**

> **Since the budget is the constraint, the ratio is what should govern, and building in order of the ratio maximises the utility obtained from whatever budget is available.**

> **This is the standard result for allocating a limited budget among independent projects, and the saturation system is essentially that result applied to road planning with a particular way of measuring benefit.**

**THE METHOD'S LIMITATIONS ARE REAL AND ARE WORTH NAMING:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The UTILITY UNITS are assigned somewhat arbitrarily** ← | **How many units is a school worth against a hectare of paddy?** ← |
| **It measures ACCESS rather than economic return** ← | **A road may serve many people and generate little economic activity** ← |
| **It does not consider the road's CONDITION or its maintainability** ← | ← |
| **Nor the terrain's difficulty, unless cost is used as the denominator** ← | ← |
| **And it treats roads as independent when they form a NETWORK** ← | **A link's value depends on what it connects to** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST SERIOUS THEORETICAL OBJECTION AND IT MATTERS PRACTICALLY: roads are not independent projects.**

> **A link whose utility is modest in isolation may complete a route and transform the value of everything it joins, and a link built in isolation may serve nobody until its connections exist.**

> **So ranking links individually can build a set of high-scoring disconnected fragments rather than a functioning network.**

> **Network analysis addresses this by evaluating the whole network's performance with and without each candidate link, which is computationally heavier and gives a much better answer — and it is why modern road planning uses network models rather than the utility-unit approach, though the utility approach remains a useful screening method and a clear way to explain the principle.**

> **THE SECOND ROW POINTS TO A GENUINE TENSION IN RURAL ROAD PLANNING THAT DESERVES ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: access and economic return are different objectives and they favour different roads.**

> **An economic appraisal favours roads serving productive areas with goods to move; an access criterion favours roads serving remote populations who currently have nothing.**

> **The second is where the human need is greatest and the economic return is weakest.**

> **So the choice between the criteria is a policy question about what the road programme is FOR, and it should be settled explicitly rather than buried in the weighting of utility units — because a technical-looking allocation method with policy assumptions hidden inside it produces decisions nobody has actually taken.**
tags: roads are a network not independent projects

examTip.trick: **Maximum utility — units for population and productive area served, ranked per unit length or cost.**
examTip.trap: **Rank by the RATIO, not the total** — that is what maximises utility from a fixed budget.
examTip.mnemonic: **Roads form a NETWORK, so ranking links individually can build disconnected high-scoring fragments** — which is why network models superseded the method.

questions.stem: The RIGHT OF WAY of a road is:
options: The width of the carriageway available to moving vehicles
The legal priority a vehicle has at a junction
The total LAND WIDTH acquired and legally reserved for the road and its future development
The width between the outer edges of the side drains only
questions.solution:
**The total LAND WIDTH acquired and legally reserved for the road and its future development** — including the carriageway, shoulders, drains, slopes, footpaths, services and a margin for future widening.

**The cross-sectional terms distinguished, since they nest inside one another:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CARRIAGEWAY** ← | **The paved width on which vehicles travel** ← |
| **SHOULDER** ← | **The strip alongside the carriageway, for stopped vehicles and lateral support of the pavement** ← |
| **ROADWAY (formation width)** ← | **Carriageway plus shoulders — the full formed top surface** ← |
| **RIGHT OF WAY (land width)** ← | **The whole legally reserved strip, including everything above plus drains, slopes, footpaths, services and reserve** ← |
| **BUILDING LINE** ← | **A line beyond the right of way within which construction is restricted** ← |
| **CONTROL LINE** ← | **A further line controlling the nature of development** ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS ARE THE PROVISIONS THAT PROTECT THE ROAD FROM THE DEVELOPMENT IT ATTRACTS, AND THEY ARE WHERE ENFORCEMENT MOST OFTEN FAILS: the right of way secures the land the road occupies, and the building line secures a setback beyond it.**

> **Without the setback, buildings crowd to the very edge of the reserved strip, and any future widening requires demolition and compensation at what by then are developed-land prices.**

> **With it, the road can be widened within land that was never built on, at a fraction of the cost and without displacing anyone.**

> **The building line therefore costs nothing to establish at the outset and saves an enormous amount later — and it is routinely ignored in Nepal, which is why widening projects on existing highways involve such extensive and contentious acquisition.**

**WHY THE RIGHT OF WAY IS MADE WIDER THAN THE ROAD CURRENTLY NEEDS:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Future WIDENING — a two-lane road may need four lanes in thirty years** ← | ← |
| **Future SERVICES — water, sewer, power, telecom, all seeking the road corridor** ← | ← |
| **Sight distance at curves requires land clear of obstruction on the inside** ← | ← |
| **Cut and fill SLOPES need land beyond the formation, and more where they are high** ← | ← |
| **Drainage, including outfall channels** ← | ← |
| **And a margin against encroachment, which will occur** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A FUNCTION OF THE ROAD CORRIDOR THAT IS RARELY PLANNED AND ALWAYS HAPPENS: every utility wants to run along the road, because the road provides a continuous corridor and access for maintenance.**

> **Unplanned, this produces a corridor repeatedly excavated by successive utilities, each trench weakening the pavement and each reinstatement worse than the original surface.**

> **The answer is a designated SERVICE DUCT or utility corridor within the right of way, established when the road is built, with ducts laid for services that do not yet exist.**

> **Laying spare ducts costs very little during construction and saves the pavement from being opened repeatedly for decades — and the failure to do so is visible on almost every urban road in the country, where the carriageway is a patchwork of utility reinstatements.**

> **THE THIRD ROW DESERVES A SPECIFIC NOTE BECAUSE IT IS A SAFETY REQUIREMENT RATHER THAN A CONVENIENCE: on the inside of a horizontal curve, the driver's sight line cuts across the land inside the curve.**

> **A wall, a hedge, a cut slope or a building on that land obstructs the view and reduces the available sight distance below the stopping distance.**

> **So the right of way on the inside of a curve must be wide enough to contain the required SET-BACK, and that land must be kept clear permanently — not merely at construction.**

> **The set-back distance follows from the sight distance required and the curve's radius, and it can be substantial on a sharp curve, which is a reason for the right of way to widen through curves rather than being a constant strip.**

examTip.trick: **The whole legally reserved land width** — carriageway, shoulders, drains, slopes, services and future widening reserve.
examTip.trap: **Carriageway ⊂ roadway (formation) ⊂ right of way** — three nested widths that are constantly confused.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lay spare utility ducts at construction** — otherwise the pavement is trenched repeatedly for decades. And keep the curve set-back clear permanently.

questions.stem: A road is to gain 240 m of height. If the ruling gradient is 6 per cent and no other constraint applies, the minimum road length required for the climb is:
questions.solution:
**4,000 m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Gradient as a ratio** | **6 per cent = 6 in 100 = 0.06** ← |
| **Length = height ÷ gradient** | **L = 240 ÷ 0.06** ← |
| ** ** | **= 4,000 m = 4 km** ← |

> **THE CHECK IS TO READ THE GRADIENT AS A STATEMENT ABOUT THE CLIMB: 6 per cent means 6 m of rise for every 100 m of length.**

> **So 240 m of rise needs 240/6 = 40 such hundred-metre lengths, which is 4,000 m.**

> **Doing it that way avoids the decimal entirely and makes the answer obvious.**

> **The distractor at 1,440 m comes from multiplying 240 × 6 instead of dividing, and 14,400 from multiplying by 60 — both being the error of getting the operation backwards, which the sanity check catches at once because a road must obviously be LONGER than the height it climbs.**

**WHAT THE ANSWER MEANS IN HILL ROAD TERMS, WHICH IS THE ENGINEERING CONTENT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **4 km of road to gain 240 m** ← | ← |
| **If the hillside offers only 1.5 km of usable length in one direction** ← | ← |
| **The alignment must double back — requiring at least two hairpins** ← | ← |
| **Each hairpin needs a stable bench and adds curve resistance** ← | ← |
| **So the height gain drives the alignment's whole form** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS HOW THE HAIRPIN COUNT IS ESTIMATED AT THE RECONNAISSANCE STAGE AND IT IS A USEFUL QUICK CALCULATION: divide the required length by the usable length available in each direction.**

> **Four kilometres of road on a spur offering 1.5 km each way means roughly three legs, hence two hairpins.**

> **Knowing that number early matters because each hairpin needs a site, and the sites may not exist — a hillside with no stable bench cannot accommodate the hairpins the gradient requires, and that eliminates the corridor.**

> **So this simple division is one of the quickest ways to test whether a candidate hill alignment is feasible at all, and it can be done from a contour map before anyone walks the ground.**

**AND A COMPARISON ACROSS GRADIENTS SHOWS WHY THE RULING GRADIENT MATTERS SO MUCH IN HILL TERRAIN:**

| Ruling gradient | Length to climb 240 m |
|---|---|
| **4%** | **6,000 m** ← |
| **5%** | **4,800 m** ← |
| **6%** | **4,000 m** ← |
| **7%** | **3,429 m** ← |
| **8%** | **3,000 m** ← |

> **THE RANGE FROM 4 TO 8 PER CENT HALVES THE LENGTH AND THAT IS AN ENORMOUS DIFFERENCE IN CONSTRUCTION COST: 6 km of hill road against 3 km, with all the earthwork, retaining structures, drainage and slope stabilisation that the extra 3 km implies.**

> **So the pressure to adopt a steeper ruling gradient in mountainous terrain is strong and it is legitimate.**

> **What must be weighed against it is the operating cost — a steeper road is slower, harder on vehicles, more dangerous when wet or icy, and it may exclude some vehicle types altogether.**

> **Those costs fall on road users over the road's whole life, and they are real even though they appear in no construction budget — so the choice of ruling gradient is a genuine whole-life trade rather than a construction decision, and it deserves to be made with the traffic's composition and volume in view rather than by applying a standard uncritically.**

examTip.trick: **L = 240 ÷ 0.06 = 4,000 m.** Or: 6 m rise per 100 m, so 40 hundred-metre lengths.
examTip.trap: **The road must be LONGER than the height climbed** — which rules out 1,440 and 400 instantly, without any arithmetic.
examTip.mnemonic: **Divide required length by usable hillside length to count the hairpins** — a contour-map test of whether a hill corridor is feasible at all.

questions.stem: A GREEN ROAD approach to rural road construction in Nepal is characterised by:
options: Surfacing the road with vegetation rather than gravel
Building only roads that carry electric vehicles
Restricting road construction to protected forest areas
LABOUR-BASED, environment-friendly construction spread over several seasons
questions.solution:
**LABOUR-BASED, environment-friendly construction spread over several seasons** — minimising mass excavation, balancing cut and fill, allowing cut slopes to stabilise naturally before the next stage, and using bio-engineering for slope protection.

**The principles of the green road approach:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **LABOUR-BASED rather than equipment-based** ← | **Generates local employment and income, and suits remote sites without machine access** ← |
| **Construction spread over SEVERAL SEASONS** ← | **Cut in one dry season, let the monsoon expose the weaknesses, repair and proceed** ← |
| **BALANCED cut and fill, with no side-tipping of spoil** ← | **Spoil tipped down a hillside is the largest single cause of slope failure below hill roads** ← |
| **BIO-ENGINEERING — vegetation used structurally for slope protection** ← | ← |
| **Narrow formation, opened progressively** ← | ← |
| **Community participation in planning, construction and maintenance** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TECHNICAL PRINCIPLE AND IT IS THE ONE MOST VIOLATED BY CONVENTIONAL CONSTRUCTION: bulldozing a hill road and pushing the spoil over the edge is fast and cheap and it destroys the slope below.**

> **The tipped material is loose, uncompacted and placed on a steep slope, often over vegetation that then decays.**

> **It saturates in the monsoon and fails, taking the original hillside with it, and the resulting slide may extend hundreds of metres downslope — damaging fields, houses and any road below.**

> **So the damage from a bulldozed hill road extends far beyond its own width, and the green road principle of retaining all spoil within the formation, in engineered fill, is what prevents it.**

**THE MULTI-SEASON PRINCIPLE IS THE APPROACH'S MOST DISTINCTIVE FEATURE AND ITS LOGIC IS WORTH SETTING OUT:**

| Stage | Timing |
|---|---|
| **Season 1: excavate the formation to a narrow width** ← | **Dry season** ← |
| **First monsoon: the cut slopes are tested by rain** ← | **Weak points reveal themselves as small failures** ← |
| **Season 2: repair those failures, widen, build drainage and structures** ← | ← |
| **Second monsoon: further settlement and testing** ← | ← |
| **Season 3: final formation, surfacing, bio-engineering established** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE INSIGHT AND IT IS A DELIBERATE USE OF FAILURE AS INFORMATION: a freshly cut slope does not reveal its weaknesses until it has been rained on.**

> **Building the road to its final standard in one season means the surfacing and structures are in place before the slopes have been tested, and the first monsoon's failures then damage completed work.**

> **Allowing the slopes a monsoon to settle, and repairing what fails before completing the road, means the failures occur on an unfinished and inexpensive formation.**

> **So the approach trades TIME — three seasons instead of one — for a much lower whole-life cost and a road that is stable when it is finished, and the trade is a good one wherever the road is not urgently needed.**

> **BIO-ENGINEERING DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD AS DECORATION: vegetation used in slope protection is a structural measure with defined functions.**

> **Roots REINFORCE the soil mass and anchor the surface layer; foliage INTERCEPTS rainfall and reduces its erosive impact; growth on a slope surface ARMOURS it against surface erosion; and dense planting in a gully DRAINS and traps sediment.**

> **Different species and planting arrangements serve different functions, so the selection is a design decision — grasses for surface armouring, deep-rooted shrubs for reinforcement, bamboo for drainage lines.**

> **And its great advantage over a structural solution is that it grows STRONGER with time while a gabion wall corrodes and a masonry wall cracks, which makes it uniquely suited to a road network whose maintenance funding is unreliable.**

examTip.trick: **Labour-based, multi-season, balanced cut and fill, bio-engineered slopes** — environment-friendly rural road construction.
examTip.trap: **Side-tipped spoil is the biggest cause of slope failure below hill roads** — the damage extends far beyond the road's own width.
examTip.mnemonic: **Let the first monsoon find the weak slopes before you finish the road** — failures then occur on cheap unfinished formation, not on completed work.

questions.stem: A TRAFFIC VOLUME COUNT for a road improvement project should be conducted:
options: Over a period long enough to capture DAILY, WEEKLY and SEASONAL variation
For a single day at the busiest location, which represents the road adequately
Only during the monsoon, when traffic is heaviest
Only at night, when counting is easier
questions.solution:
**Over a period long enough to capture DAILY, WEEKLY and SEASONAL variation** — since traffic varies by hour, by day of the week and by season, and a single short count can misrepresent the annual average by a wide margin.

**The variations a count must account for:**

| Variation | Typical magnitude |
|---|---|
| **HOURLY — the morning and evening peaks** ← | **The peak hour may carry 8 to 12 per cent of the day's traffic** ← |
| **DAILY — weekdays against weekends** ← | **Commercial traffic falls at weekends; leisure traffic rises** ← |
| **SEASONAL — festivals, harvest, monsoon, tourist season** ← | **Dashain and Tihar produce enormous peaks on Nepal's highways** ← |
| **DIRECTIONAL — the flow is rarely balanced** ← | **A commuter route may be 70:30 in the peak** ← |
| **COMPOSITION — the mix of vehicle types, which changes through the day** ← | **Heavy vehicles often travel at night** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE VARIATION THAT MATTERS MOST FOR PAVEMENT DESIGN AND IT IS EASILY MISSED BY A DAYTIME COUNT: heavy goods vehicles frequently travel overnight, to avoid daytime congestion and restrictions.**

> **A count conducted from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. sees the passenger traffic and misses a large part of the truck traffic.**

> **Since pavement damage depends almost entirely on the heavy vehicles, that omission understates the design traffic severely — and the pavement is then designed for a fraction of the loading it will actually receive.**

> **So a count for pavement design must be a full 24-hour count, on several days, with vehicles classified — and a 12-hour count factored up by a standard ratio is a poor substitute where the night-time composition differs from the daytime one, which on a freight route it always does.**

**HOW A SHORT COUNT IS CONVERTED TO AN ANNUAL AVERAGE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Conduct the classified count over 7 continuous days, 24 hours** ← | **The minimum for a serious survey** ← |
| **Apply a SEASONAL correction factor** ← | **Derived from a permanent count station on a comparable road** ← |
| **To obtain the AADT — Annual Average Daily Traffic** ← | ← |
| **Then project forward at a growth rate to the design year** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE STEP THAT REQUIRES DATA A PROJECT CANNOT COLLECT FOR ITSELF, AND IT IS WHY PERMANENT COUNT STATIONS MATTER: a seasonal factor can only come from somewhere that counts all year.**

> **A network of permanent automatic count stations, maintained continuously, provides the seasonal profile that every short count in the region is then corrected against.**

> **Without them, a count taken in March must be converted to an annual average by guesswork.**

> **So the permanent stations are infrastructure for the whole planning system rather than for any one project, and they are exactly the kind of shared, unglamorous provision that is chronically underfunded because no single project needs it and every project depends on it.**

> **THE GROWTH PROJECTION IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES A CAUTION BECAUSE IT COMPOUNDS: a 7 per cent annual growth rate doubles the traffic in ten years and quadruples it in twenty.**

> **So the design-year traffic is extremely sensitive to the growth rate assumed, and a rate taken from recent history may not persist.**

> **The honest treatment is to test the design against a range of growth rates and to state which rate the design assumes — and where the sensitivity is high, to design the pavement in a way that allows STRENGTHENING later rather than committing to a single forecast.**

> **A staged pavement design, with an overlay planned for year ten once the actual growth is known, is a rational response to genuine forecast uncertainty and is often cheaper in present-value terms than building for the highest credible forecast at the outset.**
tags: growth rate sensitivity and staged design

examTip.trick: **Long enough to capture daily, weekly and seasonal variation** — a single short count can be far from the annual average.
examTip.trap: **Heavy vehicles travel at NIGHT** — a 12-hour count misses them, and pavement damage is almost entirely their doing. Count 24 hours, classified.
examTip.mnemonic: **7% growth doubles traffic in 10 years** — test a range of rates, and consider a staged design with a planned overlay rather than one forecast.

questions.stem: In an ORIGIN-DESTINATION (O-D) survey, the purpose is to establish:
options: The total number of vehicles passing a point in a day
The speed at which vehicles travel between two points
WHERE journeys begin and end
The condition of the road surface along a route
questions.solution:
**WHERE journeys begin and end** — so that the pattern of travel demand is known, through traffic can be distinguished from local traffic, and the need for a bypass or a new link can be assessed.

**What an O-D survey answers that a volume count cannot:**

| Question | Volume count | O-D survey |
|---|---|---|
| **How many vehicles pass here?** | **YES** ← | **Incidentally** ← |
| **Where are they going?** | **NO** ← | **YES** ← |
| **How many are just passing THROUGH the town?** | **NO** ← | **YES** ← |
| **Would a bypass help, and how much traffic would use it?** | **NO** ← | **YES** ← |
| **Which new link would relieve this congestion?** | **NO** ← | **YES** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CLASSIC APPLICATION AND IT IS THE ONE MOST WORTH REMEMBERING: whether a bypass is justified depends entirely on how much of the traffic in a town has no business there.**

> **A volume count at the town centre might show 8,000 vehicles a day, and that figure says nothing about whether a bypass would help.**

> **If 6,000 of them are through traffic, a bypass transforms the town; if 500 are, it achieves almost nothing and wastes a great deal of money.**

> **Only an O-D survey distinguishes the two, which is why a bypass proposal unsupported by O-D data is a proposal whose central premise has not been tested.**

**THE SURVEY METHODS, EACH WITH ITS OWN CHARACTER:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **ROADSIDE INTERVIEW** ← | **Stop a sample of vehicles and ask. Accurate and detailed; disruptive and needs police cooperation** ← |
| **LICENSE PLATE matching** ← | **Record plates at several stations and match them. No disruption; gives only the observed points, not true origins** ← |
| **RETURN POST CARD** ← | **Hand a card to drivers to complete and post back. Cheap; low and biased response rate** ← |
| **HOME INTERVIEW** ← | **Survey households about all their travel. The most complete picture; expensive and slow** ← |
| **TAG ON VEHICLE** ← | **Attach a tag at entry and remove at exit** ← |
| **Mobile phone or GPS trace data** ← | **The modern approach — vast samples, no fieldwork, though it requires access and raises privacy questions** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW HAS LARGELY DISPLACED THE OTHERS WHERE THE DATA IS OBTAINABLE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING WHY: anonymised mobile network data records the movement of millions of devices continuously.**

> **That gives a sample size and a temporal coverage no fieldwork can approach, at a fraction of the cost, and it captures seasonal and day-of-week variation automatically.**

> **Its weaknesses are that it identifies the DEVICE's movement rather than the vehicle's or the trip's purpose, that coverage is uneven where phone ownership is, and that access depends on the network operator's cooperation and on the privacy framework permitting it.**

> **So it supplements rather than wholly replaces conventional surveys, and a modern study typically uses trace data for the broad pattern and a small interview survey to establish trip purpose and vehicle occupancy, which the traces cannot supply.**

> **THE RESULT OF AN O-D SURVEY IS PRESENTED AS A TRIP MATRIX AND THAT FORM IS WORTH KNOWING: the study area is divided into ZONES, and the matrix records the number of trips from each zone to each other zone.**

> **A desire line diagram plots those flows as straight lines between zone centroids, with width proportional to volume, and it shows the travel demand's pattern independently of the existing network.**

> **That independence is the diagram's value — it shows where people WANT to go rather than where the current roads take them, so it reveals demand that the existing network serves badly.**

> **A strong desire line with no direct road along it is precisely the case for a new link, and identifying those is the main planning use to which the whole survey is put.**

examTip.trick: **Where journeys begin and end** — which separates through traffic from local, and so tests whether a bypass is worth building.
examTip.trap: **A volume count cannot justify a bypass** — 8,000 vehicles a day says nothing about how many have no business in the town.
examTip.mnemonic: **Desire lines show where people WANT to go, not where roads take them** — a strong desire line with no road along it is the case for a new link.

questions.stem: The ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT of a hill road in Nepal that is generally the most severe and the most persistent is:
options: Noise from traffic using the completed road
Air pollution from vehicle exhaust
Loss of agricultural land under the road formation itself
SLOPE INSTABILITY AND EROSION
questions.solution:
**SLOPE INSTABILITY AND EROSION** — the cut slopes, the tipped spoil and the concentrated drainage initiating landslides and gullying that continue to deliver sediment and to threaten land and property for many years after construction.

**Why this impact dominates the others:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It extends far BEYOND the road's own footprint** ← | **A slide below a road can destroy fields and houses hundreds of metres downslope** ← |
| **It PERSISTS and often worsens for years** ← | **Unlike noise or dust, which end with construction or are confined to the road** ← |
| **It is largely IRREVERSIBLE once a large slide is initiated** ← | ← |
| **It delivers sediment to rivers, affecting downstream irrigation and hydropower** ← | **A cumulative regional impact** ← |
| **And it endangers life, which the other impacts generally do not** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WHAT MAKES THE IMPACT SO DISPROPORTIONATE AND IT IS WORTH QUANTIFYING: a road may occupy a 10 m strip and destabilise a slope 200 m deep.**

> **So the area affected can be twenty times the area taken, and the affected land belongs to people who received no compensation because their land was not acquired.**

> **That mismatch — between who is compensated and who is harmed — is a recurring source of grievance on Nepali road projects and it is entirely predictable from the engineering.**

> **An impact assessment that considers only the acquired corridor therefore misses most of the harm, and a compensation framework tied to land acquisition misses most of the people affected.**

**THE ENGINEERING CAUSES ARE SPECIFIC AND EACH HAS A KNOWN REMEDY:**

| Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **SPOIL side-tipped down the slope** ← | **Retain all spoil in engineered fill or designated tipping sites; balance cut and fill** ← |
| **Cut slopes too STEEP for the material** ← | **Slope angles set by the material, benched where high, with drainage** ← |
| **Drainage CONCENTRATED and discharged onto an unprotected slope** ← | **Lined chutes to a safe outfall, with energy dissipation** ← |
| **Culvert outfalls discharging onto bare hillside** ← | **The single commonest cause of gully initiation below a hill road** ← |
| **Vegetation stripped over a wide construction width** ← | **Minimise the width; replant immediately** ← |
| **Blasting damaging the rock mass beyond the excavation** ← | **Controlled perimeter blasting** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESERVES SINGLING OUT BECAUSE IT IS SO COMMON, SO DAMAGING AND SO CHEAP TO PREVENT: a culvert collects the drainage of a catchment above the road and discharges it at one point.**

> **Discharged onto the hillside without protection, that concentrated flow cuts a gully, the gully deepens and works back, and in time it undermines the culvert and the road above it.**

> **The remedy is a lined chute carrying the flow down to a natural watercourse, with a dissipator at the bottom — which costs a small fraction of the culvert itself.**

> **Its omission is the reason so many hill road culverts are found perched above a deep gully of their own making, and repairing that afterwards costs many times what the chute would have.**

> **THE PROPER TREATMENT OF THESE IMPACTS IN THE PROJECT CYCLE IS THE CLOSING POINT AND IT IS A MATTER OF TIMING: every remedy above is cheap when designed in and expensive when retrofitted.**

> **The tipping sites must be identified before excavation begins, the chutes must be built as the culverts are built, and the bio-engineering must be planted in the first season after cutting so that it is established before the slopes have degraded.**

> **A project that completes its earthworks and then commissions a slope stabilisation package has already incurred most of the damage and is paying to repair it.**

> **So the environmental management plan must be integrated into the construction programme and the contract, with the remedies as work items on the same programme as the earthworks — not as a separate environmental contract to follow, which is how it is too often arranged and why it too often arrives late.**
tags: remedies must be in the construction programme

examTip.trick: **Slope instability and erosion** — extending far beyond the road, persisting for years, and endangering life.
examTip.trap: **A 10 m road can destabilise a 200 m slope** — and the people harmed downslope were never compensated, since their land was not acquired.
examTip.mnemonic: **An unprotected culvert outfall cuts the gully that eventually undermines the culvert** — a lined chute costs a fraction of the structure it protects.

questions.stem: In the economic evaluation of a road project, VEHICLE OPERATING COST (VOC) savings are usually the largest quantified benefit. VOC includes:
options: Only the cost of fuel consumed
Fuel, lubricants, TYRES, maintenance and repair, depreciation, crew time and interest on capital
Only the driver's wages and the vehicle's depreciation
The toll charges paid by the vehicle's owner
questions.solution:
**Fuel, lubricants, TYRES, maintenance and repair, depreciation, crew time and interest on capital** — all of which vary with the road's roughness, gradient and curvature.

**The components and how each responds to road condition:**

| Component | Response to a rough road |
|---|---|
| **FUEL** ← | **Rises — more rolling resistance and more speed variation** ← |
| **TYRES** ← | **Rises steeply — a rough surface wears and cuts tyres rapidly** ← |
| **MAINTENANCE and spare parts** ← | **Rises very steeply — suspension, steering and body damage** ← |
| **DEPRECIATION** ← | **Rises — the vehicle's life is shortened** ← |
| **CREW TIME and passenger time** ← | **Rises — lower speeds mean longer journeys** ← |
| **Interest on capital** ← | **Rises with journey time, as the vehicle earns for fewer hours** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS USUALLY THE LARGEST SINGLE COMPONENT OF THE SAVING AND IT SURPRISES PEOPLE WHO EXPECT FUEL TO DOMINATE: maintenance and parts costs rise very sharply with roughness.**

> **Fuel consumption might rise 20 or 30 per cent on a badly deteriorated road; parts and maintenance costs can double or treble.**

> **On a rough road in Nepal the cost of springs, shock absorbers, bushes, bearings and body repairs is a substantial part of a vehicle's operating economics.**

> **So the benefit of improving a road accrues heavily to vehicle owners through reduced breakdowns and longer component life, and an appraisal that counts only fuel and time understates the benefit substantially.**

**THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ROUGHNESS AND COST IS THE HEART OF ROAD ECONOMICS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Roughness is measured by the INTERNATIONAL ROUGHNESS INDEX (IRI), in m/km** ← | ← |
| **A new asphalt road is about 2 m/km; a poor gravel road 10 to 16; a badly failed road above 16** ← | ← |
| **VOC rises with IRI, and the rise ACCELERATES at higher roughness** ← | ← |
| **So the saving from repairing a very rough road is much greater per unit of improvement than from improving an already good one** ← | ← |
| **Which is the economic argument for MAINTENANCE over new construction** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE MOST IMPORTANT CONCLUSION IN ROAD ECONOMICS AND THEY ARE PERSISTENTLY IGNORED IN PRACTICE: money spent preventing a road from becoming rough returns more than money spent building a new one.**

> **The relationship between deterioration and cost is convex, so allowing a road to deteriorate imposes costs on users that rise faster than the deterioration itself.**

> **And the cost of restoring a badly deteriorated road far exceeds the cost of the maintenance that would have prevented the deterioration — commonly by a factor of three to five.**

> **So the economically correct policy is to maintain the existing network to a good standard before extending it, and the politically attractive policy is the opposite, because a new road is visible and maintenance is not.**

> **THE HDM-4 MODEL IS THE STANDARD TOOL FOR THESE CALCULATIONS AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BY NAME: the Highway Development and Management model relates road condition, traffic, maintenance policy and vehicle operating costs over an analysis period.**

> **It predicts how a pavement will deteriorate under a given traffic and maintenance regime, computes the resulting user costs, and compares alternative investment and maintenance strategies on a whole-life basis.**

> **Its relationships are empirical, derived from extensive field studies, and they must be CALIBRATED to local conditions — vehicle types, unit costs, climate and construction quality — before the outputs mean anything.**

> **An HDM-4 analysis run on default parameters produces plausible-looking numbers that describe a road somewhere else, which is a trap the model's ease of use makes easy to fall into.**
tags: maintenance cost rises steeply with roughness

examTip.trick: **Fuel, lubricants, tyres, maintenance, depreciation, crew time and interest** — all varying with roughness, gradient and curvature.
examTip.trap: **Maintenance and parts, not fuel, dominate the saving** — fuel may rise 30% on a bad road while parts costs double or treble.
examTip.mnemonic: **VOC rises convexly with roughness** — so maintenance returns more than new construction, and restoration costs 3-5 times the prevention.

questions.stem: In a road project appraisal, GENERATED (induced) TRAFFIC refers to:
options: Traffic diverted from a parallel route onto the improved road
Traffic that existed before the improvement and continues to use the road
NEW trips that would not have been made at all without the improvement
Traffic generated by the construction works themselves
questions.solution:
**NEW trips that would not have been made at all without the improvement** — arising because the lower cost and time of travel makes journeys worthwhile that previously were not.

**The three categories of traffic on an improved road:**

| Category | Definition | Benefit valuation |
|---|---|---|
| **NORMAL traffic** ← | **Traffic that used the road before and still does, plus its natural growth** ← | **The full saving in cost and time per trip** ← |
| **DIVERTED traffic** ← | **Traffic that previously used another route or mode and now uses this one** ← | **The saving relative to its former route** ← |
| **GENERATED (induced) traffic** ← | **Trips that were not made at all before** ← | **HALF the saving, by the rule of half** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S VALUATION IS THE POINT MOST WORTH UNDERSTANDING AND THE LOGIC IS ELEGANT: a generated trip is made because the cost fell.**

> **The traveller who was just barely unwilling to travel at the old cost values the trip at just below the old cost; the one who would have travelled anyway values it at the full amount.**

> **Across the whole group of new travellers, the value ranges from the old cost down to the new cost, and the average benefit is therefore about HALF the cost reduction.**

> **Hence the RULE OF HALF: generated traffic is credited with half the unit saving that normal traffic receives, and crediting it with the full saving overstates the benefit.**

**WHY GENERATED TRAFFIC MATTERS PARTICULARLY IN RURAL NEPAL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Where there was no road at all, essentially ALL traffic is generated** ← | ← |
| **So the rule of half applies to the whole benefit stream** ← | ← |
| **And the 'saving' must be measured against the cost of the previous mode — porters, mules, or not travelling** ← | ← |
| **Which can be enormous — porterage costs many times the equivalent road freight rate** ← | ← |
| **So rural road benefits are large but must be valued carefully** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE THE PROPER 'WITHOUT PROJECT' BASELINE FOR A NEW RURAL ROAD AND GETTING IT RIGHT IS WHERE SUCH APPRAISALS SUCCEED OR FAIL: the comparison is not between a bad road and a good one but between HEAD-LOADING and a vehicle.**

> **Carrying a load on a person's back over a day's walk costs a great deal per tonne-kilometre — far more than any road transport.**

> **So the cost reduction is not a percentage but a factor, often of ten or more, and the consequent generation of traffic is correspondingly large.**

> **That is why a first road into a previously roadless area can transform the local economy in a way that improving an existing road cannot, and why the appraisal methods designed for road improvement need care when applied to first access.**

> **A FURTHER CAUTION DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD BECAUSE IT CUTS THE OTHER WAY: generated traffic is a benefit in an appraisal and a problem in a congested network.**

> **Widening a congested urban road reduces travel time, which generates additional trips, which consume the new capacity — the phenomenon of INDUCED DEMAND.**

> **So the congestion relief can be partly or wholly eroded within a few years, and an appraisal that projects the immediate time saving forward for thirty years overstates the benefit substantially.**

> **The same mechanism is therefore a benefit to be counted in a rural context, where the new trips represent genuine new economic activity, and a caution to be modelled in an urban one, where they largely represent the same activity rescheduled onto a road that then congests again — and distinguishing the two situations is a matter of judgement about what the new trips actually are.**
tags: baseline is porterage for a first road

examTip.trick: **Trips that would not have been made at all** — created by the lower cost of travel, not diverted from elsewhere.
examTip.trap: **Credit generated traffic with HALF the saving** — the rule of half, because new travellers value the trip anywhere between the old and new cost.
examTip.mnemonic: **A benefit in a rural context, a warning in an urban one** — new economic activity versus induced demand that re-congests the widened road.

questions.stem: The CAMBER (cross slope) provided on a road carriageway is intended primarily to:
options: Provide superelevation on straight sections
Increase the road's structural strength
Allow vehicles to drain fuel spillage to the side
DRAIN rainwater from the carriageway surface to the shoulders quickly
questions.solution:
**To DRAIN rainwater from the carriageway surface to the shoulders quickly** — since water standing on or infiltrating the pavement is the principal cause of its deterioration and of skidding.

**Typical camber values by surface type:**

| Surface | Camber |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete and high-quality bituminous** ← | **1.7 to 2.0 per cent (1 in 60 to 1 in 50)** ← |
| **Thin bituminous surfacing** ← | **2.0 to 2.5 per cent** ← |
| **Water-bound macadam and gravel** ← | **2.5 to 3.0 per cent** ← |
| **Earth road** ← | **3.0 to 4.0 per cent** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION IS THE RULE TO REMEMBER AND ITS LOGIC IS STRAIGHTFORWARD: the ROUGHER and more PERMEABLE the surface, the STEEPER the camber required.**

> **A smooth impermeable surface sheds water readily and needs little slope; a rough permeable one holds water in its texture and lets it soak in, so it needs more slope to shed it before it infiltrates.**

> **An earth road needs the most of all, and even then it will not stay shaped without regular grading.**

> **So the camber is set by the surface's own drainage behaviour rather than by the rainfall, which is why the same values apply across very different climates.**

**THE UPPER LIMIT ON CAMBER IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE LOWER AND IT IS WHY THE VALUES ARE SO MODEST:**

| Consequence of EXCESSIVE camber | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vehicles tend to drift toward the edge** ← | **Requiring continuous steering correction** ← |
| **Uncomfortable for occupants** ← | ← |
| **Dangerous on a wet or icy surface — a vehicle can slide sideways** ← | ← |
| **Difficult for slow two-wheeled vehicles and for animal-drawn carts** ← | ← |
| **Overtaking vehicles cross the crown and are momentarily tilted the other way** ← | **A destabilising motion at speed** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS AN EFFECT THAT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED AND IT SETS THE PRACTICAL LIMIT ON A TWO-LANE ROAD: a vehicle overtaking crosses from one camber slope to the other, rolling first one way and then the other.**

> **At a modest camber that is unnoticeable; at a steep one it is a distinct lurch, occurring at the moment the driver is most committed and least able to respond.**

> **So the camber must be small enough that crossing the crown is a non-event, which is why 2 to 2.5 per cent is the practical maximum on a sealed two-lane road however much one might want steeper drainage.**

> **Where more drainage capacity is needed the answer is a more impermeable surface, better longitudinal drainage or a narrower carriageway, not a steeper camber.**

**AND THE SHAPE OF THE CAMBER DESERVES A NOTE SINCE SEVERAL FORMS EXIST:**

| Form | Note |
|---|---|
| **PARABOLIC (barrel) camber** ← | **Steeper at the edges, flat at the crown — good drainage at the edge and comfortable at the centre** ← |
| **STRAIGHT-LINE camber** ← | **Two plane surfaces meeting at the crown — simplest to construct and to check** ← |
| **COMBINATION — straight over the outer portions, parabolic at the crown** ← | **Removes the sharp crown while keeping construction simple** ← |
| **UNIDIRECTIONAL (one-way crossfall)** ← | **The whole width sloping one way — used on divided carriageways and through curves** ← |

> **The fourth row is the standard arrangement on a dual carriageway and it has a distinct advantage worth noting: water crosses only half the width before reaching the edge, since there is no crown to drain away from.**

> **So the drainage path is shorter and the surface clears faster for the same crossfall.**

> **The straight-line form in the second row is the practical choice for most single carriageways, because a parabolic camber is difficult to construct accurately and almost impossible to verify with a straight edge.**

> **That constructability consideration usually outweighs the parabolic form's theoretical superiority, which is a reminder that a shape which cannot be built or checked to tolerance is not in practice better than a simpler one that can.**

examTip.trick: **To shed rainwater to the shoulders** — 1.7-2% for concrete and good bitumen, up to 3-4% for earth roads.
examTip.trap: **Rougher and more permeable surfaces need STEEPER camber** — it is the surface's drainage behaviour, not the rainfall, that sets the value.
examTip.mnemonic: **Overtaking means crossing the crown** — a steep camber makes that a lurch at the worst possible moment, which caps camber at about 2.5%.

questions.stem: A section of road has an existing AADT of 4,200 vehicles per day and traffic is growing at 6 per cent per year. The AADT expected after 12 years is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 8,450 vehicles per day.**

**Using compound growth:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Future AADT = present × (1 + r)ⁿ** | ← |
| **Substituting** | **4,200 × (1.06)¹²** ← |
| **Computing 1.06¹²** | **1.06⁶ = 1.4185, and 1.4185² = 2.0122** ← |
| **So** | **4,200 × 2.0122 = 8,451** ← |

> **THE INTERMEDIATE STEP OF SQUARING 1.06⁶ IS A USEFUL WAY TO HANDLE POWERS WITHOUT A CALCULATOR, and it rests on the rule that raising to the twelfth is squaring the sixth.**

> **Better still is the RULE OF 72: at 6 per cent, traffic doubles in about 72/6 = 12 years.**

> **So after exactly 12 years the traffic has roughly doubled, giving 8,400 — which is within 1 per cent of the exact answer and takes a few seconds.**

> **The rule of 72 is accurate to within a few per cent for rates between about 4 and 12 per cent, which covers almost every traffic growth rate encountered, and it is worth having for exactly this class of question.**

> **THE DISTRACTOR AT 7,224 IS SIMPLE INTEREST RATHER THAN COMPOUND: 4,200 × (1 + 0.06 × 12) = 4,200 × 1.72 = 7,224.**

> **Traffic growth compounds, because each year's growth applies to the previous year's larger base.**

> **The difference over 12 years is 1,227 vehicles a day — around 17 per cent — and over a 20-year design life it becomes much larger.**

> **So using simple growth systematically under-designs the pavement, and the error grows with the design period exactly when it matters most.**

**THE PRACTICAL CAUTION ABOUT GROWTH RATES DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD BECAUSE THE ARITHMETIC IS THE EASY PART:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A constant growth rate over 20 years is a strong assumption** ← | ← |
| **Growth is usually FASTER soon after an improvement and slower later** ← | **As the generated traffic is absorbed and the network matures** ← |
| **It saturates as vehicle ownership approaches its ceiling** ← | ← |
| **And it responds to fuel prices, economic growth and policy** ← | ← |
| **So a single compounded rate should be treated as a scenario, not a forecast** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW SUGGESTS THE BETTER PRACTICE AND IT IS NOT MUCH HARDER: use a HIGHER growth rate for the first few years after the improvement and a lower one thereafter.**

> **Something like 8 per cent for five years and 5 per cent afterwards captures the generation-then-maturation pattern far better than a flat 6 per cent, and it gives a materially different design traffic.**

> **The numbers for each period should come from observed behaviour on comparable improved roads, which is a further use for the permanent count stations.**

> **And whichever pattern is used, the design should be tested against a range — because a pavement designed for 8,450 and receiving 12,000 will fail years early, and the cost of that failure far exceeds the cost of the extra thickness that would have prevented it.**

examTip.trap: **7,224 is SIMPLE growth** — traffic compounds, and over a 20-year life the gap becomes large enough to under-design the pavement badly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rule of 72: at 6% traffic doubles in 12 years** — which gives 8,400 in seconds, within 1% of the exact answer.

questions.stem: In Nepal, the agency responsible for the construction and maintenance of strategic roads — national highways and feeder roads — is:
options: The Department of Roads (DoR), under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport
The Department of Urban Development and Building Construction
The Nepal Electricity Authority
Each District Coordination Committee individually
questions.solution:
**The Department of Roads (DoR), under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport.**

**The division of responsibility for Nepal's road network:**

| Network | Responsible body |
|---|---|
| **Strategic Road Network — national highways and feeder roads** ← | **DEPARTMENT OF ROADS (DoR)** ← |
| **Local Road Network — district, rural and agricultural roads** ← | **Local governments, supported by the Department of Local Infrastructure** ← |
| **Urban roads within municipalities** ← | **The municipality concerned** ← |
| **Roads within other agencies' areas — airports, industrial estates** ← | **The respective agency** ← |

> **THE SPLIT IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS ADMINISTRATIVELY AND IT HAS A CONSEQUENCE WORTH NOTING: the two networks are planned, funded and maintained by different bodies with different capacities.**

> **The strategic network is centrally managed with professional engineering capacity and a dedicated funding mechanism.**

> **The local network is far longer, is managed by many separate local governments with varying technical capacity, and competes for funding against every other local priority.**

> **So the local network's condition is generally much worse, and the technical standards applied to it vary widely — which is the practical reason that guidance documents and standard designs for rural roads matter so much, since they substitute for design capacity that many local bodies do not have.**

**THE KEY STANDARDS AND DOCUMENTS ARE WORTH KNOWING BY NAME:**

| Document | Scope |
|---|---|
| **Nepal Road Standard (NRS)** ← | **Geometric design standards for the strategic network** ← |
| **Nepal Rural Road Standard (NRRS)** ← | **Standards for the local and rural road network** ← |
| **Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Works** ← | **Materials and workmanship, used in DoR contracts** ← |
| **Road Maintenance Guidelines and the Roads Board Nepal framework** ← | **Maintenance funding and management** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW POINTS TO AN INSTITUTIONAL ARRANGEMENT THAT DESERVES EXPLANATION BECAUSE IT ADDRESSES THE MAINTENANCE PROBLEM DIRECTLY: Roads Board Nepal exists to provide a dedicated, protected source of maintenance funding.**

> **Its revenue comes from a fuel levy and vehicle-related charges, so it is linked to road USE rather than appropriated from general revenue each year.**

> **That linkage is the point — maintenance funding that must be argued for annually against schools and hospitals will lose, and maintenance funding that arrives automatically from a road user charge will not.**

> **So the mechanism is an institutional answer to the political economy problem identified earlier: new roads are visible and maintenance is not, so maintenance must be protected from that competition rather than expected to win it.**

> **WHETHER THE ARRANGEMENT SUCCEEDS DEPENDS ON TWO THINGS AND BOTH ARE WORTH WATCHING: whether the levy is set at a level that actually covers the maintenance need, and whether the funds are genuinely ring-fenced or are diverted in practice.**

> **A dedicated fund that receives a third of what the network requires simply makes the shortfall more visible without closing it.**

> **And a fund whose resources are periodically redirected to new construction has lost the protection that was its entire purpose.**

> **So the existence of the mechanism is a necessary condition rather than a sufficient one, and assessing a country's road maintenance regime means asking about the funding LEVEL and its actual application, not only about the institutional form.**

examTip.trick: **Department of Roads, under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport** — for national highways and feeder roads.
examTip.trap: **Local roads belong to local government, not DoR** — a far longer network with far less technical capacity, which is why standard designs matter there.
examTip.mnemonic: **Roads Board Nepal links maintenance funding to a fuel levy** — protecting it from annual competition it would always lose. Check the level, not just the form.

questions.stem: STOPPING SIGHT DISTANCE (SSD) is made up of:
options: The braking distance alone
The distance travelled during the driver's REACTION TIME plus the BRAKING DISTANCE
The distance to the nearest road sign plus the braking distance
Twice the braking distance, to allow for a second vehicle
questions.solution:
**The distance travelled during the driver's REACTION TIME plus the BRAKING DISTANCE** — the first varying linearly with speed and the second with the square of speed.

**The formula and its two parts:**

| Part | Expression | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction (lag) distance** | **v × t, with t the perception-reaction time** ← | **t = 2.5 s is the standard value** ← |
| **Braking distance** | **v² / (2 g f)** ← | **f being the longitudinal friction coefficient** ← |
| **Total SSD** | **SSD = v t + v² / (2 g f)** ← | **With v in m/s** ← |
| **On a gradient** | **SSD = v t + v² / (2 g (f ± 0.01 n))** ← | **Plus for an upgrade, minus for a downgrade** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENT WAYS THE TWO TERMS GROW WITH SPEED IS THE KEY INSIGHT AND IT EXPLAINS WHY HIGH SPEEDS DEMAND SO MUCH SIGHT DISTANCE: the reaction term doubles when speed doubles, and the braking term QUADRUPLES.**

> **At low speeds the reaction distance dominates; at high speeds the braking distance does.**

> **So the total does not merely double with speed, and a road designed for 100 km/h needs far more than twice the sight distance of one designed for 50.**

> **This is also why speed reduction is such an effective safety measure — it acts on a term that varies as the square, so a 20 per cent speed reduction cuts the braking distance by 36 per cent.**

**THE GRADIENT CORRECTION IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN GOT BACKWARDS AND IT IS WORTH REASONING THROUGH RATHER THAN MEMORISING:**

| Situation | Effect | Sign |
|---|---|---|
| **DOWNGRADE** ← | **Gravity helps the vehicle continue — braking is harder, distance LONGER** ← | **Subtract the grade from f** ← |
| **UPGRADE** ← | **Gravity helps stop the vehicle — braking is easier, distance SHORTER** ← | **Add the grade to f** ← |

> **THE PHYSICAL CHECK IS ALWAYS AVAILABLE AND IT NEVER FAILS: going downhill, stopping is harder, so the distance must be longer, so the denominator must be smaller — hence subtract.**

> **Reasoning it out that way takes three seconds and is more reliable than remembering a sign convention.**
