> **The correction matters most on a steep descent, which is precisely where hill roads need sight distance and where the geometry offers least — so the combination of a steep downgrade and a sharp curve is doubly penalised, once by the longer stopping distance and once by the restricted visibility.**

> **That combination is where hill road accidents concentrate, and identifying it on an alignment is one of the most useful things a road safety audit does.**

**AND THE VALUE OF f DESERVES A NOTE SINCE IT IS NOT A CONSTANT:**

| Condition | Longitudinal friction coefficient |
|---|---|
| **Design value, wet surface** ← | **0.40 at 20-30 km/h falling to about 0.35 at 100 km/h** ← |
| **Dry good surface** ← | **Much higher — 0.6 to 0.8** ← |
| **Wet, polished or contaminated** ← | **Can fall below 0.3** ← |

> **The design values are deliberately based on a WET surface, because that is the condition in which the sight distance must still suffice.**

> **Designing to dry friction would give a road that is adequate in fine weather and dangerous in rain, which is no design at all.**

> **The fall in f with speed in the first row is worth noticing too — friction is not independent of speed, so the braking distance grows slightly faster than the simple v² relation suggests.**

> **And the third row is why surface texture and its maintenance are a safety matter rather than a comfort one: a polished aggregate reduces f, the sight distances provided were computed for a higher f, and the road silently becomes substandard without anything visibly changing.**

examTip.trick: **SSD = vt + v²/(2gf)** with t = 2.5 s — reaction distance plus braking distance.
examTip.trap: **Downgrade SUBTRACTS from f** — reason it physically: downhill is harder to stop, so the distance is longer, so the denominator is smaller.
examTip.mnemonic: **Braking varies as v², so a 20% speed cut removes 36% of it** — which is why speed management is such an effective safety measure.

questions.stem: SUPERELEVATION is provided on a horizontal curve to:
options: Counteract the CENTRIFUGAL FORCE acting on a vehicle
Improve the drainage of the curve
Compensate for the gradient of the road at the curve
Allow vehicles to overtake more easily on the curve
questions.solution:
**To counteract the CENTRIFUGAL FORCE acting on a vehicle** — the component of the vehicle's weight along the banked surface supplying part of the required centripetal force, so that less reliance is placed on side friction.

**The governing relationship:**

| Element | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Equilibrium on a banked curve** | **e + f = V² / (127 R)** ← |
| **With** | **e the superelevation as a ratio, f the side friction coefficient** ← |
| ** ** | **V in km/h and R in metres — the 127 packages the unit conversion and g** ← |
| **Fully superelevated, no friction needed** | **e = V² / (127 R)** ← |
| **No superelevation, friction alone** | **f = V² / (127 R)** ← |

> **THE CONSTANT 127 IS THE ONE TO CARRY AND ITS ORIGIN IS WORTH KNOWING SO IT IS NOT MISREMEMBERED: the basic relation is v²/(gR) with v in m/s.**

> **Converting V from km/h to m/s divides by 3.6, so v² = V²/12.96.**

> **Then v²/(gR) = V²/(12.96 × 9.81 × R) = V²/(127.1 R).**

> **So 127 = 12.96 × 9.81, and knowing that means the constant can be reconstructed if it is forgotten — and it also makes clear that the formula requires V in km/h specifically, which is where errors arise.**

**HOW e AND f ARE APPORTIONED IN PRACTICE, SINCE THE EQUATION HAS TWO UNKNOWNS:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Calculate e for 75 per cent of the design speed, ignoring friction** ← | **The IRC approach — so that slower vehicles are not over-banked** ← |
| **2. Check that e does not exceed the maximum permitted** ← | **7 per cent in plain terrain, 10 per cent in hills without snow, 7 per cent where ice occurs** ← |
| **3. If e exceeds the maximum, set e at the maximum and check the required f** ← | ← |
| **4. If the required f exceeds the permissible value (0.15), restrict the SPEED or increase the RADIUS** ← | ← |

> **THE 75 PER CENT IN THE FIRST STEP IS A SUBTLE POINT AND IT ADDRESSES A REAL PROBLEM: superelevation designed for the full design speed over-banks the curve for slow vehicles.**

> **A heavily laden truck crawling round a steeply banked curve, or a vehicle stopped on it, tends to slide DOWN the slope and its load tends to shift.**

> **On a wet or icy surface that is a genuine hazard, and in mixed traffic with bullock carts and cycles it is worse.**

> **So the design deliberately provides less superelevation than the fastest vehicles need, and lets side friction make up the difference for them — protecting the slow vehicles at a small cost to the fast ones, which is the right way round given the consequences of each failure.**

> **THE MAXIMUM VALUES IN THE SECOND STEP ARE SET BY THE SLOW-VEHICLE CONSIDERATION AND BY ICE, AND THE ICE CASE IS WORTH NOTING FOR NEPAL'S HIGH PASSES: on an icy surface the side friction available is nearly zero, so a steeply banked curve will let a vehicle slide bodily down the camber whatever its speed.**

> **Hence the reduced maximum where snow and ice occur, and hence the general principle that superelevation cannot simply be increased without limit to accommodate a sharp curve.**

> **Where the geometry demands more than the maximum, the answer is the fourth step — a larger radius or a lower posted speed — and not a steeper bank.**

> **That constraint is why sharp curves on high-altitude roads carry advisory speed limits rather than dramatic banking, and it is a case where the correct engineering response is to manage the traffic rather than to build around the problem.**
tags: design for 75 per cent of design speed

examTip.trick: **e + f = V²/(127 R)** with V in km/h, R in m. The 127 is 12.96 × 9.81 — reconstructable if forgotten.
examTip.trap: **Design e for 75% of the design speed** — full-speed banking over-banks the curve for slow and stopped vehicles, which then slide down it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Where e would exceed the maximum, increase R or cut the speed — never the bank** — because on ice, friction vanishes and a steep bank sheds vehicles.

questions.stem: A TRANSITION CURVE is introduced between a straight and a circular curve principally to:
options: Reduce the length of the circular curve required
Provide a place to locate road signs
Introduce the CENTRIFUGAL FORCE and the SUPERELEVATION gradually
Make the curve appear longer to the driver
questions.solution:
**To introduce the CENTRIFUGAL FORCE and the SUPERELEVATION gradually** — since a straight has infinite radius and a circular curve a finite one, and an abrupt change would require an instantaneous application of both.

**The four purposes of a transition curve:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Gradual introduction of CENTRIFUGAL FORCE** ← | **Avoiding the jerk of an instantaneous change** ← |
| **Gradual application of SUPERELEVATION** ← | **The crossfall is rotated progressively along the transition** ← |
| **Gradual introduction of the extra WIDENING required on the curve** ← | ← |
| **An improved APPEARANCE, avoiding the visual kink where a straight meets a circle** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRACTICAL REASON THE TRANSITION MUST HAVE A CERTAIN LENGTH AND IT IS THE ONE THAT USUALLY GOVERNS: the crossfall has to change from the normal camber to the full superelevation, and that change takes distance.**

> **Changing it too quickly means the outer edge of the carriageway rises at an uncomfortable rate relative to the centreline, which produces a visible twist in the road surface and an unpleasant roll for the vehicle.**

> **So a maximum rate of rotation is specified — commonly 1 in 150 on plain terrain and 1 in 60 in hills — and the transition must be long enough to achieve the required change at no more than that rate.**

> **That is one of the three criteria from which the transition's length is determined, and the longest of the three governs.**

**THE THREE LENGTH CRITERIA:**

| Criterion | Expression |
|---|---|
| **RATE OF CHANGE OF CENTRIFUGAL ACCELERATION** | **L = V³ / (46.5 C R), with C = 80/(75 + V), bounded to 0.5-0.8** ← |
| **RATE OF INTRODUCTION OF SUPERELEVATION** | **L = e N (W + We) or e N W, depending on whether rotation is about the centre or the edge** ← |
| **IRC EMPIRICAL formula** | **L = 2.7 V²/R for plain and rolling; L = V²/R for mountainous and steep** ← |
| **Adopt the LARGEST of the three** | ← |

> **THE SPIRAL USED IS ALMOST ALWAYS THE CLOTHOID (Euler spiral) AND ITS DEFINING PROPERTY IS WORTH KNOWING: its radius varies INVERSELY with the distance along it, so L × R is constant.**

> **That is exactly what is wanted, because it means the centrifugal acceleration increases at a uniform rate as the vehicle travels along it at constant speed.**

> **A driver turning the steering wheel at a steady rate traces approximately a clothoid, so the curve matches what vehicles naturally do.**

> **That correspondence is why the clothoid is the standard transition and not merely a mathematical convenience — a road built to it requires no unnatural steering input, which is the most direct definition of good alignment there is.**

> **THE SHIFT IS THE GEOMETRIC CONSEQUENCE THAT MUST BE ACCOMMODATED AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED IN SETTING OUT: inserting a transition requires the circular curve to be moved inward, away from the intersection point.**

> **The amount of that inward movement is the SHIFT, approximately L²/(24 R).**

> **So the circular curve of a transitioned alignment is not the same circle as the untransitioned one — it has a slightly different position, and the tangent points move outward along the straights.**

> **Setting out a transitioned curve without applying the shift places the circular arc wrongly and the transitions then do not meet it, which is a setting-out error that shows up on the ground as a discontinuity and is tedious to correct after earthworks have begun.**

examTip.trick: **Gradual introduction of centrifugal force, superelevation and widening** — plus better appearance. Four purposes.
examTip.trap: **Length is the LARGEST of three criteria** — rate of change of centrifugal acceleration, rate of superelevation application, and the IRC empirical formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **A clothoid has L × R constant** — matching a steady turn of the wheel, which is why it is the natural transition. And remember the shift, L²/24R.

questions.stem: EXTRA WIDENING is provided on a horizontal curve because:
options: Vehicles travel faster on curves and need more room
The pavement is weaker on curves
Drainage requires a wider surface on curves
A vehicle's REAR WHEELS track INSIDE its front wheels on a curve (mechanical widening) and drivers need extra clearance to steer accurately at speed (psychological widening)
questions.solution:
**A vehicle's REAR WHEELS track INSIDE its front wheels on a curve (mechanical widening) and drivers need extra clearance to steer accurately at speed (psychological widening)** — so the vehicle occupies more width than on a straight.

**The two components:**

| Component | Expression | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| **MECHANICAL widening** | **Wm = n L² / (2 R)** ← | **Off-tracking — the rear wheels cut the corner** ← |
| **PSYCHOLOGICAL widening** | **Wps = V / (9.5 √R)** ← | **Drivers keep further from the edge and from each other on a curve** ← |
| **Total** | **We = n L²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** ← | **n = number of lanes, L = wheelbase, V in km/h, R in m** ← |

> **THE MECHANICAL TERM'S DEPENDENCE ON WHEELBASE SQUARED IS THE POINT THAT MATTERS MOST IN PRACTICE: a long vehicle off-tracks far more than a short one, and the effect grows with the square of the wheelbase.**

> **So a car with a 2.5 m wheelbase on a 30 m radius needs about 0.10 m of widening, and a truck with a 6 m wheelbase on the same curve needs 0.60 m — six times as much for a wheelbase 2.4 times as long.**

> **An articulated vehicle, whose effective wheelbase is longer still, needs more again.**

> **So the widening must be computed for the DESIGN VEHICLE, and designing for a car on a route that carries trucks produces a curve on which trucks cannot stay in their lane — which on a two-lane hill road means they occupy the oncoming lane on every bend.**

**WHY THE WIDENING IS APPLIED ON THE INSIDE OF THE CURVE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Off-tracking moves the rear wheels toward the INSIDE of the curve** ← | ← |
| **So the space the vehicle needs beyond its lane is on the inside** ← | ← |
| **Hence widening is applied to the INNER edge on a simple curve** ← | ← |
| **Though on a curve with transitions it is commonly split, half on each side** ← | **Which is easier to construct and looks better** ← |
| **And on a hairpin the full widening goes inside** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE RULE AND ITS LOGIC IS DIRECTLY PHYSICAL: the rear wheels cut the corner, so the extra space must be where they cut to.**

> **Widening the outside of a curve provides room where nothing needs it and leaves the inside as tight as before, which achieves nothing for the vehicle that needed it.**

> **The practice in the fourth row — splitting the widening — is a construction convenience adopted where a transition curve allows the widening to be introduced gradually on both sides, and it works because the transition gives room to develop the extra width smoothly.**

> **On a sharp curve without transitions, applying it all to the inside is both correct and necessary.**

> **THE PSYCHOLOGICAL TERM DESERVES DEFENDING BECAUSE IT SOUNDS SOFTER THAN IT IS: drivers genuinely do position themselves further from the edge and from oncoming traffic on a curve, and they do so because their lateral control is less precise when steering.**

> **That is a measurable behaviour rather than a matter of nervousness, and a lane that does not accommodate it is a lane in which vehicles encroach on the adjacent one.**

> **Its formula's dependence on speed and on the inverse root of radius captures the behaviour well — faster and sharper both increase the clearance drivers take.**

> **So both terms are real, they add, and omitting the psychological term because it sounds unscientific produces curves that measure adequate and drive narrow.**

examTip.trick: **Off-tracking plus driver clearance** — We = nL²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R).
examTip.trap: **Mechanical widening goes as WHEELBASE SQUARED** — a truck needs six times a car's widening on the same curve. Design for the actual design vehicle.
examTip.mnemonic: **Widen the INSIDE** — that is where the rear wheels cut to. Widening the outside helps nobody.

questions.stem: A road is designed for 80 km/h. Taking the perception-reaction time as 2.5 s and the longitudinal friction coefficient as 0.35, the stopping sight distance on a level road is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 127 m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Convert speed** | **v = 80 ÷ 3.6 = 22.22 m/s** ← |
| **Reaction distance** | **v t = 22.22 × 2.5 = 55.6 m** ← |
| **Braking distance** | **v² / (2 g f) = 22.22² / (2 × 9.81 × 0.35)** ← |
| ** ** | **22.22² = 493.8** ← |
| ** ** | **2 × 9.81 × 0.35 = 6.867** ← |
| ** ** | **493.8 ÷ 6.867 = 71.9 m** ← |
| **Total SSD** | **55.6 + 71.9 = 127.5 m ≈ 127 m** ← |

> **THE TWO DISTRACTORS AT 55.6 AND 72 ARE THE TWO COMPONENTS TAKEN SEPARATELY, and their presence is the trap: each is a correctly computed intermediate value and neither is the answer.**

> **A candidate who computes the reaction distance and stops has 55.6; one who computes only the braking distance has 72.**

> **Both numbers appear in the working, so both feel confirmed by the arithmetic.**

> **The guard is to remember that SSD has TWO terms by definition, so an answer that equals either single term cannot be the total — and checking that the final answer is larger than both intermediate values catches it immediately.**

**A USEFUL SIMPLIFICATION FOR SPEED IN km/h DESERVES NOTING SINCE IT AVOIDS THE CONVERSION:**

| Form | Expression |
|---|---|
| **With V in km/h directly** | **SSD = 0.278 V t + V² / (254 f)** ← |
| **Check** | **0.278 × 80 × 2.5 = 55.6 m** ← |
| ** ** | **80² / (254 × 0.35) = 6400 / 88.9 = 72.0 m** ← |
| ** ** | **Total 127.6 m — the same answer** ← |

> **THE CONSTANTS 0.278 AND 254 ARE JUST 1/3.6 AND 2 × 9.81 × 12.96 RESPECTIVELY, so the form is the same equation with the unit conversion built in.**

> **Using it avoids converting the speed and therefore avoids one opportunity for error.**

> **It is worth noting that 254 = 2 × 127, which connects it to the superelevation formula's constant and makes both easier to hold.**

> **So 127 appears in the curve equation and 254 in the braking equation, and both derive from the same 12.96 × 9.81 conversion — a small coherence that makes the two formulas mutually reinforcing rather than two separate things to remember.**

**AND THE RESULT SHOULD BE CHECKED AGAINST THE STANDARD, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL CLOSING STEP:**

| Design speed | SSD typically specified |
|---|---|
| **40 km/h** | **45 m** ← |
| **60 km/h** | **90 m** ← |
| **80 km/h** | **120 m** ← |
| **100 km/h** | **180 m** ← |

> **The computed 127 m against a specified 120 m shows the standard values are rounded from calculations of this kind, with the parameters the standard adopts.**

> **So a computed value that comes out near the tabulated one confirms both.**

> **A computed value far from it means the parameters differ — a different reaction time, a different friction value, or a gradient — and the discrepancy should be understood rather than ignored.**

> **And the growth down the table is worth noting: from 40 to 100 km/h the speed goes up by 2.5 times and the sight distance by 4 times, which is the v² term asserting itself and is the geometric reason high-speed roads are so much more demanding to align.**

examTip.trap: **55.6 and 72 are the two components** — each correctly computed and neither the answer. The total must exceed both.
examTip.mnemonic: **254 = 2 × 127** — the braking constant is twice the superelevation constant, both from 12.96 × 9.81.

questions.stem: OVERTAKING SIGHT DISTANCE (OSD) on a two-lane two-way road is much greater than stopping sight distance because it must accommodate:
options: The distance the overtaking vehicle travels while the driver considers the manoeuvre
Only the length of the vehicle being overtaken
Twice the stopping sight distance
The distance required for the overtaken vehicle to brake
questions.solution:
**The distance the overtaking vehicle travels while the driver considers the manoeuvre, the distance it travels during the actual overtaking, AND the distance travelled by an ONCOMING vehicle during the same period.**

**The three components:**

| Component | Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **d₁** | **v_b × t, with t about 2 s** ← | **Distance travelled at the slower vehicle's speed while the driver decides** ← |
| **d₂** | **v_b T + 2s, where T = √(4s/a)** ← | **Distance travelled during the overtaking manoeuvre itself** ← |
| **d₃** | **v × T** ← | **Distance travelled by the ONCOMING vehicle during the manoeuvre** ← |
| **OSD** | **d₁ + d₂ + d₃ on a two-way road** ← | **On a one-way or divided road, d₁ + d₂ only** ← |

> **THE THIRD COMPONENT IS WHAT MAKES OSD SO LARGE AND IT IS THE ONE OMITTED ON A DIVIDED CARRIAGEWAY: on a two-way road the overtaking vehicle uses the opposing lane, so the gap must be clear of oncoming traffic for the whole manoeuvre.**

> **The oncoming vehicle is approaching at full speed throughout, so it covers as much ground as the overtaker does.**

> **That roughly doubles the requirement, which is why OSD on a two-lane road runs to several hundred metres — commonly 470 m at 80 km/h against an SSD of 120 m.**

> **So overtaking demands about four times the sight distance that stopping does, and providing it over a substantial proportion of a road's length is one of the hardest geometric requirements to meet in hill terrain.**

**THE CONSEQUENCE FOR DESIGN IS A PRACTICAL COMPROMISE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Providing full OSD everywhere is usually impossible in hills and costly in plains** ← | ← |
| **So the standard requires OSD over a PROPORTION of the length** ← | **Commonly a third or more, distributed along the road** ← |
| **Sections with adequate OSD are designated OVERTAKING ZONES** ← | ← |
| **And sections without are marked with a CONTINUOUS centre line prohibiting overtaking** ← | ← |
| **The marking is what converts the geometry into driver behaviour** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHERE THE DESIGN INTENTION SO OFTEN FAILS AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: the geometry determines where overtaking is safe, and the road MARKING is what tells the driver.**

> **A road with restricted sight distance and no centre line, or with a broken line throughout, invites overtaking exactly where it is dangerous.**

> **So the line marking is not decoration applied at the end of construction but the delivery of a safety analysis, and it must be set out from the actual measured sight distances rather than by eye.**

> **A survey of available sight distance along the finished road, from which the no-overtaking sections are determined and marked, is a standard and inexpensive exercise that is frequently skipped — and its omission means the whole sight distance analysis done at design stage never reaches the driver.**

> **ONE FURTHER DISTANCE IS WORTH KNOWING AND IT SITS BETWEEN THE OTHER TWO: INTERMEDIATE SIGHT DISTANCE, defined as twice the stopping sight distance.**

> **It is used where full overtaking sight distance cannot be provided, and it gives a driver who has begun an overtaking manoeuvre enough distance for both vehicles to stop.**

> **So it is a partial provision — not enough to overtake safely, but enough to survive a misjudgement — and it is the standard applied on many hill roads where OSD is unattainable.**

> **Recognising that it is a mitigation rather than a provision is important, because a road built to intermediate sight distance is a road where overtaking should be prohibited, not one where it is marginally acceptable.**

examTip.trick: **d₁ decision + d₂ manoeuvre + d₃ oncoming vehicle** — the third is dropped on a divided carriageway.
examTip.trap: **OSD is about four times SSD** — 470 m against 120 m at 80 km/h, because the oncoming vehicle covers as much ground as the overtaker.
examTip.mnemonic: **Intermediate sight distance = 2 × SSD** — a mitigation, not a provision. Where it is all that exists, overtaking should be prohibited.

questions.stem: The length of a SUMMIT (crest) vertical curve is normally governed by:
options: The comfort of passengers, since the vertical acceleration is the critical factor
The need to drain water from the curve
SIGHT DISTANCE — the crest itself obstructs the view, so the curve must be long enough that a driver can see the required stopping distance over it
The maximum permissible rate of change of grade for construction plant
questions.solution:
**SIGHT DISTANCE** — the crest itself obstructs the view, so the curve must be long enough that a driver can see the required stopping distance over it.

**Why summit and valley curves are governed by different criteria:**

| Curve | Governing criterion | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **SUMMIT (crest)** ← | **SIGHT DISTANCE** ← | **The road surface itself blocks the view over the crest** ← |
| **VALLEY (sag)** ← | **HEADLIGHT sight distance by night; COMFORT by day** ← | **Nothing blocks the daytime view, so comfort and night visibility govern** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST IS THE MOST EXAMINABLE POINT IN VERTICAL ALIGNMENT AND THE PHYSICAL REASON IS EASY TO PICTURE: standing at a crest, the ground rises between you and a distant object, so the crest cuts your line of sight.**

> **Standing in a sag, the ground falls away between you and the object, so nothing obstructs the view at all.**

> **Hence daytime sight distance is never a problem in a sag, and it is the controlling problem on a crest.**

> **At night, however, the sag is the problem — the headlight beam points along the vehicle's axis and the road curves upward away from it, so the illuminated distance is limited even though the geometric sight line is clear.**

**THE SUMMIT CURVE FORMULAE, WHICH FOLLOW FROM THE GEOMETRY:**

| Case | Expression |
|---|---|
| **When L > S** | **L = N S² / (√(2h₁) + √(2h₂))²** ← |
| **For SSD, with h₁ = 1.2 m (driver's eye) and h₂ = 0.15 m (object)** | **L = N S² / 4.4** ← |
| **For OSD or ISD, with h₁ = h₂ = 1.2 m** | **L = N S² / 9.6** ← |
| **When L < S** | **L = 2S − (√(2h₁) + √(2h₂))² / N** ← |

> **THE TWO HEIGHTS ARE THE VALUES TO MEMORISE — 1.2 m FOR THE DRIVER'S EYE AND 0.15 m FOR THE OBJECT — and the 0.15 m is worth a moment's thought because it is deliberately small.**

> **It represents an object low enough to matter: a rock, a pothole edge, a piece of debris, a small animal.**

> **Designing to a taller object would give shorter curves and a road on which low hazards are invisible until too late.**

> **And for overtaking, both heights are 1.2 m because the object being sighted is another vehicle's driver — which is why the constant changes from 4.4 to 9.6 and the required curve length for overtaking is correspondingly much shorter per unit of sight distance, though the sight distance itself is far greater.**

> **THE TWO CASES — L GREATER THAN OR LESS THAN S — MUST BOTH BE CHECKED AND THAT IS A COMMON PROCEDURAL ERROR: one assumes a case, computes L, and then finds the assumption was wrong.**

> **The correct procedure is to assume L > S, compute, and check.**

> **If the computed L turns out to be less than S, the assumption fails and the other formula must be used instead.**

> **Reporting the first answer without checking gives a curve length that does not satisfy the equation it came from, and the error is in the unconservative direction for short curves — which is exactly where it matters, since short curves are adopted where the alignment is constrained and the margin is already thin.**
tags: check both L>S and L<S cases

examTip.trick: **Sight distance — the crest blocks the view.** L = NS²/4.4 for SSD when L > S.
examTip.trap: **Sags are governed by HEADLIGHT distance and comfort, not daytime sight** — nothing blocks the view in a sag by day.
examTip.mnemonic: **Eye 1.2 m, object 0.15 m** — the low object is deliberate, so rocks and debris are visible. Both 1.2 m for overtaking, giving 9.6.

questions.stem: A vehicle travels at 65 km/h on a curve of 150 m radius. If the superelevation provided is 7 per cent, the side friction coefficient required is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 0.15.**

**Using e + f = V² / (127 R):**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Right-hand side** | **65² / (127 × 150)** ← |
| ** ** | **65² = 4,225** ← |
| ** ** | **127 × 150 = 19,050** ← |
| ** ** | **4,225 ÷ 19,050 = 0.2218** ← |
| **Subtract the superelevation** | **f = 0.2218 − 0.07** ← |
| ** ** | **= 0.1518 ≈ 0.15** ← |

> **THE DISTRACTOR AT 0.22 IS THE TOTAL e + f WITH THE SUPERELEVATION NOT SUBTRACTED, and it is the natural error to make because 0.2218 is the number the calculation produces before the last step.**

> **The question asks for the FRICTION required, which is what remains after the banking has done its share.**

> **So the last subtraction is the whole point of the question, and an answer of 0.22 has stopped one line early.**

> **A useful discipline on any two-term equation is to identify at the outset which term is being asked for, and to write the rearranged form before substituting — f = V²/(127R) − e makes the subtraction impossible to forget.**

**THE ANSWER MUST NOW BE ASSESSED AGAINST THE PERMISSIBLE VALUE, WHICH IS THE ENGINEERING STEP:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The permissible side friction coefficient for design is 0.15** ← | **IRC value, deliberately well below the available friction** ← |
| **The required 0.15 therefore exactly equals the permissible value** ← | ← |
| **So the curve is ACCEPTABLE but has no margin** ← | ← |
| **At any higher speed it would be unsatisfactory** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PROPER CONCLUSION AND IT IS MORE INFORMATIVE THAN THE NUMBER ALONE: this curve works at exactly its design speed and fails above it.**

> **Since a proportion of drivers exceed any design speed, a curve with no margin will be traversed at speeds requiring more friction than the design permits.**

> **That does not mean vehicles will slide — the ACTUAL friction available on a dry surface is 0.4 or more, far above the design value of 0.15.**

> **The design value is conservative precisely to provide that margin, so exceeding it modestly is uncomfortable rather than dangerous — but the margin is there to cover a wet surface, a polished aggregate, a worn tyre and a driver's misjudgement together, and a curve designed with none of it in hand has spent the margin before those conditions arise.**

> **THE DESIGN RESPONSE, IF MORE MARGIN IS WANTED, IS WORTH SETTING OUT BECAUSE IT SHOWS WHICH VARIABLES ARE AVAILABLE: the radius can be increased, the speed reduced, or the superelevation raised.**

> **Raising e is already at its hill maximum of 7 per cent in many standards, so that avenue may be closed.**

> **Reducing the design speed reduces the requirement as the square, so 60 km/h instead of 65 would need f = 60²/(127 × 150) − 0.07 = 0.189 − 0.07 = 0.119, comfortably within the limit.**

> **So a 5 km/h reduction in design speed converts a marginal curve into a satisfactory one, which illustrates how powerfully the v² term works in the designer's favour when speed is reduced — and it is the cheapest of the three remedies by a wide margin, requiring only a sign.**
tags: speed reduction is the cheapest remedy

examTip.trap: **0.22 is e + f, with the superelevation not subtracted** — write the rearranged form before substituting.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.15 is exactly the permissible value, so the curve has NO margin** — and 60 km/h instead of 65 brings it to 0.12. A sign is the cheapest fix.

questions.stem: A VALLEY (sag) vertical curve is designed for NIGHT conditions on the criterion of headlight sight distance because:
options: Sag curves are more common on roads used at night
Vehicles travel faster at night on sag curves
Headlights are brighter than daylight at close range
The headlight beam is directed along the vehicle's axis and the road curves UPWARD away from it
questions.solution:
**The headlight beam is directed along the vehicle's axis and the road curves UPWARD away from it, so the length of road illuminated ahead is limited** — whereas by day nothing obstructs the view at all.

**The geometry of the problem:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Headlights are mounted about 0.75 m above the road** ← | ← |
| **The beam is aimed slightly upward — a 1 degree divergence is assumed** ← | ← |
| **On a sag, the road ahead rises relative to the vehicle's current attitude** ← | ← |
| **So the beam strikes the road surface at a limited distance and illuminates no further** ← | ← |
| **Beyond that point the road is dark, whatever the geometric sight line** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL DISTINCTION AND IT IS WHY THIS CRITERION EXISTS SEPARATELY FROM SIGHT DISTANCE: a driver can only stop for what can be SEEN, and at night that means what is ILLUMINATED.**

> **The geometric sight distance in a sag is effectively unlimited, so a daytime analysis finds no problem at all.**

> **At night the illuminated distance may be well short of the stopping distance, and the driver is then over-driving the headlights.**

> **So the sag curve must be long enough — flat enough — that the headlight beam reaches at least the stopping sight distance ahead, and that requirement has nothing to do with the daytime geometry.**

**THE FORMULAE AND THE SECOND CRITERION:**

| Criterion | Expression |
|---|---|
| **HEADLIGHT sight distance, L > S** | **L = N S² / (1.5 + 0.035 S)** ← |
| **HEADLIGHT sight distance, L < S** | **L = 2S − (1.5 + 0.035 S) / N** ← |
| **COMFORT criterion** | **L = 0.38 (N V²)^0.5 ... commonly given as L = N V² / (3.9 × c), with c the allowable centrifugal acceleration** ← |
| **Adopt the GREATER of the two** | ← |

> **THE 1.5 IN THE HEADLIGHT FORMULA IS TWICE THE HEADLIGHT HEIGHT OF 0.75 m, AND THE 0.035 IS THE TANGENT OF THE 1 DEGREE BEAM DIVERGENCE MULTIPLIED BY 2 — so both constants are physical rather than arbitrary, and knowing that makes the formula reconstructable.**

> **The comfort criterion arises because a sag subjects occupants to an UPWARD centrifugal acceleration, which adds to gravity and is felt as increased weight.**

> **That is tolerable up to about 0.3 m/s² and unpleasant beyond it, which is what the comfort formula limits.**

> **In practice the headlight criterion almost always governs on a road designed for night use, and the comfort criterion governs only where the road is lit or where design speeds are low — so the headlight formula is the one to reach for first, with the comfort check confirming rather than deciding.**

> **A FURTHER CONSIDERATION APPLIES IN SAGS THAT THE FORMULAE DO NOT CAPTURE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: a sag is where water collects and where cold air pools.**

> **So a sag on a hill road is the place where ice forms first and persists longest, and where fog lies when the surrounding road is clear.**

> **Both conditions reduce the friction and the visibility precisely where the alignment is already demanding.**

> **So a sag at the bottom of a long descent, which is the commonest place for one, combines a high approach speed, a possible ice patch and a limited headlight distance — and recognising that combination as a hazard cluster rather than three separate minor issues is what a road safety audit contributes beyond the design calculations.**
tags: sags collect water ice and fog

examTip.trick: **The beam points along the vehicle while the road rises away** — so the illuminated distance, not the sight line, is the limit at night.
examTip.trap: **Daytime sight distance is never a problem in a sag** — which is why a daytime analysis finds nothing wrong with a dangerously short one.
examTip.mnemonic: **1.5 = 2 × 0.75 m headlight height; 0.035 = 2 tan 1°** — both constants physical, so the formula can be rebuilt.

questions.stem: The minimum radius of a horizontal curve for a given design speed is determined by:
options: Setting both the superelevation and the side friction to their MAXIMUM permissible values in e + f = V²/(127R) and solving for R
The length of the longest vehicle expected to use the road
The width of the available right of way
The rate at which the transition curve can introduce superelevation
questions.solution:
**Setting both the superelevation and the side friction to their MAXIMUM permissible values in e + f = V²/(127R) and solving for R** — since any sharper curve would demand more of one or the other than is allowed.

**The derivation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **e + f = V² / (127 R)** | ← |
| **Rearranged** | **R = V² / (127 (e + f))** ← |
| **With e_max and f_max substituted** | **R_min = V² / (127 (e_max + f_max))** ← |
| **For a hill road: e_max = 0.10, f_max = 0.15** | **R_min = V² / (127 × 0.25) = V² / 31.75** ← |
| **For plain terrain: e_max = 0.07, f_max = 0.15** | **R_min = V² / (127 × 0.22) = V² / 27.94** ← |

> **THE TWO FORMULAE AT THE BOTTOM ARE WORTH HAVING BECAUSE THEY GIVE THE MINIMUM RADIUS DIRECTLY FROM THE SPEED: at 50 km/h in hills, R_min = 2500/31.75 = 79 m; in plain terrain, 2500/27.94 = 89 m.**

> **The hill value is smaller because the higher permitted superelevation allows a sharper curve.**

> **That is the opposite of what one might expect — hill roads permit SHARPER curves at a given speed, not gentler ones — and the reason is simply that the standards allow steeper banking there.**

> **In practice the design speeds adopted in hills are lower anyway, so the absolute radii used in hills are much smaller than in plains on both counts.**

**THE WORD 'MINIMUM' CARRIES AN IMPORTANT PRACTICAL CAUTION AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The minimum radius is an ABSOLUTE limit, not a design target** ← | ← |
| **A curve at the minimum radius uses the full permitted superelevation AND the full permitted friction** ← | ← |
| **So it has no margin whatever** ← | ← |
| **Curves should be designed GENEROUSLY where the terrain allows** ← | ← |
| **And the minimum reserved for the few places where nothing better is possible** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A PRINCIPLE THAT SEPARATES GOOD ALIGNMENT FROM MERELY COMPLIANT ALIGNMENT: a designer who uses the minimum radius wherever it fits has produced a road that is legal and unpleasant.**

> **The minimum exists to permit a difficult location to be negotiated, not to define normal practice.**

> **A well-designed alignment uses generous radii on the open sections and tightens only where the topography insists, which also produces a road whose curves are CONSISTENT with what the driver has been led to expect.**

> **That consistency matters more than any individual curve's radius, which is the point of the next consideration.**

**DESIGN CONSISTENCY IS THE MOST IMPORTANT ALIGNMENT PRINCIPLE AND IT IS NOT CAPTURED BY ANY MINIMUM:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Drivers adopt a speed based on what the road has recently been like** ← | ← |
| **A long straight or a series of gentle curves invites a high speed** ← | ← |
| **A sharp curve following them is a SURPRISE, and surprise is what causes accidents** ← | ← |
| **The same sharp curve after a series of similar curves is entirely safe** ← | ← |
| **So the danger lies in the CHANGE, not in the curve's radius alone** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE INSIGHT AND IT HAS A DIRECT DESIGN CONSEQUENCE: successive curves should not differ greatly in radius, and a sharp curve should be approached through progressively tighter ones.**

> **Standards express this by limiting the ratio of successive radii — commonly requiring that a curve's radius be no less than about two-thirds of the preceding one.**

> **So an alignment is checked not only curve by curve against the minimum but curve against curve for consistency, and a road that passes the first check and fails the second is more dangerous than one which is uniformly tighter.**

> **That is why accident records so often single out 'the one sharp bend' on an otherwise fast road, and why straightening the approaches to such a bend can make it more dangerous rather than less.**
tags: minimum is a limit not a target

examTip.trick: **R_min = V²/(127(e_max + f_max))** — both at their permitted maxima. Hills: V²/31.75; plains: V²/27.94.
examTip.trap: **The minimum is a limit, not a target** — a curve at minimum radius uses all the banking and all the friction, with no margin at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Danger lies in the CHANGE, not the radius** — a sharp bend after fast curves is the hazard. Straightening its approaches makes it worse.

questions.stem: The SET-BACK DISTANCE on the inside of a horizontal curve is the clearance that must be kept free of obstruction so that:
options: Vehicles can park off the carriageway
Drainage water can be discharged clear of the road
The required SIGHT DISTANCE is available along the chord of the curve
Snow cleared from the carriageway can be stored
questions.solution:
**The required SIGHT DISTANCE is available along the chord of the curve** — since the driver's line of sight cuts across the ground inside the curve and any wall, cut face, building or vegetation there would block it.

**The geometry:**

| Case | Expression |
|---|---|
| **When the curve length exceeds the sight distance (L > S)** | **m = R − (R − d) cos(θ/2), where θ = 180 S / (π (R − d))** ← |
| **A simpler approximation for a single lane on the centreline** | **m ≈ S² / (8 R)** ← |
| **With** | **m = set-back from the centreline of the inner lane, d = distance from the centreline to that lane** ← |

> **THE APPROXIMATION m ≈ S²/(8R) IS THE FORM WORTH CARRYING AND IT MAKES THE MAGNITUDE IMMEDIATELY APPARENT: at 80 km/h needing 120 m of sight distance on a 300 m radius curve, m = 14,400/2,400 = 6 m.**

> **So six metres of clearance is needed inside the curve, measured from the lane centreline.**

> **On a hill road with a cut face on the inside of the bend, that means cutting six metres further back than the road itself requires, over the length of the curve.**

> **That is a substantial additional excavation and it is expensive, which is exactly why it gets omitted — and its omission is one of the commonest causes of inadequate sight distance on hill roads.**

**THE S² DEPENDENCE HAS A CONSEQUENCE WORTH DRAWING OUT:**

| Sight distance | Radius | Set-back |
|---|---|---|
| **60 m (40 km/h)** | **150 m** | **3.0 m** ← |
| **120 m (80 km/h)** | **150 m** | **12.0 m** ← |
| **120 m (80 km/h)** | **300 m** | **6.0 m** ← |
| **120 m (80 km/h)** | **600 m** | **3.0 m** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW AGAINST THE FIRST SHOWS THE PENALTY OF SPEED: doubling the sight distance requirement QUADRUPLES the set-back, because m varies with S².**

> **And the last two rows show the remedy: increasing the radius reduces the set-back in direct proportion.**

> **So on a constrained hillside, a flatter curve is often cheaper overall than a sharp one, because the sharp curve's set-back excavation exceeds what the flatter alignment costs.**

> **That trade is easily missed because the curve and the excavation are considered separately — the geometry is set first and the earthwork computed afterwards — whereas they should be optimised together.**

**AND THE OBSTRUCTIONS THAT MUST BE CLEARED ARE WORTH LISTING, SINCE SOME ARE EASILY OVERLOOKED:**

| Obstruction | Note |
|---|---|
| **The CUT FACE itself** ← | **The commonest, and the one requiring excavation** ← |
| **Retaining walls and parapets** ← | **Which can be lowered or made see-through** ← |
| **VEGETATION** ← | **Which grows back — so this is a maintenance obligation, not a one-time clearance** ← |
| **Buildings and boundary walls** ← | **Requiring the right of way to extend into the set-back** ← |
| **Parked vehicles and roadside stalls** ← | **An enforcement matter rather than a design one** ← |
| **Snow banks in winter** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT DEFEATS MANY OTHERWISE ADEQUATE DESIGNS AND IT IS A MAINTENANCE FAILURE RATHER THAN A DESIGN ONE: vegetation on the inside of a curve grows, and within a few seasons it obscures a sight line that was clear when the road opened.**

> **The road then becomes progressively more dangerous without any physical change to its geometry.**

> **So the sight line clearance must appear in the maintenance schedule as a recurring item, with the set-back area identified on the drawings so that whoever does the cutting knows where to cut.**

> **And marking those areas on the as-built drawings costs nothing at the time and is the only way the requirement survives the departure of the people who designed the road.**
tags: sight line cuts inside the curve
vegetation is a recurring maintenance item

examTip.trick: **m ≈ S²/(8R)** — the clearance needed inside the curve for the sight line across the chord.
examTip.trap: **Set-back varies as S²** — doubling the sight distance quadruples the excavation. A flatter curve is often cheaper overall than a sharp one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vegetation regrows and closes the sight line** — mark the set-back area on the as-built drawings and put clearance in the maintenance schedule.

questions.stem: In the design of a road INTERSECTION, the primary objective of channelisation using islands and markings is to:
options: Increase the intersection's total paved area
REDUCE the CONFLICT AREA and control the angle and location of conflicts
Provide space for vendors and parking
Increase vehicle speeds through the junction
questions.solution:
**To REDUCE the CONFLICT AREA and control the angle and location of conflicts** — separating turning movements, forcing traffic to cross at favourable angles, reducing speeds and providing refuge for pedestrians.

**The conflict points at an intersection:**

| Type | Description | At a 4-arm crossroads |
|---|---|---|
| **CROSSING (intersecting) conflicts** ← | **Paths cross at an angle — the most severe** ← | **16** ← |
| **MERGING conflicts** ← | **Two streams join** ← | **8** ← |
| **DIVERGING conflicts** ← | **One stream splits** ← | **8** ← |
| **TOTAL** ← | ← | **32** ← |

> **THE 32 CONFLICT POINTS AT AN UNCONTROLLED CROSSROADS IS THE FIGURE WORTH REMEMBERING AND IT IS THE STARTING POINT FOR EVERY INTERSECTION IMPROVEMENT: each is a place where two vehicles could collide.**

> **The 16 crossing conflicts are the dangerous ones, because a crossing collision is a side impact at a large angle and side impacts injure severely.**

> **Merging and diverging conflicts are lower-speed-differential events and they produce far less severe collisions.**

> **So the aim of intersection design is to reduce the number of conflicts and, where they cannot be removed, to convert crossing conflicts into merging ones — which is exactly what a roundabout does.**

**A ROUNDABOUT'S EFFECT IS WORTH SETTING OUT BECAUSE IT IS SO STRIKING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A roundabout converts every crossing movement into a MERGE followed by a DIVERGE** ← | ← |
| **So the 16 crossing conflicts become ZERO** ← | ← |
| **Total conflict points fall from 32 to 8** ← | **4 merging and 4 diverging** ← |
| **And all traffic moves in the same rotational direction** ← | **So relative speeds at any conflict are low** ← |
| **Which is why roundabouts have far fewer serious injury accidents than signalised crossroads** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MECHANISM BEHIND THE SAFETY BENEFIT AND IT IS MORE IMPORTANT THAN THE CONFLICT COUNT: at a roundabout, vehicles that might collide are travelling in nearly the same direction.**

> **So the relative speed is low even when the absolute speeds are moderate, and collision severity depends on relative speed.**

> **A crossroads produces right-angle impacts at the full sum of both speeds, and those are the collisions that kill.**

> **So the roundabout's benefit is chiefly in SEVERITY rather than frequency — it may have a similar number of minor collisions and far fewer serious ones, which is the trade that matters.**

> **ITS LIMITATIONS DESERVE STATING SINCE ROUNDABOUTS ARE NOT UNIVERSALLY APPROPRIATE: a roundabout handles balanced flows well and unbalanced ones badly, because a dominant flow on the circulating carriageway can block entry from a minor arm indefinitely.**

> **It requires more LAND than a signalised junction, which is often decisive in an urban area.**

> **It is difficult for pedestrians and cyclists, who must cross traffic that is not required to stop — a serious drawback where they are numerous, as they are throughout Nepal's towns.**

> **And it cannot give priority to a particular movement, which a signal can.**

> **So the choice between a roundabout and signals turns on the flow balance, the land available and the pedestrian volume, and applying either as a default without that assessment produces the wrong answer regularly.**

examTip.trick: **Reduce the conflict area and control the angle of conflicts** — separating movements and slowing traffic.
examTip.trap: **A 4-arm crossroads has 32 conflict points: 16 crossing, 8 merging, 8 diverging** — a roundabout removes all 16 crossing ones.
examTip.mnemonic: **Roundabouts cut SEVERITY more than frequency** — all traffic moves the same way, so relative speeds are low. But they suit balanced flows and few pedestrians.

questions.stem: A road has a design speed of 50 km/h. Taking e_max = 0.07 and f_max = 0.15, the minimum horizontal curve radius is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 89 m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **R_min = V² / (127 (e + f))** | ← |
| **Denominator** | **127 × (0.07 + 0.15) = 127 × 0.22 = 27.94** ← |
| **Numerator** | **50² = 2,500** ← |
| **So** | **R = 2,500 ÷ 27.94 = 89.5 m ≈ 89 m** ← |

> **THE CHECK IS TO SUBSTITUTE BACK INTO THE ORIGINAL EQUATION: 50²/(127 × 89.5) = 2500/11,367 = 0.22, which is e + f as required.**

> **That confirms the arithmetic in one line.**

> **The distractor at 112 m comes from using only the friction, 127 × 0.15 giving 19.05 and 2500/19.05 = 131 — or from some similar partial substitution.**

> **The one at 45 m is roughly half the answer, and 70 m corresponds to using the hill maximum e = 0.10 with a different arrangement — all of them plausible-looking results of using the wrong value for e + f, which is the single quantity the question turns on.**

**THE ANSWER SHOULD BE COMPARED WITH THE STANDARD'S TABULATED VALUE, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL STEP:**

| Design speed | Absolute minimum radius, plain terrain |
|---|---|
| **30 km/h** | **30 m** ← |
| **40 km/h** | **60 m** ← |
| **50 km/h** | **90 m** ← |
| **65 km/h** | **155 m** ← |
| **80 km/h** | **230 m** ← |
| **100 km/h** | **360 m** ← |

> **THE COMPUTED 89 m AGAINST THE TABULATED 90 m CONFIRMS BOTH, and the tabulated values are simply this calculation rounded.**

> **The progression down the table is worth noticing: from 30 to 100 km/h the speed rises by 3.3 times and the radius by 12 times, which is the V² relation.**

> **So high design speeds require enormously larger curves, and that is the fundamental geometric reason high-speed alignment is so difficult in mountainous terrain.**

> **A 360 m radius curve simply cannot be fitted onto many Himalayan hillsides at any reasonable cost, which is why hill roads carry low design speeds as a matter of physical necessity rather than of standards-setting choice.**

**AND THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN ABSOLUTE AND DESIRABLE MINIMUM RADII DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Term | Note |
|---|---|
| **ABSOLUTE minimum** ← | **Computed with e_max and f_max, as above — used only where nothing better is achievable** ← |
| **DESIRABLE (normal) minimum** ← | **Computed with a lower f, giving a larger radius — the value to design to in normal circumstances** ← |
| **The desirable minimum is commonly around 1.5 times the absolute** ← | ← |

> **The distinction restates the point made earlier about minima being limits rather than targets, and standards express it explicitly by tabulating both.**

> **Designing every curve to the absolute minimum produces a road that satisfies the standard and is at the edge of its envelope everywhere.**

> **Designing to the desirable minimum where the terrain allows, and dropping to the absolute only where it does not, produces a road with margin over most of its length and constraint only where constraint is unavoidable.**

> **Which of the two a designer produces is usually a matter of how the design is reviewed — a review that checks only compliance gets the first, and one that asks where margin was available and not taken gets the second.**

examTip.trap: **Use e + f together, not either alone** — every distractor here comes from a wrong value of that single sum.
examTip.mnemonic: **Radius goes as V²: 30 km/h needs 30 m, 100 km/h needs 360 m** — which is why high design speeds are physically impossible in hill terrain.

questions.stem: PASSING PLACES on a single-lane hill road should be provided:
options: Only at the start and end of the road
At regular intervals AND at locations INTERVISIBLE with one another
Only where the road is already wide enough, requiring no construction
At intervals of exactly one kilometre regardless of the terrain
questions.solution:
**At regular intervals AND at locations INTERVISIBLE with one another** — so that a driver can see the next passing place and knows whether to proceed or wait, with additional places at curves and at points of natural widening.

**Why intervisibility is the governing requirement:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A single-lane road works by drivers yielding to one another** ← | ← |
| **A driver meeting an oncoming vehicle must reverse to a passing place** ← | ← |
| **Reversing on a hill road is slow, difficult and dangerous** ← | ← |
| **If each passing place is VISIBLE from the last, a driver can see whether the section ahead is clear before entering it** ← | ← |
| **So no reversing is needed — the waiting is done at a passing place** ← | ← |
| **Which is the entire point of the system** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS DESCRIBE HOW A WELL-DESIGNED SINGLE-LANE ROAD ACTUALLY OPERATES AND THE DIFFERENCE FROM A BADLY DESIGNED ONE IS LARGE: with intervisible passing places, the road functions as a series of one-way sections with waiting bays between them.**

> **A driver looks ahead, sees the next bay is clear and no vehicle is approaching, and proceeds.**

> **Without intervisibility, two vehicles enter the same section from opposite ends, meet in the middle, and one must reverse — on a narrow hill road, possibly for hundreds of metres, with a drop on one side.**

> **So the spacing rule is not primarily about distance but about SIGHT, and a passing place every 300 m around blind bends is worse than one every 500 m on intervisible straights.**

**THE DESIGN OF THE PASSING PLACE ITSELF:**

| Requirement | Typical provision |
|---|---|
| **Sufficient WIDTH for two vehicles to pass** ← | **Total width of about 5.5 m, so roughly 2 m of widening** ← |
| **Sufficient LENGTH for the design vehicle plus tapers** ← | **Commonly 15 to 20 m of full width, with tapers each end** ← |
| **Located on a STRAIGHT, or on the outside of a bend** ← | **Never on the inside of a bend, where it worsens the sight line** ← |
| **On the side where widening is CHEAPEST** ← | **Usually the fill side or a natural bench** ← |
| **Clearly VISIBLE and preferably signed or marked** ← | ← |
| **Kept clear of parked vehicles and material** ← | **An enforcement matter that determines whether it works** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHERE THE PROVISION MOST OFTEN FAILS IN PRACTICE AND IT IS WORTH ANTICIPATING AT THE DESIGN STAGE: a passing place is a convenient flat wide spot, which is exactly what people want for parking, for stacking materials and for stalls.**

> **Once occupied, it no longer functions, and the single-lane system breaks down over that whole section.**

> **Marking the places clearly, signing them, and locating them away from buildings and settlements all reduce the problem.**

> **And where a settlement is unavoidable, providing a separate widened area for its needs is cheaper than losing the passing place, which is a small piece of foresight that repays itself immediately.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON WHEN A SINGLE-LANE ROAD IS APPROPRIATE AT ALL: it is the correct standard where traffic is light enough that meetings are infrequent, typically below a few hundred vehicles a day.**

> **Above that, the delays and the risk of reversing manoeuvres mount, and the intermediate lane or full two-lane standard becomes justified.**

> **So the standard should be chosen from the projected traffic, with the recognition that a single-lane road is much cheaper to build in hill terrain — its formation width may be half that of a two-lane road, which on a steep hillside means far less cut, less spoil and far less slope to stabilise.**

> **That saving is large enough that building single-lane with passing places, and widening later if traffic justifies it, is frequently the right staged strategy — provided the alignment and the structures are set out for the eventual width so the widening does not require them to be rebuilt.**

examTip.trick: **Regular intervals AND intervisible** — so a driver can see the next bay is clear before entering the section.
examTip.trap: **The rule is about SIGHT, not distance** — closely spaced bays around blind bends are worse than wider spacing on intervisible straights.
examTip.mnemonic: **Build single-lane but set out structures for the eventual width** — widening later then costs no rebuilding.

questions.stem: The GRADE COMPENSATION applied at a horizontal curve on a road with a steep gradient means that the gradient is:
options: Increased, to help vehicles maintain momentum through the curve
Left unchanged, since the curve does not affect tractive requirements
REDUCED through the curve
Replaced by a level section of at least 50 m
questions.solution:
**REDUCED through the curve** — because curve resistance adds to the grade resistance, and the combination would otherwise exceed what the design vehicle can overcome.

**The rule and its limit:**

| Element | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Grade compensation** | **30 + R / R per cent, subject to a maximum of 75/R** ← |
| **With R in metres** | ← |
| **And the compensated gradient** | **Not to be reduced below 4 per cent** ← |
| **Compensation is not applied** | **Where the gradient is flatter than 4 per cent** ← |

> **THE 4 PER CENT FLOOR IS THE PRACTICAL PART OF THE RULE AND IT PREVENTS AN ABSURDITY: without it, a very sharp curve on a moderate gradient would require the gradient to be reduced to nearly nothing.**

> **That would be both unnecessary — a 4 per cent grade with curve resistance added is still manageable — and extremely expensive, since flattening a gradient on a hillside means lengthening the road.**

> **So the compensation applies only where the gradient is steep enough to matter, and it stops at 4 per cent.**

> **A worked instance: on a 50 m radius curve, the compensation is (30 + 50)/50 = 1.6 per cent, checked against 75/50 = 1.5 per cent, so 1.5 per cent governs — and a 6 per cent gradient becomes 4.5 per cent through the curve.**

**WHY CURVE RESISTANCE EXISTS AT ALL IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN ACCEPTING:**

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **TYRE SCRUB — the wheels are not all tracking the same circle, so they slide laterally** ← | **The dominant component** ← |
| **Increased rolling resistance from the sideways force on the tyres** ← | ← |
| **Bearing and transmission losses from the differential working** ← | ← |
| **And for a long vehicle, the off-tracking makes the effect worse** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MAIN MECHANISM AND IT IS WHY THE EFFECT GROWS SO SHARPLY AS RADIUS FALLS: on a sharp curve, the front and rear axles follow noticeably different paths, so the tyres must scrub sideways.**

> **That scrubbing dissipates energy, and it does so in proportion to how different the paths are — which is to say, inversely with the radius.**

> **Hence the compensation formula's 1/R form, which is not an empirical curve fit but a reflection of the underlying mechanism.**

> **It is also why the effect is far worse for long vehicles, and why a hairpin bend on a steep gradient can defeat a truck entirely — the combination of maximum curve resistance and maximum grade resistance occurring together at the point where the vehicle is also steering at full lock.**

> **THE PRACTICAL RULE FOR HILL ROADS THAT FOLLOWS FROM ALL THIS IS SIMPLE AND WORTH STATING EXPLICITLY: gain height on the straights and turn on the flat.**

> **A hill road should be designed with its steep gradients on the straight sections between bends, and its bends as nearly level as the alignment permits.**

> **That distribution gives the same average gradient overall while keeping the two resistances from coinciding.**

> **It costs nothing to arrange at the design stage and it is very difficult to correct afterwards — and a road on which every hairpin sits on a steep grade is one where the vertical and horizontal alignments were designed separately, which is the underlying error the compensation rule exists to catch.**
tags: 30 + R over R subject to 75 over R
gain height on straights turn on the flat

examTip.trick: **Reduced — curve resistance adds to grade resistance.** (30 + R)/R per cent, capped at 75/R.
examTip.trap: **Never compensate below 4 per cent** — otherwise a sharp curve would flatten a moderate grade to nothing, at enormous cost in road length.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gain height on the straights, turn on the flat** — the two resistances must not coincide. A hairpin on a steep grade means the alignments were designed separately.

questions.stem: In coordinating HORIZONTAL and VERTICAL alignment, the combination that must be AVOIDED above all is:
options: A horizontal curve extending slightly beyond the vertical curve at both ends
A gentle horizontal curve coinciding with a long sag curve
A straight section coinciding with a constant gradient
A sharp HORIZONTAL curve located at or near the top of a SUMMIT curve
questions.solution:
**A sharp HORIZONTAL curve located at or near the top of a SUMMIT curve** — since the crest hides the curve from the approaching driver until it is too late to react.

**Why this particular combination is so dangerous:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A summit curve limits the distance a driver can see ahead** ← | ← |
| **A driver approaching a crest sees only the road surface up to the crest itself** ← | ← |
| **Beyond it, the road may go anywhere and the driver cannot tell** ← | ← |
| **If it turns sharply, the driver discovers this only on reaching the crest** ← | ← |
| **By which time the available distance may be less than the stopping distance** ← | ← |
| **And the driver's approach speed was chosen on the assumption the road continued straight** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE ASPECT THAT MAKES IT WORSE THAN A SIGHT DISTANCE DEFICIENCY ALONE: the crest does not merely hide the curve, it actively suggests there is none.**

> **A road disappearing over a crest reads visually as continuing straight, because that is what the visible alignment implies.**

> **So the driver is not merely uninformed but MISLED, and approaches at a speed appropriate to a straight road.**

> **A sight distance restriction that the driver can perceive — a cutting, a bend into trees — prompts caution; one that looks like open road does not, and that difference is why this combination appears so consistently in accident records.**

**THE PRINCIPLES OF ALIGNMENT COORDINATION:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **The horizontal curve should be somewhat LONGER than the vertical curve, overlapping it at both ends** ← | **So the driver sees the horizontal curve begin before reaching the crest** ← |
| **Curves in the two planes should be PHASED — beginning and ending at about the same chainage** ← | ← |
| **Avoid a sharp horizontal curve at or just beyond a summit** ← | **The rule above** ← |
| **Avoid a sharp horizontal curve at the bottom of a steep descent** ← | **High approach speed, and water and ice collect there** ← |
| **Avoid short vertical curves within a long horizontal curve** ← | **Producing a visually broken, undulating appearance** ← |
| **Avoid a series of short curves and grades producing a 'roller-coaster' profile** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE POSITIVE VERSION OF THE RULE AND IT IS THE ONE TO APPLY IN DESIGN: let the horizontal curve start BEFORE the crest.**

> **The driver then sees the road curving as they approach, understands what is coming, and adjusts speed in advance.**

> **The same sharp curve, properly phased with the vertical alignment, becomes an ordinary and safe piece of road.**

> **So the hazard is not the curve or the crest individually but their relative POSITION, and shifting one by fifty metres can transform the location at essentially no cost if it is done at the design stage.**

> **THE SECOND ROW'S PHASING PRINCIPLE HAS AN AESTHETIC DIMENSION THAT IS MORE THAN COSMETIC: a road whose horizontal and vertical curves are phased looks coherent and flows naturally, and one whose curves are offset looks broken and confusing.**

> **A driver reads the road ahead largely from its apparent shape, so a road that looks coherent is a road that is correctly understood.**

> **Visual appearance is therefore a safety attribute rather than a matter of taste, and the 'looks wrong' judgement of an experienced designer looking at a perspective view or a drive-through model is a legitimate technical assessment.**

> **That is why three-dimensional visualisation of an alignment before construction is worth doing — it reveals coordination faults that plan and profile drawings, examined separately, conceal by their very separation.**
tags: the crest misleads rather than merely hides
horizontal curve should overlap the vertical

examTip.trick: **A sharp horizontal curve at a summit** — the crest hides it until the driver arrives.
examTip.trap: **The crest actively MISLEADS** — the road reads as continuing straight, so the driver approaches at straight-road speed. Worse than a visible restriction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Let the horizontal curve START before the crest** — the same curve, properly phased, is ordinary and safe. Shift one by 50 m at design stage.

questions.stem: A summit vertical curve joins a +3% grade with a −2% grade. If the required stopping sight distance is 90 m and the curve length exceeds the sight distance, the required length of the vertical curve is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 92 m.**

**Using L = N S² / 4.4 for stopping sight distance with L > S:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Algebraic difference of grades** | **N = 0.03 − (−0.02) = 0.05** ← |
| **Substituting** | **L = 0.05 × 90² ÷ 4.4** ← |
| ** ** | **90² = 8,100** ← |
| ** ** | **0.05 × 8,100 = 405** ← |
| ** ** | **405 ÷ 4.4 = 92.0 m** ← |
| **Check the assumption** | **L = 92 m > S = 90 m ✓ — so the formula used was the right one** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE STEP THAT MUST NOT BE OMITTED AND THIS QUESTION IS CONSTRUCTED TO MAKE IT MATTER: the answer of 92 m only just exceeds the 90 m sight distance.**

> **Had it come out below 90 m, the L > S formula would have been inapplicable and the other form would have been required.**

> **Since 92 > 90, the assumption holds and the answer stands — but the margin is two metres, so the check is doing real work rather than being a formality.**

> **This is exactly the situation where a candidate who computes and reports without checking gets the right answer by luck, and would have got a wrong one from the same procedure on slightly different numbers.**

**THE TWO SIGN CONVENTIONS THAT CAUSE ERRORS IN THIS CALCULATION ARE WORTH SETTING OUT:**

| Convention | Note |
|---|---|
| **N is the ALGEBRAIC difference: N = g₁ − g₂** ← | **With upgrades positive and downgrades negative** ← |
| **Here: +3% and −2% give N = 3 − (−2) = 5%, or 0.05** ← | ← |
| **A common error is 3 − 2 = 1%, treating the downgrade as positive** ← | **Which gives L = 18 m, a curve far too short** ← |
| **For a SUMMIT curve, N is positive** ← | **For a SAG curve, N is negative and its magnitude is used** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ERROR TO GUARD AGAINST AND THE PHYSICAL CHECK CATCHES IT: a curve joining +3% to −2% changes the road's slope by five percentage points, not one.**

> **The road is rising at 3 in 100 and ends falling at 2 in 100, so the total change in direction is 5 in 100.**

> **Picturing that makes the algebraic subtraction obvious and removes any need to remember a rule.**

> **The distractor at 405 m is the numerator alone, N S², with the division by 4.4 omitted; 184 m is roughly double the answer; and 45 m is half the sight distance, which is not a length of anything relevant.**

**AND THE RESULT SHOULD BE CHECKED AGAINST A MINIMUM LENGTH CRITERION, WHICH THE CALCULATION ALONE DOES NOT SUPPLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Standards impose a minimum vertical curve length regardless of the sight distance calculation** ← | ← |
| **Commonly a length equal to the design speed in km/h expressed in metres** ← | **So 60 m for a 60 km/h road** ← |
| **Or a minimum based on a few seconds of travel time** ← | ← |
| **The purpose is APPEARANCE and comfort, not sight distance** ← | ← |

> **The fourth row explains why the criterion exists: a very short vertical curve, even if it satisfies sight distance, appears as a visible kink in the road's profile and feels abrupt.**

> **On a small change of grade the sight distance formula can give a length of a few metres, which would be a bump rather than a curve.**

> **So the minimum length criterion governs wherever the grade change is small, and the sight distance criterion governs wherever it is large — and a complete design checks both and adopts the greater, exactly as with the transition curve's three criteria.**

examTip.trap: **N is the ALGEBRAIC difference — +3 to −2 is a change of 5, not 1** — and always verify that the computed L really does exceed S.
examTip.mnemonic: **A minimum length also applies, for appearance** — roughly the design speed in metres. On small grade changes it governs instead.

questions.stem: The LOS ANGELES ABRASION test on road aggregate measures:
options: The aggregate's resistance to crushing under a slowly applied compressive load
The aggregate's water absorption
The aggregate's resistance to ABRASION and IMPACT combined
The shape of the aggregate particles
questions.solution:
**The aggregate's resistance to ABRASION and IMPACT combined** — the sample being tumbled in a rotating drum with steel balls, and the percentage passing a 1.7 mm sieve afterwards reported as the LA value.

**The test and its interpretation:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A graded sample is placed in a steel drum with a specified charge of steel balls** ← | **The number of balls depends on the grading** ← |
| **The drum rotates 500 revolutions at 30 to 33 rpm** ← | **A shelf inside lifts and drops the charge each revolution** ← |
| **The material is then sieved on a 1.7 mm sieve** ← | ← |
| **LA value = percentage passing that sieve, by weight of the original sample** ← | ← |
| **A LOWER value means a TOUGHER aggregate** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE SENSE OF THE RESULT AND IT IS WORTH FIXING BECAUSE SEVERAL AGGREGATE TESTS SHARE IT: the value reported is the amount of material DESTROYED, so lower is better.**

> **The same holds for the aggregate impact value, the aggregate crushing value and the abrasion values generally.**

> **So a specification of 'LA value not more than 30 per cent' is a requirement that no more than 30 per cent of the sample be reduced to dust.**

> **Reading it as a strength figure, where higher would be better, inverts the requirement — and the habit that prevents this is to remember that these tests measure DAMAGE rather than capacity.**

**TYPICAL SPECIFICATION LIMITS BY LAYER:**

| Layer | Maximum LA value |
|---|---|
| **Bituminous wearing course** ← | **30 per cent** ← |
| **Bituminous base and binder courses** ← | **35 to 40 per cent** ← |
| **Water-bound macadam base** ← | **40 to 50 per cent** ← |
| **Sub-base** ← | **50 to 60 per cent** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION IS THE LOGIC WORTH CARRYING RATHER THAN THE NUMBERS: the requirement tightens as the layer approaches the SURFACE.**

> **The wearing course takes the direct abrasion of tyres, the impact of loads, and the weather, so it needs the toughest aggregate.**

> **Deeper layers are protected by those above and carry more distributed, less punishing stresses, so a weaker aggregate serves.**

> **This means a quarry that cannot supply wearing-course aggregate may still supply base and sub-base perfectly well, which matters a great deal in Nepal where good hard aggregate is not available everywhere and hauling it is expensive.**

**THE RELATED AGGREGATE TESTS ARE WORTH DISTINGUISHING SINCE THEY ARE EASILY CONFUSED:**

| Test | Measures | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **LOS ANGELES ABRASION** ← | **Abrasion and impact together** ← | **The most widely specified** ← |
| **AGGREGATE IMPACT VALUE (AIV)** ← | **Resistance to sudden shock** ← | **A hammer dropped repeatedly on a confined sample** ← |
| **AGGREGATE CRUSHING VALUE (ACV)** ← | **Resistance to gradual compressive load** ← | **A slowly applied 400 kN load** ← |
| **POLISHED STONE VALUE (PSV)** ← | **Resistance to POLISHING under traffic** ← | **A HIGHER value is better here — the opposite sense** ← |
| **SOUNDNESS (sodium or magnesium sulphate)** ← | **Resistance to weathering by salt crystallisation** ← | ← |
| **FLAKINESS and ELONGATION indices** ← | **Particle shape** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE EXCEPTION TO THE 'LOWER IS BETTER' RULE AND IT DESERVES SPECIFIC ATTENTION: the polished stone value measures the friction RETAINED after polishing, so a higher PSV is a better aggregate.**

> **This matters enormously for safety, because it is the wearing course's polished friction — not its friction when new — that determines skid resistance over the road's life.**

> **An aggregate that is very hard and polishes smooth gives a road that is durable and slippery, which is the worst combination for a wearing course.**

> **So a surfacing aggregate must satisfy BOTH a low LA value for durability and a high PSV for skid resistance, and those two requirements are not always met by the same rock — a fact that sometimes forces a blend, or a surface dressing with a different aggregate over a durable base.**
tags: durability and skid resistance can conflict

examTip.trick: **Abrasion and impact together** — tumbled with steel balls for 500 revolutions, percentage passing 1.7 mm reported.
examTip.trap: **These tests measure DAMAGE, so lower is better** — except PSV, where higher is better because it measures friction retained.
examTip.mnemonic: **A very hard aggregate can polish smooth** — durable and slippery. A wearing course needs low LA AND high PSV, which one rock may not give.

questions.stem: The CALIFORNIA BEARING RATIO (CBR) test is used in pavement design to:
options: Measure the bitumen content of a mix
Determine the optimum moisture content of a soil
Measure the compressive strength of concrete used in rigid pavements
Express a soil's or an aggregate's resistance to penetration as a PERCENTAGE of that of a standard crushed stone
questions.solution:
**Express a soil's or an aggregate's resistance to penetration as a PERCENTAGE of that of a standard crushed stone** — giving an empirical index of SUBGRADE or layer strength from which pavement thickness is read off design curves.

**The test in outline:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The soil is compacted in a standard mould at a specified density and moisture** ← | ← |
| **Usually SOAKED for 4 days with a surcharge, to simulate the worst likely condition** ← | ← |
| **A plunger of 50 mm diameter is driven in at 1.25 mm/min** ← | ← |
| **The load is recorded at 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm penetration** ← | ← |
| **Each is expressed as a percentage of the standard load — 1370 kg at 2.5 mm, 2055 kg at 5.0 mm** ← | ← |
| **The HIGHER of the two percentages is reported as the CBR** ← | **Normally the 2.5 mm value governs; if the 5 mm value is higher, the test is repeated and if confirmed, the 5 mm value is taken** ← |

> **THE SOAKING IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FEATURE OF THE TEST AS PRACTISED AND ITS OMISSION IS A SERIOUS ERROR: a subgrade's strength falls dramatically when it is saturated.**

> **A soil with an unsoaked CBR of 15 may have a soaked CBR of 4.**

> **The pavement must survive the worst condition the subgrade will experience, which in a monsoon climate is saturation.**

> **So the soaked value is the design value, and using an unsoaked CBR because the laboratory was pressed for time produces a pavement designed for a subgrade strength that will not exist when it rains — which is precisely when the pavement is most vulnerable.**

**THE SIXTH ROW'S RULE IS A COMMON EXAMINATION POINT AND IT IS WORTH BEING PRECISE ABOUT:**

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| **CBR at 2.5 mm is greater than at 5.0 mm** ← | **Normal. Report the 2.5 mm value** ← |
| **CBR at 5.0 mm is greater** ← | **Unusual. REPEAT the test** ← |
| **If the repeat confirms it** ← | **Report the 5.0 mm value** ← |

> **THE REQUIREMENT TO REPEAT RATHER THAN SIMPLY TAKE THE HIGHER VALUE IS THE PART MOST OFTEN MISSTATED, and it exists because the anomaly usually indicates a problem with the test rather than a property of the soil.**

> **A stone under the plunger, a poorly prepared surface, or non-uniform compaction can all produce it.**

> **So the anomalous result is treated as suspect until confirmed, and only a confirmed anomaly is accepted as real.**

> **That is a sound general principle for any test — an unexpected result is a reason to check the test before revising the understanding, and the CBR procedure writes that principle into the standard.**

**THE TEST'S NATURE AS AN EMPIRICAL INDEX DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT BOUNDS WHAT CAN BE DONE WITH IT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **CBR is not a fundamental engineering property** ← | **It is not a modulus, a strength or a stiffness** ← |
| **It is an INDEX, correlated empirically with pavement performance** ← | ← |
| **So it can only be used with design methods CALIBRATED against it** ← | ← |
| **It cannot be inserted into a mechanistic analysis directly** ← | **Though correlations to resilient modulus exist, such as E ≈ 10 CBR in MPa** ← |
| **And those correlations are approximate and scatter widely** ← | ← |

> **The fourth row's correlation is widely used and worth knowing, with the caveat the fifth row states: E (MPa) ≈ 10 × CBR is the common rule for fine-grained subgrades at low CBR values.**

> **It lets a CBR-based site investigation feed a mechanistic-empirical design, which is how most modern pavement design is done.**

> **But the scatter is large — a factor of two either way is not unusual — so a design resting entirely on a converted CBR carries that uncertainty.**

> **Where the design is critical or the pavement expensive, measuring the modulus directly with a falling weight deflectometer or a plate load test removes the conversion and its uncertainty, and is worth the extra cost for exactly that reason.**
tags: soaked CBR is the design value

examTip.trick: **Penetration resistance as a percentage of standard crushed stone** — an index feeding empirical thickness design curves.
examTip.trap: **Use the SOAKED value** — an unsoaked CBR of 15 may be 4 when saturated, and the pavement must survive the monsoon.
examTip.mnemonic: **If the 5 mm value exceeds the 2.5 mm value, REPEAT the test** — the anomaly usually means a faulty test, not a real property.

questions.stem: The PENETRATION GRADE of a bitumen (for example 60/70) indicates:
options: The depth in tenths of a millimetre to which a standard needle penetrates the sample under a 100 g load for 5 seconds at 25 °C
The temperature at which the bitumen becomes liquid
The percentage of bitumen that penetrates the aggregate
The number of days the bitumen can be stored
questions.solution:
**The depth in tenths of a millimetre to which a standard needle penetrates the sample under a 100 g load for 5 seconds at 25 °C** — a HIGHER number meaning a SOFTER bitumen.

**The test's standard conditions, which must all be quoted together:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Temperature** | **25 °C** ← |
| **Load** | **100 g** ← |
| **Duration** | **5 seconds** ← |
| **Result unit** | **Tenths of a millimetre (decimillimetres)** ← |
| **So a penetration of 65 means** | **6.5 mm of needle penetration** ← |

> **THE UNIT IS WHERE MOST CONFUSION ARISES AND IT IS WORTH FIXING FIRMLY: the number is in TENTHS of a millimetre, so a 60/70 bitumen admits the needle 6 to 7 millimetres.**

> **That is a substantial penetration and it conveys how soft bitumen actually is at ordinary temperatures.**

> **The grade designation '60/70' is a permitted RANGE — the material must fall between 60 and 70 — rather than a single value.**

> **And the sense of the scale is the key fact: HIGHER penetration means SOFTER, so an 80/100 bitumen is softer than a 60/70, which is softer than a 30/40.**

**WHICH GRADE TO USE WHERE IS A CLIMATE DECISION AND IT FOLLOWS A CLEAR LOGIC:**
