| Condition | Grade | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **HOT climate, heavy traffic** ← | **HARDER — 30/40 or 60/70** ← | **A soft bitumen would flow and rut in the heat** ← |
| **COLD climate** ← | **SOFTER — 80/100 or 120/150** ← | **A hard bitumen would become brittle and crack in the cold** ← |
| **Nepal's Terai** ← | **60/70 predominantly** ← | **Hot summers with heavy traffic** ← |
| **Nepal's high hills** ← | **80/100** ← | **Cold winters, where brittleness is the greater risk** ← |

> **THE TWO FAILURE MODES IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS ARE OPPOSITE AND THE GRADE SELECTION IS A BALANCE BETWEEN THEM: too soft and the pavement ruts and bleeds in summer; too hard and it cracks in winter.**

> **A location with both hot summers and cold winters is therefore genuinely difficult, because no single penetration grade is right for both seasons.**

> **That is precisely the problem that MODIFIED bitumens and the performance-graded (PG) system address — a polymer-modified binder can be stiff at high temperature and flexible at low, which a straight-run bitumen cannot.**

> **And it explains why the penetration grading system, which tests at a single temperature, has been superseded in many countries by the PG system, which specifies performance at both the high and low service temperatures the road will actually experience.**

**THE OTHER ROUTINE BITUMEN TESTS ARE WORTH LISTING ALONGSIDE:**

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** ← | **Consistency at 25 °C — as above** ← |
| **SOFTENING POINT (ring and ball)** ← | **The temperature at which it softens — a measure of high-temperature behaviour** ← |
| **DUCTILITY** ← | **The length to which a sample stretches before breaking — a measure of cohesion and flexibility** ← |
| **FLASH and FIRE POINT** ← | **Safe handling temperatures** ← |
| **VISCOSITY** ← | **Flow behaviour at mixing and compaction temperatures** ← |
| **LOSS ON HEATING / thin film oven test** ← | **How much the bitumen HARDENS during mixing — simulating ageing** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE TEST THAT ADDRESSES THE PROPERTY THAT MOST DETERMINES A PAVEMENT'S LIFE AND IT IS FREQUENTLY OVERLOOKED: bitumen hardens with age, through oxidation and the loss of volatiles.**

> **Most of that hardening occurs during MIXING, when the binder is hot and spread in a thin film over the aggregate.**

> **So the binder in a newly laid pavement is already harder than the binder in the drum, and it continues to harden slowly in service.**

> **Eventually it becomes brittle enough to crack, and that is the end of the pavement's life by a mechanism unrelated to loading — which is why an old lightly-trafficked road can crack up while a heavily trafficked one of the same age has not, and why excessive mixing temperature, which accelerates the hardening, shortens a pavement's life in a way that is invisible at the time.**
tags: age hardening and the thin film oven test

examTip.trick: **Needle penetration in tenths of a mm, 100 g, 5 s, 25 °C** — so 60/70 means 6 to 7 mm. HIGHER means SOFTER.
examTip.trap: **Hot climate needs a HARDER grade; cold needs softer** — rutting is the summer failure, brittle cracking the winter one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Most age hardening happens during MIXING** — so excessive mixing temperature shortens the pavement's life invisibly.

questions.stem: A BITUMEN EMULSION differs from a cutback bitumen in that the emulsion:
options: Contains no bitumen at all
Must be heated to above 150 °C before use
Is used only for concrete pavements
Disperses bitumen in WATER with an emulsifying agent
questions.solution:
**It disperses bitumen in WATER with an emulsifying agent, so it can be applied COLD and sets by the water separating and evaporating** — whereas a cutback dissolves bitumen in a volatile petroleum solvent that must evaporate.

**The two compared:**

| Aspect | EMULSION | CUTBACK |
|---|---|---|
| **Bitumen dispersed in** | **WATER, with an emulsifier** ← | **A petroleum SOLVENT — kerosene, diesel or naphtha** ← |
| **Application** | **Cold or slightly warmed** ← | **Warmed, less than for hot bitumen** ← |
| **Sets by** | **BREAKING — the water separating — then evaporating** ← | **Evaporation of the solvent** ← |
| **Environmental effect** | **Water released; low emissions** ← | **Hydrocarbon solvent released to atmosphere** ← |
| **Fire risk** | **Low** ← | **Significant — the solvents are flammable** ← |
| **Works on damp aggregate** | **YES — an important advantage** ← | **NO — requires dry aggregate** ← |
| **Cost of the volatile phase** | **Water — free** ← | **Petroleum solvent — expensive and lost to the air** ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL ADVANTAGE THAT MATTERS MOST IN NEPAL AND IT IS DECISIVE FOR MONSOON-SEASON WORK: an emulsion will bond to a damp surface, because it is itself water-based.**

> **A cutback or hot bitumen applied to damp aggregate does not adhere — the water film prevents contact, and the bond fails immediately or shortly afterwards.**

> **Since it is difficult to guarantee dry aggregate in a monsoon climate, and since waiting for dryness costs working days, the emulsion's tolerance of dampness extends the working season considerably.**

> **The fourth and seventh rows together are why emulsions have largely displaced cutbacks worldwide — releasing petroleum solvent to the atmosphere is both a pollution problem and a waste of an expensive material, whereas the emulsion's volatile phase is water.**

**EMULSIONS ARE CLASSIFIED BY HOW FAST THEY BREAK AND BY THEIR CHARGE:**

| Classification | Types | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **By SETTING rate** | **RS (rapid setting)** ← | **Surface dressing, tack coat — must break quickly on contact** ← |
| ← | **MS (medium setting)** ← | **Premix with coarse aggregate** ← |
| ← | **SS (slow setting)** ← | **Premix with fine aggregate, soil stabilisation, prime coat** ← |
| **By CHARGE** | **CATIONIC (positively charged)** ← | **Suits negatively charged aggregates such as granite and quartzite — most common** ← |
| ← | **ANIONIC (negatively charged)** ← | **Suits positively charged aggregates such as limestone** ← |

> **THE CHARGE MATCHING IN THE LAST TWO ROWS IS THE ELEGANT PART OF EMULSION TECHNOLOGY AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: the emulsified bitumen droplets carry an electrical charge, and they are attracted to aggregate of the OPPOSITE charge.**

> **Most common road aggregates — granite, quartzite, gneiss, the siliceous rocks — carry a negative surface charge.**

> **So a CATIONIC emulsion, whose droplets are positive, is electrostatically attracted to them and breaks on contact, depositing the bitumen directly onto the stone.**

> **That is why cationic emulsions dominate in practice, and why using an anionic emulsion on a siliceous aggregate gives poor adhesion — the two repel, and the emulsion breaks by evaporation alone rather than by attraction.**

> **THE SETTING RATE MUST MATCH THE APPLICATION AND A MISMATCH FAILS IN AN OBVIOUS WAY: a rapid-setting emulsion used in a premix breaks while the mixing is still in progress, producing lumps of coated and uncoated material that cannot be laid.**

> **A slow-setting emulsion used for surface dressing has not broken by the time traffic is admitted, so the chippings are picked up by tyres and the treatment is lost.**

> **So the grade is selected from the operation, not from convenience or availability — and substituting whichever grade is in stock, which is a real temptation on a remote site, wastes both the material and the work.**
tags: water based works on damp aggregate

examTip.trick: **Bitumen dispersed in WATER, applied cold, setting when it breaks** — against a cutback's petroleum solvent that must evaporate.
examTip.trap: **An emulsion works on DAMP aggregate** — decisive in a monsoon climate, where hot bitumen and cutbacks simply will not bond.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cationic for siliceous aggregate** — most road stone is negatively charged, so positive droplets are attracted and break on contact.

questions.stem: In the MARSHALL METHOD of bituminous mix design, the STABILITY value represents:
options: The maximum LOAD in kN that the compacted specimen carries before failure when loaded diametrically at 60 °C at a rate of 50 mm per minute
The percentage of voids in the compacted mix
The bitumen content at which the mix is most economical
The deformation of the specimen at failure
questions.solution:
**The maximum LOAD in kN that the compacted specimen carries before failure when loaded diametrically at 60 °C at a rate of 50 mm per minute.**

**The test's standard conditions and its two readings:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Specimen** | **101.6 mm diameter, 63.5 mm high, compacted with 50 or 75 blows per face** ← |
| **Test temperature** | **60 °C** ← |
| **Loading rate** | **50 mm per minute** ← |
| **Loading arrangement** | **Diametrically, in a curved loading head** ← |
| **STABILITY** | **The maximum load carried, in kN** ← |
| **FLOW** | **The deformation at that maximum load, in units of 0.25 mm** ← |

> **THE 60 °C IS THE MOST SIGNIFICANT OF THESE CONDITIONS AND ITS CHOICE IS DELIBERATE: it approximates the maximum temperature a pavement surface reaches in service in a hot climate.**

> **Bitumen's behaviour is strongly temperature-dependent, so a stability measured at 25 °C would say nothing useful about summer performance.**

> **Testing at the critical service temperature means the stability value directly addresses the condition in which rutting occurs.**

> **So the test's relevance comes from its temperature as much as from its mechanics, and quoting a Marshall stability without its test temperature is quoting an incomplete result.**

**STABILITY AND FLOW MUST BOTH BE SATISFIED AND THEY PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS:**

| Reading | Too LOW means | Too HIGH means |
|---|---|---|
| **STABILITY** | **The mix will rut and shove under traffic** ← | **Generally acceptable, though often accompanied by brittleness** ← |
| **FLOW** | **The mix is BRITTLE and will crack** ← | **The mix is too plastic and will deform** ← |

> **THE FLOW READING HAVING LIMITS ON BOTH SIDES IS THE POINT MOST OFTEN MISSED AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THE MIX DESIGN A BALANCE RATHER THAN A MAXIMISATION: a designer who simply maximises stability produces a stiff, brittle mix that resists rutting and cracks instead.**

> **The specification therefore requires stability above a minimum AND flow within a range — commonly 2 to 4 mm, or 8 to 16 units.**

> **A mix satisfying both has the stiffness to resist deformation and the flexibility to accommodate movement without fracturing.**

> **That pairing of a minimum and a range is characteristic of bituminous mix design generally, and it reflects the two competing failure modes the material must resist simultaneously.**

**THE VOLUMETRIC PROPERTIES COMPLETE THE DESIGN AND THEY MATTER AS MUCH AS THE STRENGTH READINGS:**

| Property | Typical requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Va — AIR VOIDS in the mix** ← | **3 to 5 per cent** ← | **Too few and the mix bleeds and ruts; too many and it oxidises and ravels** ← |
| **VMA — voids in the mineral aggregate** ← | **Above a minimum depending on aggregate size** ← | **Ensures enough space for adequate bitumen film thickness** ← |
| **VFB — voids filled with bitumen** ← | **65 to 75 per cent** ← | **Balances durability against stability** ← |
| **Unit weight** ← | ← | **Recorded to compute the above** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW'S TWO-SIDED REQUIREMENT REPEATS THE PATTERN AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING PHYSICALLY: a mix with too few air voids has no room for the bitumen to expand into on a hot day, so it bleeds to the surface and the mix shoves.**

> **A mix with too many air voids is permeable — air and water reach the binder, it oxidises and hardens rapidly, and the surface ravels as the bond fails.**

> **So 3 to 5 per cent is a window, and the design bitumen content is chosen to land within it.**

> **The VMA requirement in the second row exists because a mix can satisfy the air void requirement while having so little space between aggregate particles that the bitumen film is too thin to be durable — which is the failure that a dense, well-graded aggregate with insufficient VMA produces, and it is why VMA is specified separately rather than being left to follow from the voids and binder content.**
tags: flow has limits on both sides

examTip.trick: **Maximum load in kN at 60 °C, 50 mm/min, loaded diametrically** — with FLOW the deformation at that load.
examTip.trap: **Flow has an upper AND a lower limit** — too low means brittle cracking, too high means deformation. Maximising stability alone gives a brittle mix.
examTip.mnemonic: **Air voids 3-5%: too few and it bleeds, too many and it ravels** — a window, not a minimum. Same two-sided logic throughout mix design.

questions.stem: The FLAKINESS INDEX of an aggregate is the percentage by weight of particles whose:
options: Length is greater than 1.8 times their mean dimension
LEAST dimension (thickness) is less than 0.6 times their mean dimension
Volume is less than 60 per cent of a sphere of the same diameter
Surface is rough rather than smooth
questions.solution:
**LEAST dimension (thickness) is less than 0.6 times their mean dimension** — flaky particles being undesirable because they break easily under load and compaction and do not interlock well.

**The two shape indices distinguished:**

| Index | Definition | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **FLAKINESS** ← | **Thickness less than 0.6 × mean dimension** ← | **Particles passing through the slots of a thickness gauge** ← |
| **ELONGATION** ← | **Length greater than 1.8 × mean dimension** ← | **Particles retained on the length gauge** ← |

> **THE FACTORS 0.6 AND 1.8 ARE THE NUMBERS TO KEEP STRAIGHT AND A USEFUL WAY TO REMEMBER THEM IS THAT FLAKY IS 'LESS THAN' AND ELONGATED IS 'MORE THAN': a flake is too THIN, so its thickness falls below a fraction; a rod is too LONG, so its length exceeds a multiple.**

> **The mean dimension is the average of the two sieve sizes between which the particle was retained, so the test is done fraction by fraction on a graded sample.**

> **The two indices are determined separately and may also be combined into a combined index by adding them, though the elongation test is properly performed on the material remaining after the flaky particles are removed.**

> **That sequencing matters, because a particle can be both flaky and elongated, and counting it twice overstates the problem.**

**WHY SHAPE MATTERS SO MUCH:**

| Problem with flaky and elongated particles | Note |
|---|---|
| **They BREAK under compaction and under traffic** ← | **A thin particle has little strength across its thinnest dimension** ← |
| **Breaking changes the GRADING after the mix was designed** ← | **Producing fines that were not accounted for** ← |
| **They do not INTERLOCK — they tend to lie flat and slide over one another** ← | ← |
| **They give a mix with higher voids and a greater bitumen demand** ← | ← |
| **They orient horizontally during rolling, creating planes of weakness** ← | ← |
| **And they are harder to compact to the required density** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CONSEQUENCE THAT PROPAGATES FURTHEST AND IT IS OFTEN NOT RECOGNISED AS THE CAUSE: a mix designed with a particular grading is laid, and the rolling breaks the flaky particles.**

> **The in-place grading is then finer than the designed one, with more fines than intended.**

> **Extra fines fill the voids, reduce the VMA, and the bitumen that was correct for the designed grading is now excessive for the actual one — so the mix bleeds and ruts.**

> **The symptom appears as a binder problem and the cause is an aggregate shape problem, which is why a bleeding pavement should prompt a check of the aggregate's flakiness as well as of the binder content.**

**TYPICAL SPECIFICATION LIMITS AND THEIR SOURCE:**

| Application | Maximum combined flakiness and elongation |
|---|---|
| **Bituminous wearing courses** ← | **30 per cent, sometimes 25** ← |
| **Bituminous base courses** ← | **30 to 35 per cent** ← |
| **Granular base and sub-base** ← | **35 to 40 per cent** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION AGAIN TIGHTENS TOWARD THE SURFACE, FOR THE SAME REASONS AS THE ABRASION LIMITS, and the practical route to meeting the limits is worth naming: particle shape is largely determined by the CRUSHER.**

> **An impact crusher produces more cubical particles than a jaw crusher, and running a crusher with too large a feed-to-product ratio produces flaky material whatever its type.**

> **So a persistent flakiness problem is usually a crushing problem rather than a rock problem, and it is corrected by adjusting the crushing plant — a closed-circuit arrangement with a final impact or cone stage — rather than by seeking a different quarry.**

> **Recognising that saves a great deal of futile searching for better stone when the stone was adequate and the crushing was not.**

examTip.trick: **Thickness less than 0.6 × mean dimension** — flaky is 'less than', elongated is 'more than' (1.8 × length).
examTip.trap: **Flaky particles break during rolling and change the grading** — the mix then has excess fines and bleeds, which looks like a binder fault.
examTip.mnemonic: **Flakiness is usually a CRUSHER problem, not a rock problem** — an impact or cone final stage gives cubical particles from the same quarry.

questions.stem: In soil classification for road subgrades, a soil with a high PLASTICITY INDEX is undesirable chiefly because it:
options: Cannot be compacted by any available equipment
Is too permeable and drains the pavement layers above it
Undergoes large VOLUME CHANGE with moisture
Is chemically aggressive to bitumen
questions.solution:
**It undergoes large VOLUME CHANGE with moisture — swelling when wet and shrinking when dry — and loses strength dramatically on wetting**, so the pavement above it heaves, cracks and loses support seasonally.

**What the plasticity index represents:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **LIQUID LIMIT (LL)** ← | **The moisture content at which the soil begins to behave as a liquid** ← |
| **PLASTIC LIMIT (PL)** ← | **The moisture content at which it begins to behave plastically rather than crumbling** ← |
| **PLASTICITY INDEX (PI)** | **PI = LL − PL — the RANGE of moisture over which the soil is plastic** ← |

> **THE PI AS A RANGE RATHER THAN A LEVEL IS THE CONCEPTUAL POINT AND IT EXPLAINS WHY IT PREDICTS BEHAVIOUR SO WELL: a soil with a wide plastic range holds a great deal of water in a plastic, deformable state.**

> **That water is held by the clay minerals' surfaces, and the amount held reflects how much clay there is and how active it is.**

> **So the PI is effectively a measure of the clay content weighted by the clay's activity, obtained from two simple tests requiring no specialised equipment.**

> **That is why it has survived as the fundamental soil index — it correlates with volume change, with strength loss on wetting, with compressibility and with frost susceptibility, all from a pair of tests that can be done in any field laboratory.**

**TYPICAL LIMITS FOR SUBGRADE AND PAVEMENT MATERIALS:**

| Material | Maximum PI |
|---|---|
| **Sub-base material** ← | **6, sometimes up to 12 for lower classes** ← |
| **Granular base course** ← | **6, often less** ← |
| **Embankment fill** ← | **Commonly limited to 20 to 25** ← |
| **Subgrade, top 300 mm** ← | **Restricted, or the material replaced or stabilised** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS' TIGHT LIMITS ARE WORTH EXPLAINING BECAUSE THEY SOMETIMES SEEM EXCESSIVE: a base or sub-base derives its strength from PARTICLE INTERLOCK, and clay between the particles destroys that.**

> **A small amount of plastic fines lubricates the contacts, so the layer loses its stiffness exactly when it gets wet — which is when the pavement most needs it.**

> **So the limit of 6 is not a measure of quality in the abstract but a protection of the mechanism by which the layer works.**

> **And a base course that meets its grading and its strength requirements while failing the PI limit will perform badly in the monsoon however good its other properties, which is why the plasticity requirement is enforced strictly and not treated as a secondary criterion.**

**THE REMEDIES FOR A PLASTIC SUBGRADE ARE WORTH LISTING SINCE THE SOIL OFTEN CANNOT SIMPLY BE AVOIDED:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **REPLACE the top layer with better material** ← | **Simple and effective; costs depend on haul distance** ← |
| **LIME stabilisation** ← | **Lime reacts with clay minerals, reducing PI substantially — the standard treatment for plastic soils** ← |
| **CEMENT stabilisation** ← | **Better for low-plasticity soils; lime is preferred for high PI** ← |
| **Thicken the pavement to spread the load** ← | **Treats the symptom, and is expensive** ← |
| **Improve DRAINAGE so the subgrade never saturates** ← | **Addresses the cause directly and is often the cheapest measure** ← |
| **A capping layer or a geotextile separator** ← | **Preventing the subgrade from contaminating the sub-base** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WORTH KNOWING IN A LITTLE DETAIL BECAUSE THE MECHANISM DETERMINES WHERE IT WORKS: lime added to a plastic clay causes immediate cation exchange, which flocculates the clay particles and reduces the plasticity within hours.**

> **A longer, slower pozzolanic reaction then cements the soil over weeks, adding strength.**

> **So lime does two distinct things on two timescales — immediate workability and plasticity reduction, followed by gradual strength gain — and the first happens whether or not the second does.**

> **That makes lime particularly suited to high-PI soils, where cement would be consumed in coating clay particles without achieving much, and it is the reason the two stabilisers are chosen by the soil's plasticity rather than interchangeably.**
tags: PI = LL - PL as a range
PI limits for base and sub-base
lime for high PI cement for low

examTip.trick: **Large volume change with moisture and strength loss on wetting** — heave, cracking and seasonal loss of support.
examTip.trap: **PI is a RANGE (LL − PL), not a level** — effectively a measure of clay content weighted by activity, from two simple tests.
examTip.mnemonic: **LIME for high-PI clays, CEMENT for low-plasticity soils** — lime flocculates within hours, then cements over weeks.

questions.stem: The MODIFIED PROCTOR compaction test differs from the STANDARD Proctor test in that it:
options: Uses a different soil sample preparation method only
Applies a much GREATER compactive effort
Is carried out on saturated samples only
Measures the soil's shear strength rather than its density
questions.solution:
**It applies a much GREATER compactive effort — a heavier rammer falling further, in more layers** — giving a HIGHER maximum dry density at a LOWER optimum moisture content.

**The two tests compared:**

| Parameter | STANDARD Proctor | MODIFIED Proctor |
|---|---|---|
| **Rammer mass** | **2.6 kg** ← | **4.89 kg** ← |
| **Drop height** | **310 mm** ← | **450 mm** ← |
| **Number of layers** | **3** ← | **5** ← |
| **Blows per layer** | **25 (or 56 in the larger mould)** ← | **25 (or 56)** ← |
| **Compactive energy** | **About 600 kJ/m³** ← | **About 2,700 kJ/m³** ← |
| **Result** | **Lower MDD, higher OMC** ← | **Higher MDD, lower OMC** ← |

> **THE ENERGY RATIO OF ROUGHLY 4.5 TIMES IS THE ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCE AND THE EFFECT ON THE CURVE IS WORTH PICTURING: greater compactive effort shifts the whole compaction curve UP and to the LEFT.**

> **Up, because more energy achieves a higher density.**

> **Left, because with more energy available, less water is needed as a lubricant to reach that density — and beyond the optimum, water occupies space that could hold soil.**

> **So the modified test's peak is higher and drier, and both effects follow from the same cause.**

**WHICH TEST TO SPECIFY IS A QUESTION OF WHAT PLANT WILL BE USED AND WHAT THE LAYER MUST DO:**

| Situation | Test |
|---|---|
| **Modern heavy compaction plant, pavement layers, airfields** ← | **MODIFIED — it represents what the plant can actually achieve** ← |
| **Earth embankments, light plant, earth dams** ← | **STANDARD — the modified density may be unattainable in the field** ← |
| **A specification quoting '95 per cent compaction'** ← | **Is meaningless without saying WHICH test** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A SERIOUS AND COMMON SPECIFICATION DEFECT AND IT IS WORTH BEING EMPHATIC ABOUT: 95 per cent of modified Proctor density is a far more demanding requirement than 95 per cent of standard.**

> **The two maximum dry densities may differ by 5 to 10 per cent, so the required field densities differ correspondingly.**

> **A contractor pricing against one interpretation and an engineer testing against the other is a dispute waiting to happen, and it happens regularly.**

> **So every compaction specification must name the test, and every field density result must state the reference density and the test it came from — which sounds obvious and is omitted often enough to be worth stating.**

**THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN COMPACTION AND THE PROPERTIES THAT ACTUALLY MATTER DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Compaction is specified because density correlates with strength, stiffness and low compressibility** ← | ← |
| **But density is not itself the objective** ← | ← |
| **And the MOISTURE at which the density is achieved matters as much as the density** ← | ← |
| **Compacted DRY of optimum gives a stiffer, more brittle, more permeable soil** ← | **Which may swell later if it wets** ← |
| **Compacted WET of optimum gives a more flexible, less permeable soil** ← | **Lower strength initially, but more stable against later moisture change** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS DESCRIBE A CHOICE THAT IS DELIBERATELY MADE IN EARTH DAM DESIGN AND IS RARELY THOUGHT ABOUT IN ROAD WORK, THOUGH IT MATTERS THERE TOO: the same density can be reached on either side of the optimum, and the resulting soil is not the same.**

> **A clay compacted dry of optimum has a flocculated structure, higher initial strength and a strong tendency to swell if it later gains moisture.**

> **The same clay compacted slightly wet of optimum has a dispersed structure, lower permeability and far less swelling potential.**

> **For a road subgrade in a climate with a pronounced wet season, compacting slightly wet of optimum is therefore often preferable despite the marginally lower immediate strength — because the strength that matters is the strength after the monsoon, not the strength at handover.**

examTip.trick: **Greater effort: 4.89 kg rammer, 450 mm drop, 5 layers** — about 4.5 times the energy, giving higher MDD at lower OMC.
examTip.trap: **'95 per cent compaction' is meaningless without naming the test** — modified and standard densities differ by 5-10 per cent.
examTip.mnemonic: **More energy shifts the curve UP and LEFT** — higher density, less water needed as lubricant.

questions.stem: STRIPPING of a bituminous mix refers to:
options: Removal of the surface layer during maintenance milling
The separation of the bitumen film from the AGGREGATE surface in the presence of WATER
The peeling of road markings from the surface
The loss of volatile components from the bitumen during mixing
questions.solution:
**The separation of the bitumen film from the AGGREGATE surface in the presence of WATER** — the water displacing the binder because it has a greater affinity for the stone, leading to loss of cohesion, ravelling and potholing.

**Why stripping occurs:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Most road aggregates are HYDROPHILIC — they attract water** ← | **Particularly siliceous rocks: quartzite, granite, gneiss** ← |
| **Bitumen is hydrophobic and adheres to stone only by weaker forces** ← | ← |
| **So when water reaches the interface, it DISPLACES the bitumen** ← | **Being thermodynamically preferred at the stone surface** ← |
| **The bond fails and the aggregate is released** ← | ← |
| **The mix loses cohesion and ravels, and potholes form** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MECHANISM AND IT EXPLAINS WHY STRIPPING IS SO DIFFICULT TO DESIGN AGAINST: the water is not merely intruding, it is WINNING a competition for the stone's surface.**

> **So the problem cannot be solved by making the bitumen stickier alone — the issue is the relative affinity of the two fluids for the aggregate.**

> **That is why the effective remedies work by changing the INTERFACE rather than the binder: an anti-stripping agent, or a coating of hydrated lime, alters the stone's surface chemistry so that it prefers the bitumen.**

> **And it is why the aggregate's mineralogy matters so much — a limestone, being basic, bonds far better to bitumen than a siliceous rock does, and stripping is correspondingly rarer with calcareous aggregates.**

**THE FACTORS THAT PROMOTE STRIPPING AND THEIR REMEDIES:**

| Factor | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **Siliceous (acidic) aggregate** ← | **Use an anti-stripping additive, or hydrated lime at 1 to 2 per cent** ← |
| **DUSTY aggregate surfaces** ← | **Wash the aggregate — dust prevents the binder reaching the stone at all** ← |
| **DAMP aggregate at mixing** ← | **Dry it properly; the binder cannot displace a water film** ← |
| **Inadequate binder film thickness** ← | **Increase binder content or VMA** ← |
| **High air VOIDS, letting water into the mix** ← | **Compact properly to the specified density** ← |
| **Standing water and poor DRAINAGE** ← | **Drain the pavement — the single most effective measure** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE MOST OFTEN NEGLECTED, AND IT SUBSUMES SEVERAL OF THE OTHERS: stripping requires water at the interface, so a pavement that does not admit or retain water does not strip.**

> **Effective drainage — a sound crossfall, clear side drains, a drainage layer or a sealed surface — removes the necessary condition rather than mitigating the mechanism.**

> **So the most reliable anti-stripping measure is not an additive but a drain, and a road with an excellent mix and blocked side drains will strip while one with an ordinary mix and good drainage will not.**

> **That ordering is worth remembering because the additive is a visible, specifiable, purchasable item and the drainage is an ongoing maintenance obligation — so the procurement system naturally favours the less effective remedy.**

> **THE SECOND ROW DESERVES A SPECIFIC MENTION BECAUSE IT IS A CONSTRUCTION FAULT WITH THE SAME SYMPTOM: an aggregate coated in quarry dust presents a dust surface to the binder, not a stone surface.**

> **The bitumen bonds to the dust, the dust is loosely attached to the stone, and the bond fails at the first opportunity.**

> **The failure looks exactly like stripping and its cause is entirely different — it is a cleanliness failure rather than a chemical incompatibility.**

> **Distinguishing the two matters because the remedies differ: washing the aggregate solves one and does nothing for the other, and adding lime solves the other and does nothing for dust — so the diagnosis should be made by examining the stripped aggregate, which will show either clean stone or dust-coated stone and answer the question directly.**

examTip.trick: **Water displaces the bitumen film from the stone** — because most aggregates prefer water to binder.
examTip.trap: **It is a competition for the stone's surface, not just intrusion** — so remedies change the INTERFACE: lime or an anti-stripping agent, not a stickier binder.
examTip.mnemonic: **The best anti-stripping measure is a DRAIN** — no water at the interface, no stripping. Additives are purchasable; drainage is maintenance.

questions.stem: A DENSE GRADED aggregate differs from an OPEN GRADED one in that the dense graded material:
options: Contains a full range of sizes from coarse down to fine, so the smaller particles fill the voids between the larger
Contains only a single particle size
Contains no coarse aggregate at all
Is produced only from river gravel and never from crushed rock
questions.solution:
**It contains a full range of sizes from coarse down to fine, so the smaller particles fill the voids between the larger** — giving high density, high stability and LOW permeability.

**The three grading types and their characters:**

| Grading | Description | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **DENSE (well) graded** ← | **All sizes present in a smooth distribution** ← | **High density and stability; low voids; nearly impermeable** ← |
| **OPEN (uniformly) graded** ← | **A narrow band of sizes, with the fines absent** ← | **High voids; PERMEABLE; lower stability; relies on interlock of similar-sized stones** ← |
| **GAP graded** ← | **Some intermediate sizes deliberately missing** ← | **Between the two; used in stone mastic asphalt for coarse-aggregate skeleton contact** ← |

> **THE PERMEABILITY DIFFERENCE IS THE PROPERTY THAT DECIDES WHERE EACH IS USED AND IT IS WORTH TREATING AS A DESIGN CHOICE RATHER THAN A CONSEQUENCE: dense grading keeps water OUT, and open grading lets it THROUGH.**

> **A dense graded wearing course sheds water from its surface and prevents it reaching the layers below.**

> **An open graded drainage layer, placed beneath the pavement, collects water that does get in and carries it to a drain.**

> **So the two serve opposite and complementary functions, and a pavement may contain both — a dense impermeable surface over a granular base over an open graded drainage layer — with each doing what its grading suits it for.**

**THE FULLER AND THOMPSON CURVE IS THE THEORETICAL BASIS FOR DENSE GRADING AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **P = 100 (d/D)ⁿ, with P the percentage passing sieve size d and D the maximum size** ← | ← |
| **n = 0.5 gives the theoretical MAXIMUM density grading** ← | ← |
| **n = 0.45 is used in practice, plotted on a 0.45-power chart** ← | **Giving a straight line for maximum density** ← |
| **Real specifications band around that line rather than following it exactly** ← | ← |

> **THE 0.45-POWER CHART IN THE THIRD ROW IS A PRACTICAL DEVICE WORTH UNDERSTANDING: sieve sizes are plotted raised to the power 0.45, which makes the maximum density grading plot as a STRAIGHT LINE from the origin to the maximum size.**

> **A proposed grading can then be plotted on the same chart and compared by eye against that straight line.**

> **A grading that plots above the line is finer than maximum density; below it, coarser.**

> **That visual immediacy is why the chart is used, and it also makes the specification bands easy to draw and to check — an advantage that a linear or logarithmic sieve axis does not give.**

> **THE 'MAXIMUM DENSITY' GRADING IS NOT ALWAYS THE DESIRABLE ONE AND THAT IS A SUBTLETY WORTH STATING: a grading at exactly maximum density has the minimum possible voids in the mineral aggregate.**

> **Since the binder must occupy some of those voids, a minimum-void grading leaves too little room for an adequate binder film — the VMA requirement discussed earlier.**

> **So bituminous mixes are deliberately graded slightly AWAY from maximum density, usually by a dip in the fine sand sizes, to open up the VMA.**

> **A mix designed on the maximum density line will meet its air void target with a very low binder content, and the resulting thin binder film gives a durable-looking mix that ages and ravels early — which is a failure produced by following the theory too exactly, and a good illustration of why the theoretical optimum and the engineering optimum are not always the same point.**
tags: maximum density is not the design target

examTip.trick: **All sizes present, fines filling the voids** — high density and stability, low permeability.
examTip.trap: **Dense keeps water OUT, open lets it THROUGH** — opposite functions, and a pavement may deliberately use both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design slightly AWAY from maximum density** — the theoretical optimum leaves too little VMA for an adequate binder film.

questions.stem: A PRIME COAT applied to a granular base before the bituminous layer is intended to:
options: Provide the final wearing surface
Increase the base course's thickness
PENETRATE and bind the top of the granular surface
Colour the base for inspection purposes
questions.solution:
**To PENETRATE and bind the top of the granular surface, plug its capillary voids and provide a bond for the bituminous layer above** — a low-viscosity binder being used so it soaks in rather than forming a film.

**Prime coat and tack coat distinguished, since they are constantly confused:**

| Aspect | PRIME COAT | TACK COAT |
|---|---|---|
| **Applied to** | **A GRANULAR (unbound) surface** ← | **An existing BITUMINOUS or concrete surface** ← |
| **Purpose** | **PENETRATE and bind the surface; waterproof it; provide a bond** ← | **Provide ADHESION between two bituminous layers** ← |
| **Binder** | **LOW viscosity — slow-setting emulsion or a light cutback** ← | **Higher viscosity — rapid-setting emulsion** ← |
| **Rate** | **Higher — 0.6 to 1.2 kg/m², since it soaks in** ← | **Lower — 0.2 to 0.4 kg/m², since it stays on the surface** ← |
| **Should it penetrate?** | **YES — that is its purpose** ← | **NO — it must stay at the interface** ← |
| **Curing** | **Allowed to cure for 24 hours or more** ← | **Laid upon as soon as it has broken** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE CLEANEST WAY TO HOLD THE DISTINCTION AND IT FOLLOWS FROM WHAT EACH SURFACE IS: a granular base is porous and needs its top millimetres BOUND, so the binder must go in.**

> **A bituminous surface is already bound and impermeable, so a binder applied to it can only sit on top — and that is exactly what is wanted, since its job is to glue two layers together.**

> **Using a prime coat's low-viscosity binder on a bituminous surface wastes it and gives a weak bond; using a tack coat's binder on a granular base leaves it sitting on loose material that will simply separate.**

> **So the two are not interchangeable, and the choice follows automatically once the surface beneath is identified.**

**WHY THE PRIME COAT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS COST SUGGESTS:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Binds the loose fines at the base's surface** ← | **Preventing them from being picked up by the paver and forming a weak layer** ← |
| **Plugs the capillary voids** ← | **So moisture cannot rise from below into the bituminous layer** ← |
| **Waterproofs the base temporarily** ← | **Protecting it if rain falls before the surfacing is laid** ← |
| **Provides the BOND between a granular and a bituminous layer** ← | **Which are otherwise chemically and physically dissimilar** ← |
| **And it hardens the surface enough to carry construction traffic** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A BENEFIT THAT IS OFTEN REALISED UNINTENTIONALLY AND IS VALUABLE IN A MONSOON CLIMATE: a primed base can survive a rain shower that would soften and ruin an unprimed one.**

> **On a project where the surfacing cannot follow the base immediately, priming as soon as the base is finished protects the investment in that base.**

> **The alternative — leaving an unprimed base exposed and hoping — regularly results in the base being damaged and requiring reworking before it can be surfaced.**

> **So priming promptly is good practice independent of the bond it provides, and it is worth doing even where the surfacing is delayed indefinitely.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW'S BOND FUNCTION DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE ON WHY INTERLAYER BOND MATTERS SO MUCH: a pavement's layers must act TOGETHER as a composite, and that requires shear transfer between them.**

> **If a bituminous layer slips over the layer beneath, the pavement behaves as two thin independent layers rather than one thick composite one, and its load-spreading capacity falls dramatically.**

> **Debonding failures — slippage cracking, crescent-shaped cracks under braking areas — are a recognised and serious distress mode caused precisely by an omitted or contaminated tack or prime coat.**

> **So these thin, cheap, easily-skipped applications are what make the pavement a structure rather than a stack, and skipping them to save a day or a small sum removes a large part of the structural capacity that everything else was designed to provide.**

examTip.trick: **Prime penetrates a GRANULAR base; tack bonds two BITUMINOUS layers** — low viscosity going in, higher viscosity staying on.
examTip.trap: **Prime SHOULD penetrate; tack should NOT** — that single question settles which is which and which binder to use.
examTip.mnemonic: **Without the bond the pavement is a stack, not a structure** — debonded layers spread load like two thin slabs, not one thick one.

questions.stem: A sample of aggregate weighs 5,000 g before the Los Angeles abrasion test. After the test, 3,650 g is retained on the 1.7 mm sieve. The LA abrasion value is:
options: 73 per cent
27 per cent
36.5 per cent
13.5 per cent
questions.solution:
**27 per cent.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Material PASSING the 1.7 mm sieve** | **5,000 − 3,650 = 1,350 g** ← |
| **As a percentage of the original** | **1,350 ÷ 5,000 × 100** ← |
| ** ** | **= 27 per cent** ← |

> **THE DISTRACTOR AT 73 PER CENT IS THE RETAINED FRACTION AND IT IS THE ERROR THE QUESTION IS BUILT AROUND: the LA value is the material DESTROYED, not the material surviving.**

> **3,650/5,000 = 73 per cent is the proportion that remained intact, which is a perfectly meaningful number and is not what the test reports.**

> **So the calculation requires the subtraction first, and reading the question carefully enough to notice that the retained mass was given rather than the passing mass is the whole difficulty.**

> **The guard is the sense-check established earlier: these tests report damage, so the answer should be a smallish number for a good aggregate — and a 'LA value of 73 per cent' would describe an aggregate that had almost entirely disintegrated.**

**INTERPRETING THE RESULT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **27 per cent is a good, tough aggregate** ← | ← |
| **It satisfies the 30 per cent limit for a bituminous wearing course** ← | ← |
| **And comfortably satisfies every lower-layer requirement** ← | ← |
| **So this material may be used anywhere in the pavement** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION AND IT IS WHAT THE TEST IS FOR — the number is a means to a decision about where the material can be used, not an end in itself.**

> **A quarry returning 27 per cent can supply the whole pavement, which simplifies the logistics considerably.**

> **One returning 38 per cent can supply base and sub-base but not the wearing course, so a second source must be found for that layer.**

> **And one returning 55 per cent is a sub-base material only, which may still be worth using if it is close at hand, since sub-base is the thickest layer and hauling it furthest costs the most.**

**A FURTHER CONSIDERATION MAKES THIS MORE THAN AN ARITHMETIC EXERCISE AND IT IS WORTH RAISING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A single test result represents the sample, not the quarry** ← | ← |
| **Rock quality varies within a quarry, sometimes sharply** ← | **Weathered zones, different beds, altered material near joints** ← |
| **So the test must be repeated as the quarry is worked** ← | ← |
| **And a source approved on one sample may deliver material that would fail** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A REAL AND COMMON PROBLEM ON ROAD PROJECTS AND IT IS A QUALITY ASSURANCE MATTER RATHER THAN A TESTING ONE: a quarry is approved on the basis of samples from a trial pit, and the production face then moves into different material.**

> **The aggregate delivered is no longer the aggregate approved, and unless routine testing continues through production, nobody notices until the pavement fails.**

> **So the specification should require testing at a stated FREQUENCY — per so many cubic metres or per so many days of production — rather than approval on an initial sample.**

> **And the frequency should increase when the quarry face changes or when visual inspection suggests different material, which is a judgement the site engineer must be empowered and expected to make.**

examTip.trick: **(5000 − 3650)/5000 × 100 = 27 per cent** — the material destroyed, not the material retained.
examTip.trap: **73 per cent is the RETAINED fraction** — the question gives the retained mass, so subtract first.
examTip.mnemonic: **Approve the quarry, then keep testing** — the production face moves into different rock, and the approved sample stops representing what is delivered.

questions.stem: GEOTEXTILES used in road construction perform several functions. When a geotextile is placed between a soft subgrade and a granular sub-base, its primary function is:
options: Reinforcement, carrying tensile stress from wheel loads
Drainage along the plane of the fabric
Filtration of groundwater rising from below
SEPARATION
questions.solution:
**SEPARATION** — preventing the soft subgrade soil from intruding into the granular layer and the granular particles from being pushed into the subgrade, so that each layer retains its designed thickness and properties.

**The five functions a geotextile can perform:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| **SEPARATION** ← | **Keeping two dissimilar materials from mixing** ← |
| **FILTRATION** ← | **Allowing water through while retaining soil particles — flow ACROSS the plane** ← |
| **DRAINAGE** ← | **Conducting water WITHIN the plane of the fabric** ← |
| **REINFORCEMENT** ← | **Carrying tensile stress, adding strength to the soil mass** ← |
| **PROTECTION** ← | **Cushioning a membrane against puncture** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN FILTRATION AND DRAINAGE IN THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS IS A COMMON EXAMINATION POINT AND THE KEY IS THE DIRECTION OF FLOW: filtration is flow ACROSS the fabric, and drainage is flow ALONG it.**

> **A filter lets water pass through while holding the soil back, characterised by its permittivity.**

> **A drain conducts water within its own thickness to an outlet, characterised by its transmissivity.**

> **A thin woven fabric filters well and drains hardly at all; a thick needle-punched nonwoven does both; and a geocomposite with a drainage core is made specifically for the second.**

**WHY SEPARATION IS THE FUNCTION THAT MATTERS AT A SOFT SUBGRADE INTERFACE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Under repeated wheel loading, a soft saturated subgrade PUMPS upward into the granular layer** ← | ← |
| **And the granular stones are pressed DOWN into the subgrade** ← | ← |
| **The two processes are driven by the same cyclic loading and they act together** ← | ← |
| **The granular layer becomes contaminated with fines and loses its stiffness and drainage** ← | ← |
| **And it loses effective THICKNESS, since its bottom portion is now a mixture** ← | ← |
| **A separator prevents both** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE LOSS THAT MATTERS STRUCTURALLY AND IT IS SUBSTANTIAL: a 200 mm sub-base that loses its bottom 75 mm to intermixing is a 125 mm sub-base, and the pavement was designed for 200.**

> **That loss is progressive and invisible, occurring under the traffic the pavement was built to carry.**

> **So a road built on a soft subgrade without a separator loses structural capacity from the day it opens, and its measured life falls short of the design life for reasons that a materials investigation after failure will not readily reveal.**

> **A geotextile costing a small fraction of the sub-base prevents this entirely, which makes it one of the better-value items in road construction on weak ground.**

**AND THE SELECTION CRITERIA FOR A SEPARATOR ARE WORTH KNOWING SINCE THEY DIFFER FROM THOSE FOR OTHER FUNCTIONS:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Adequate SURVIVABILITY — it must survive installation and the first passes of plant** ← | **Which is usually the governing requirement, not the in-service stress** ← |
| **Appropriate apparent opening size** ← | **Fine enough to retain the subgrade, coarse enough to pass water** ← |
| **Sufficient permeability relative to the subgrade** ← | **It must not become a barrier to water, which would cause pore pressure build-up** ← |
| **Adequate tensile strength and puncture resistance** ← | ← |

> **The first row is the point most often underestimated and it produces the commonest failure: a lightweight fabric adequate for its in-service function is torn during placement by the tracked plant spreading the first lift of stone over it.**

> **Once torn, it separates nothing.**

> **So the specification must consider the installation loading — which depends on the subgrade's softness, the stone's angularity and the lift thickness — and this is why separator specifications are written in terms of survivability classes rather than of the modest stresses the fabric carries in service.**

> **And the associated construction rule follows directly: the first lift over a geotextile on soft ground must be thick enough and placed by end-tipping and pushing forward over already-placed material, never by tracking plant directly on the fabric.**

examTip.trick: **Separation** — keeping the soft subgrade and the granular layer from intermixing under cyclic loading.
examTip.trap: **Filtration is flow ACROSS the fabric; drainage is flow ALONG it** — permittivity against transmissivity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Survivability during installation governs the specification** — a fabric torn by the first tracked plant separates nothing.

questions.stem: WATER BOUND MACADAM (WBM) derives its strength from:
options: A cement binder mixed with the aggregate
A bituminous binder sprayed between the layers
MECHANICAL INTERLOCK of coarse aggregate
The compaction of a single uniform aggregate size with no filler
questions.solution:
**MECHANICAL INTERLOCK of coarse aggregate, with screening material filling the voids and binding material and water forming a slurry that is compacted in to key the whole together.**

**The construction sequence, which explains the name:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Prepare and camber the underlying surface; provide lateral confinement** ← | **Kerbs, shoulders or a trench section — essential to prevent spreading** ← |
| **2. Spread the COARSE AGGREGATE to a uniform loose thickness** ← | **A single nominal size band — 90-45 mm, 63-45 mm or 53-22.4 mm** ← |
| **3. Dry roll to achieve initial interlock** ← | **From the edges toward the centre on a straight; from inner to outer edge on a curve** ← |
| **4. Apply SCREENINGS in successive thin layers, brooming them into the voids** ← | **With dry rolling between applications** ← |
| **5. Apply WATER and sprinkle, brooming continuously** ← | ← |
| **6. Apply BINDING MATERIAL (fine material) with water, forming a slurry** ← | **Which fills the remaining voids** ← |
| **7. Roll until the slurry forms a wave ahead of the roller** ← | **The traditional sign of completion** ← |
| **8. Allow to DRY and set before the next layer or the surfacing** ← | ← |

> **THE WATER IN STEP 5 IS WHAT GIVES THE MATERIAL ITS NAME AND ITS ROLE IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD: the water does not bind anything permanently.**

> **It acts as a LUBRICANT and a carrier — lubricating the aggregate so it can rearrange into a denser interlock, and carrying the fine binding material down into the voids as a slurry.**

> **Once the layer dries, the water is gone and the strength that remains is mechanical interlock plus the packing of the screenings and fines.**

> **So 'water bound' describes the construction method, not the final binding mechanism — and understanding that explains why the layer must be allowed to DRY before being covered, since a layer sealed while still wet retains that water and stays weak.**

**THE LATERAL CONFINEMENT IN STEP 1 IS THE REQUIREMENT MOST OFTEN NEGLECTED AND IT IS FUNDAMENTAL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **An interlocked aggregate layer resists load by the stones wedging against one another** ← | ← |
| **That wedging generates outward lateral thrust** ← | ← |
| **Which must be resisted at the edges** ← | ← |
| **Without confinement, the edges spread, the interlock loosens and the layer disintegrates** ← | ← |
| **So the shoulders must be built UP with the layer, not afterwards** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A CONSTRUCTION SEQUENCING REQUIREMENT AND ITS VIOLATION IS A COMMON CAUSE OF EDGE FAILURE: shoulders built after the pavement leave the pavement unconfined during construction and during its early life.**

> **Building the shoulder material up alongside each layer as it is placed provides confinement from the start.**

> **It also compacts the shoulder properly, whereas a shoulder placed afterwards against a finished edge is compacted against an unyielding face and remains loose.**

> **So the practice of building shoulders last, which is convenient because it keeps the working area clear, produces both a weaker pavement edge and a weaker shoulder — and edge failure is one of the commonest distress modes on Nepali roads.**

> **WBM'S PLACE TODAY DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE: it is labour-intensive, slow and requires several distinct materials and considerable skill in the rolling and brooming.**

> **WET MIX MACADAM (WMM) has largely replaced it on mechanised projects — the aggregate and fines are mixed with water in a plant and laid in one operation, which is far faster and gives more consistent results.**

> **WBM remains appropriate where labour is available and plant is not, which describes a great deal of rural road construction in Nepal, and it produces an entirely satisfactory layer when properly executed.**

> **So the choice between them is one of construction method and available resources rather than of quality, and the green road approach's preference for labour-based methods naturally favours WBM.**
tags: water is a lubricant and carrier

examTip.trick: **Mechanical interlock, with screenings and a fines slurry keying the voids** — coarse aggregate, screenings, binding material, water.
examTip.trap: **The water lubricates and carries; it binds nothing permanently** — so the layer must be allowed to DRY before being covered.
examTip.mnemonic: **Build shoulders UP with each layer** — interlock generates lateral thrust that must be confined, and a shoulder added later compacts badly.

questions.stem: A bituminous mix contains aggregate of bulk specific gravity 2.65 and bitumen of specific gravity 1.02. The mix contains 5 per cent bitumen by weight of total mix and its compacted bulk density is 2.35 g/cm³. The air void content is approximately:
options: 2.1 per cent
4.2 per cent
7.3 per cent
10.5 per cent
questions.solution:
**About 4.2 per cent.**

**Taking 100 g of mix as the basis:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Bitumen mass** | **5 g** ← |
| **Aggregate mass** | **95 g** ← |
| **Volume of aggregate** | **95 ÷ 2.65 = 35.85 cm³** ← |
| **Volume of bitumen** | **5 ÷ 1.02 = 4.90 cm³** ← |
| **Total volume of solids** | **35.85 + 4.90 = 40.75 cm³** ← |
| **Theoretical maximum specific gravity** | **Gmm = 100 ÷ 40.75 = 2.454** ← |
| **Air voids** | **Va = (1 − Gmb/Gmm) × 100** ← |
| ** ** | **2.35 ÷ 2.454 = 0.9577** ← |
| ** ** | **Va = (1 − 0.9577) × 100 = 4.23 per cent** ← |

> **THE STRUCTURE OF THE CALCULATION IS WORTH SEPARATING FROM ITS ARITHMETIC BECAUSE IT IS THE SAME EVERY TIME: work out what the mix WOULD weigh with no air, compare with what it ACTUALLY weighs, and the shortfall is the air.**

> **Gmm is the air-free figure, computed by adding the volumes the components occupy and dividing the total mass by that volume.**

> **Gmb is the measured bulk density of the compacted specimen, which includes the air.**

> **So Gmb/Gmm is the fraction of the volume that is solid, and one minus it is the fraction that is air — a form that cannot be inverted by mistake and that gives a free check, since Gmm must always exceed Gmb.**

**A SECOND ROUTE TO THE SAME ANSWER CONFIRMS IT AND IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Take 1 cm³ of compacted mix, which weighs 2.35 g** | ← |
| **Bitumen in it** | **5 per cent of 2.35 = 0.1175 g, occupying 0.1175/1.02 = 0.1152 cm³** ← |
| **Aggregate in it** | **95 per cent of 2.35 = 2.2325 g, occupying 2.2325/2.65 = 0.8425 cm³** ← |
| **Total solid volume** | **0.1152 + 0.8425 = 0.9577 cm³** ← |
| **Air volume** | **1 − 0.9577 = 0.0423 cm³, so 4.23 per cent** ← |

> **THE TWO ROUTES AGREE EXACTLY, AS THEY MUST, AND THE SECOND IS ARGUABLY THE MORE TRANSPARENT: it works directly in volumes within a unit volume of the mix, so the air voids fall out as a leftover volume rather than as the difference of two specific gravities.**

> **Which route to use is a matter of preference, and doing the question by one and checking by the other takes very little extra time.**

> **The distractors correspond to plausible slips: using 5 per cent of the aggregate weight rather than of the total mix, omitting the bitumen's volume, or inverting the final ratio.**

> **Each produces a number in a believable range, which is why the check by a second route is worth the thirty seconds it costs.**

**AND THE RESULT SHOULD BE ASSESSED AGAINST THE SPECIFICATION, WHICH IS THE POINT OF COMPUTING IT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The design range for a dense bituminous mix is 3 to 5 per cent** ← | ← |
| **4.2 per cent sits comfortably within it** ← | ← |
| **So the mix is satisfactory on air voids** ← | ← |
| **Though VMA and VFB must also be checked before it is accepted** ← | ← |

> **The fourth row is the reminder that air voids alone do not qualify a mix: a mix can have ideal air voids and insufficient VMA, meaning the binder film is too thin to be durable.**

> **So the volumetric assessment is a set of three related criteria rather than one, and reporting only the air voids answers a third of the question.**

> **All three come from the same specific gravities once Gmm is known, so computing them together is little extra work.**

> **It is worth adding that a MEASURED Gmm, from the Rice test on the loose mix, is preferable to the computed value used here — because the computation assumes the aggregate absorbs no bitumen, and a porous aggregate absorbs a significant amount, which makes the true Gmm differ from the computed one and shifts every volumetric figure derived from it.**

examTip.trap: **The 5 per cent is by weight of TOTAL MIX, not of aggregate** — so the split is 5 g and 95 g in a 100 g basis.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gmm must always exceed Gmb** — one is air-free and the other includes air. That inequality is a free check on both.

questions.stem: In the DUCTILITY test on bitumen, the property measured is:
options: The temperature at which the bitumen flows
The weight loss when the bitumen is heated
The force required to break the bitumen sample
The DISTANCE in centimetres to which a standard briquette of bitumen stretches before the thread breaks
questions.solution:
**The DISTANCE in centimetres to which a standard briquette of bitumen stretches before the thread breaks, when pulled at 50 mm per minute at 27 °C** — indicating the binder's cohesion and ability to accommodate movement without fracturing.

**The test's conditions:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Temperature** | **27 °C** ← |
| **Rate of pull** | **50 mm per minute** ← |
| **Specimen** | **A briquette of standard cross-section, 10 mm × 10 mm at the minimum** ← |
| **Result** | **The elongation at break, in CENTIMETRES** ← |
| **Typical requirement** | **A minimum of 50 to 75 cm for paving grades** ← |

> **THE RESULT BEING A DISTANCE RATHER THAN A FORCE IS THE POINT THE QUESTION TURNS ON AND IT IS WORTH FIXING: ductility measures how FAR the binder stretches, not how hard it is to stretch.**

> **A ductility of 75 cm means a thread of bitumen 10 mm square drew out to three-quarters of a metre before parting.**

> **That is a remarkable extension and it conveys something important about bitumen: it is not a brittle solid but a very viscous liquid at ordinary temperatures.**

> **The property matters because a pavement moves — thermally, under load, and with the subgrade — and a binder that cannot accommodate that movement cracks.**

**WHY LOW DUCTILITY IS A WARNING SIGN:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Low ductility indicates poor COHESION within the binder** ← | ← |
| **Such a binder cracks under thermal contraction and traffic flexing** ← | ← |
| **It often indicates a bitumen from an unsuitable crude or an over-processed one** ← | ← |
| **And ductility falls sharply as bitumen AGES** ← | ← |
| **So a low value on fresh binder predicts early cracking in service** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW LINKS THE TEST TO THE AGEING MECHANISM DISCUSSED EARLIER AND IT IS WHY DUCTILITY IS SOMETIMES MEASURED AFTER THE THIN FILM OVEN TEST: what matters is not the fresh binder's ductility but the ductility it retains after mixing and after years of service.**

> **A binder with excellent fresh ductility that loses most of it in the thin film oven test will be brittle in the pavement within a year or two.**

> **So 'retained ductility' after accelerated ageing is a more useful specification than ductility on the fresh material, and modern specifications increasingly work that way.**

> **The same shift underlies the performance-graded system generally — specifying the property that matters, measured after the ageing the material will actually undergo, rather than the property of the material as delivered.**

**THE PENETRATION-BASED TESTS AS A GROUP DESERVE A CLOSING ASSESSMENT SINCE THEY ARE BEING SUPERSEDED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Penetration, softening point and ductility are EMPIRICAL tests** ← | **Measuring behaviour under arbitrary standard conditions** ← |
| **They are simple, cheap and require little equipment** ← | ← |
| **Their conditions do not correspond to service conditions** ← | ← |
| **And they do not measure fundamental rheological properties** ← | ← |
| **The PG system instead measures properties at the actual service temperatures** ← | ← |

> **The tension between the second and third rows is what has kept the old tests in use long after their limitations were understood: they can be performed in any laboratory with modest equipment, and the PG tests require a dynamic shear rheometer and a bending beam rheometer.**

> **In a country where testing capacity is limited and dispersed, a test that can be done at a district laboratory has a practical value that a theoretically superior test in a single central facility does not.**

> **So the empirical tests remain in use in Nepal and in much of South Asia, and they serve adequately when their limitations are understood.**

> **The sensible position is to use them for routine acceptance while recognising that they cannot distinguish a modified binder's performance from a straight one's, and to specify PG testing where a modified binder is being paid for — otherwise the premium is paid for a property the acceptance testing cannot verify.**

examTip.trick: **The DISTANCE stretched before breaking, in centimetres** — at 27 °C, pulled at 50 mm/min. Typically 50-75 cm minimum.
examTip.trap: **It measures distance, not force** — how far the binder stretches, not how hard it is to stretch.
examTip.mnemonic: **Retained ductility after ageing matters more than fresh ductility** — a binder that loses it in the thin film oven test is brittle within two years.

questions.stem: In Nepal, the practical constraint that most often governs the choice of pavement materials on a remote hill road project is:
options: The HAUL DISTANCE from the nearest acceptable source
The absence of any suitable rock anywhere in the country
A shortage of laboratory testing standards
The prohibition on using river-run gravel in any pavement layer
questions.solution:
**The HAUL DISTANCE from the nearest acceptable source** — since transporting aggregate and bitumen over long distances on poor roads can cost more than the material itself, making local materials attractive even where they are of lower quality.

**Why haul dominates the cost in remote terrain:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Aggregate is a LOW-VALUE, HIGH-BULK material** ← | **Its cost per tonne at the quarry is small** ← |
| **So transport cost quickly exceeds material cost** ← | ← |
| **On a poor hill road, haulage rates per tonne-kilometre are several times the plains rate** ← | **Slow speeds, low payloads, high vehicle wear** ← |
| **And the volumes are large — a kilometre of pavement needs thousands of tonnes** ← | ← |
| **So a 50 km haul can double or triple the delivered cost of aggregate** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW GIVES THE SCALE AND IT IS WORTH MAKING CONCRETE: a 5 m wide, 300 mm thick granular layer over one kilometre is 1,500 m³, which is around 3,000 tonnes.**

> **At 100 lorry-loads per kilometre of road, the haulage is a major operation in itself.**

> **So the location of the quarry relative to the road is a first-order project cost driver, and the search for material sources along the alignment is part of the reconnaissance for exactly that reason.**

> **A source 5 km from the middle of the works transforms the economics relative to one 50 km away, and identifying it may be worth more than any refinement of the pavement design.**

**THE CONSEQUENCE IS A GENUINE ENGINEERING TRADE AND IT DESERVES TO BE MADE EXPLICITLY:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Import high-quality aggregate from a distant source** ← | **A thinner pavement, higher material cost** ← |
| **Use local lower-quality material in a THICKER layer** ← | **More material, but it is cheap and close** ← |
| **STABILISE the local material with cement, lime or bitumen** ← | **Upgrading it in place rather than replacing it** ← |
| **Use the better material only in the layers that need it** ← | **Imported wearing course over local base and sub-base** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS USUALLY THE RIGHT ANSWER AND IT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM THE LAYER-BY-LAYER SPECIFICATION LOGIC ESTABLISHED EARLIER: requirements tighten toward the surface, and the surface is the THINNEST layer.**

> **So the expensive high-quality material is needed in the smallest quantity, and the cheap local material serves in the thickest layers.**

> **Hauling 40 mm of wearing course aggregate 50 km is a fraction of the cost of hauling the whole 500 mm of pavement.**

> **That allocation — quality where it is needed, quantity where it is cheap — is the single most useful cost-management principle in remote road construction, and it is why the layer specifications are differentiated in the first place.**

> **THE THIRD ROW DESERVES ITS OWN EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS UNDERUSED: stabilisation treats the material where it lies.**

> **A local gravel with too many fines and too high a plasticity index can be made into an acceptable base by adding 3 to 5 per cent cement, and the cement is a high-value low-bulk material that is cheap to transport.**

> **So stabilisation converts a transport problem into a chemistry problem, and chemistry travels far more cheaply than stone does.**

> **The constraints are that it requires reasonable process control — mixing, moisture and compaction within tolerances — and that a cement-stabilised layer cracks and must be designed and sealed accordingly, so it is not a free substitution.**

> **But on a remote project where the alternative is a 60 km aggregate haul, the arithmetic usually favours it decisively, and it deserves to be examined as a serious option rather than dismissed as a specialist technique.**
tags: aggregate is low value high bulk
quality where needed quantity where cheap

examTip.trick: **Haul distance** — aggregate is cheap at the quarry and expensive delivered over a hill road.
examTip.trap: **A kilometre of granular layer is about 3,000 tonnes** — roughly 100 lorry loads. Finding a source near the works beats refining the design.
examTip.mnemonic: **Quality where it is needed, quantity where it is cheap** — imported wearing course over local base. Or stabilise: cement travels far cheaper than stone.

questions.stem: The three fundamental parameters of traffic flow are related by the equation:
options: FLOW (q) = SPEED (v) × DENSITY (k)
Flow = Speed ÷ Density
Density = Flow × Speed
Speed = Flow × Density
questions.solution:
**FLOW (q) = SPEED (v) × DENSITY (k)** — where flow is vehicles per hour, speed is km/h and density is vehicles per km.

**The three parameters defined:**

| Parameter | Definition | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **FLOW (volume), q** ← | **Vehicles passing a POINT per unit time** ← | **veh/h** ← |
| **DENSITY (concentration), k** ← | **Vehicles occupying a LENGTH of road at an instant** ← | **veh/km** ← |
| **SPEED, v** ← | **The SPACE MEAN speed — the average of the speeds of vehicles on a length** ← | **km/h** ← |

> **A DIMENSIONAL CHECK CONFIRMS THE RELATION IMMEDIATELY AND IT IS THE FASTEST WAY TO SETTLE WHICH FORM IS RIGHT: (km/h) × (veh/km) = veh/h, which is flow.**

> **The other three options do not reduce to sensible units, so they can be eliminated without any understanding of traffic theory.**

> **This is the same technique that settled the settling basin formula earlier, and it works on almost every relation of this kind.**

> **Writing the units under each symbol before choosing takes ten seconds and removes the possibility of error entirely.**

**THE SPEED IN THE RELATION MUST BE THE SPACE MEAN SPEED AND THAT IS A GENUINE SUBTLETY:**

| Speed measure | Definition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **TIME MEAN speed** ← | **The arithmetic mean of the speeds of vehicles passing a POINT** ← | **Higher — fast vehicles pass more often, so they are over-represented** ← |
| **SPACE MEAN speed** ← | **The harmonic mean; the average speed of vehicles occupying a LENGTH at an instant** ← | **Lower — this is the one q = k·v requires** ← |

> **THE REASON THE TIME MEAN IS HIGHER IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING BECAUSE IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE UNTIL SEEN: a fast vehicle passes a point more frequently than a slow one covering the same road.**

> **So a point-based sample catches more fast vehicles than their share of the traffic stream, and the average is biased upward.**

> **A space-based sample — a photograph of a length of road — catches each vehicle once regardless of its speed, so it is unbiased.**

> **The relation vs = vt − σ²/vt links them, where σ² is the variance of the speeds, and it shows that the two converge when the speeds are uniform and diverge when they scatter.**

**THE FUNDAMENTAL DIAGRAM FOLLOWS FROM THE RELATION AND IT IS THE CENTRAL PICTURE OF TRAFFIC FLOW THEORY:**

| Condition | Speed | Density | Flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Empty road** | **Free-flow speed, vf** ← | **Zero** ← | **ZERO** ← |
| **Light traffic** | **Near free-flow** ← | **Low** ← | **Rising** ← |
| **CAPACITY** | **About half the free-flow speed** ← | **Critical density, kj/2** ← | **MAXIMUM** ← |
| **Congested** | **Falling** ← | **Rising** ← | **FALLING** ← |
| **Jam** | **ZERO** ← | **Jam density, kj** ← | **ZERO** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND LAST ROWS BOTH SHOW ZERO FLOW AND THAT IS THE KEY INSIGHT OF THE DIAGRAM: no vehicles means no flow, and stationary vehicles also means no flow.**

> **So flow rises from zero, reaches a maximum, and falls back to zero — and every flow value below capacity occurs TWICE, once in free-flow and once in congested conditions.**

> **That means a flow measurement alone is ambiguous: 1,500 veh/h might be a lightly loaded road or a congested one, and only the speed or the density distinguishes them.**

> **This is why traffic monitoring measures speed or occupancy alongside flow — a detector reporting flow alone cannot tell whether the road is working well or has broken down, which is exactly the distinction the operator needs.**
tags: time mean versus space mean speed

examTip.trick: **q = k × v** — (veh/km) × (km/h) = veh/h. The units settle it without any theory.
examTip.trap: **The speed must be SPACE mean, not time mean** — a point sample over-represents fast vehicles and biases the average upward.
examTip.mnemonic: **Flow is zero at both ends** — empty road and jam. So every sub-capacity flow occurs twice, and flow alone cannot tell you which.

questions.stem: The PASSENGER CAR UNIT (PCU) is used in traffic analysis to:
options: Count the number of passengers carried by each vehicle
Express the number of cars a road can park
Convert a MIXED traffic stream into an equivalent stream of passenger cars
Measure the fuel consumption of a car per kilometre
questions.solution:
**To convert a MIXED traffic stream into an equivalent stream of passenger cars** — since a truck, a bus, a rickshaw and a motorcycle each occupy different road space and impose different effects on other traffic.

**Typical PCU values:**

| Vehicle | PCU |
|---|---|
| **Passenger car, light van, taxi** ← | **1.0** ← |
| **Motorcycle or scooter** ← | **0.5** ← |
| **Bicycle** ← | **0.5** ← |
| **Auto-rickshaw** ← | **1.2** ← |
| **Truck or bus** ← | **3.0** ← |
| **Tractor with trailer** ← | **4.5** ← |
| **Animal-drawn cart** ← | **6.0 to 8.0** ← |
| **Hand cart** ← | **3.0** ← |

> **THE ANIMAL-DRAWN CART'S HIGH VALUE IS THE ONE THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND ITS REASON IS INSTRUCTIVE: the PCU reflects the effect a vehicle has on OTHER traffic, not merely the space it occupies.**

> **A bullock cart is not much longer than a car, but it travels at perhaps 5 km/h on a road where other traffic wants 50.**

> **So it obstructs, it forces overtaking, and it creates a moving queue behind it.**

> **Its equivalent effect is therefore that of six or eight cars, even though it occupies the space of one — which shows that the PCU is a measure of INTERFERENCE rather than of physical dimensions.**

**THE PCU IS NOT A FIXED NUMBER AND THAT IS FREQUENTLY OVERLOOKED:**

| Factor | Effect on a heavy vehicle's PCU |
|---|---|
| **Steep UPGRADE** ← | **RISES sharply — a truck crawling uphill obstructs far more** ← |
| **Narrow carriageway** ← | **Rises — overtaking becomes harder** ← |
| **Restricted sight distance** ← | **Rises — overtaking opportunities are fewer** ← |
| **High traffic volume** ← | **Rises — fewer gaps in the opposing stream** ← |
| **Level, wide, straight road with light traffic** ← | **Falls toward the tabulated value or below** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW MATTERS ENORMOUSLY IN NEPAL'S HILLS AND IT IS WHERE STANDARD TABLES MISLEAD: a truck's PCU on a 6 per cent grade may be 6 or more rather than the tabulated 3.**

> **So a hill road's capacity, computed with plains PCU values, is substantially overstated.**

> **The remedy is to use grade-specific PCU factors, which the capacity manuals provide, and where they are not available to recognise that the computed capacity is optimistic.**

> **An observed capacity far below the computed one on a hill road is therefore not a measurement error but the predictable consequence of applying the wrong equivalence factors, and it is worth checking before any other explanation is sought.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON WHY THE CONCEPT IS NEEDED AT ALL: capacity, level of service and signal timing are all defined in terms of a homogeneous traffic stream.**

> **South Asian traffic is anything but homogeneous — cars, motorcycles, buses, trucks, rickshaws, carts, cycles and pedestrians share the same carriageway, often without lane discipline.**

> **The PCU converts that heterogeneity into a single number so that the standard analytical methods can be applied.**

> **It is an approximation, and where the mix is extremely varied and lane discipline absent, its accuracy degrades — which is why capacity analysis in South Asian conditions is a genuinely harder problem than in homogeneous lane-disciplined traffic, and why locally calibrated PCU values and capacity figures matter far more than imported ones.**

examTip.trick: **Converts mixed traffic to an equivalent car-only stream** — car 1.0, motorcycle 0.5, truck/bus 3.0, cart 6-8.
examTip.trap: **PCU measures INTERFERENCE, not size** — a bullock cart is car-sized and counts as six, because it is slow and forces overtaking.
examTip.mnemonic: **A truck's PCU doubles on a steep grade** — so hill road capacity computed with plains values is badly overstated.

questions.stem: The 85TH PERCENTILE SPEED from a spot speed study is used to:
options: Identify the slowest vehicles for enforcement purposes
Calculate the road's capacity
Determine the average speed of the traffic stream
Set the SPEED LIMIT
questions.solution:
**Set the SPEED LIMIT** — on the reasoning that 85 per cent of drivers choose a speed that is reasonable for the conditions, so a limit at that speed regulates only the unreasonable minority.

**The percentile speeds and their uses:**

| Percentile | Use |
|---|---|
| **15th percentile** ← | **The MINIMUM speed limit, where one is imposed — below this, vehicles obstruct** ← |
| **50th percentile (median)** ← | **The typical speed; used in some design and economic calculations** ← |
| **85th percentile** ← | **The SPEED LIMIT, and the design speed for geometric elements on an existing road** ← |
| **98th percentile** ← | **The DESIGN SPEED for safety-critical geometric design — sight distances and the like** ← |

> **THE LOGIC BEHIND THE 85TH PERCENTILE IS WORTH SETTING OUT BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN MISREPRESENTED AS ARBITRARY: it rests on the observation that most drivers choose a speed appropriate to the road they can see.**

> **Their collective judgement, expressed in the speed distribution, reflects the road's actual characteristics better than any calculation — because they are responding to the geometry, the surface, the sight lines and the roadside conditions all at once.**

> **So a limit set at the 85th percentile agrees with what most drivers already do, and it targets the minority driving faster than conditions warrant.**

> **A limit set much BELOW the 85th percentile criminalises the majority, is widely disobeyed, and brings the whole limit system into disrepute — which is why arbitrarily low limits reduce compliance without reducing speeds.**

**THE PRINCIPLE HAS REAL LIMITATIONS AND THEY DESERVE HONEST STATEMENT:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **It assumes drivers' collective judgement is SAFE, which it may not be** ← | **Drivers respond to their own perceived risk, not to the risk they impose on others** ← |
| **It ignores VULNERABLE road users entirely** ← | **Pedestrians and cyclists bear risk they did not choose and have no vote in the distribution** ← |
| **It can RATCHET upward** ← | **Raise the limit to the 85th percentile, speeds rise, the new 85th percentile is higher** ← |
| **It presumes the road is well designed** ← | **On a poorly designed road, drivers may choose speeds it cannot safely accommodate** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST SERIOUS OBJECTION AND IT MATTERS PARTICULARLY IN NEPAL'S TOWNS AND HIGHWAY SETTLEMENTS: a driver weighing their own risk does not weigh the pedestrian's.**

> **A speed that feels comfortable to a driver in a car may be lethal to a person crossing the road, and the pedestrian's risk does not enter the speed distribution at all.**

> **So the 85th percentile approach is appropriate where the road users are homogeneous — a rural highway with few pedestrians — and inappropriate where they are not.**

> **In a settlement, the limit should be set from the SURVIVABILITY of a pedestrian impact, which points to 30 km/h or less, regardless of what drivers would otherwise choose.**

> **THE SURVIVABILITY FIGURES ARE WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE THEY SETTLE THE ARGUMENT DIRECTLY: a pedestrian struck at 30 km/h has roughly a 90 per cent chance of survival.**

> **At 50 km/h that falls to around 50 per cent, and at 65 km/h to perhaps 10 per cent.**
