> **The relationship is steeply non-linear, because the kinetic energy transferred rises with the square of the speed while the human body's tolerance does not change.**

> **So in any place where vehicles and pedestrians mix, speed management is not one safety measure among several — it is the measure that determines whether collisions are survivable, and reducing 50 to 30 converts most fatal outcomes into survivable ones.**

examTip.trick: **Setting the speed limit** — 85% of drivers choose a reasonable speed, so the limit targets the rest. 98th percentile is used for geometric design.
examTip.trap: **It ignores pedestrians entirely** — they bear risk they did not choose and do not appear in the speed distribution.
examTip.mnemonic: **30 km/h: 90% pedestrian survival. 50 km/h: about 50%.** Where people and vehicles mix, speed decides whether crashes are survivable.

questions.stem: A traffic signal cycle has an effective green time of 27 s for an approach with a saturation flow of 1,800 PCU/h. If the cycle length is 90 s, the approach capacity is:
options: 1,800 PCU/h
540 PCU/h
600 PCU/h
270 PCU/h
questions.solution:
**540 PCU/h.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Capacity = saturation flow × (effective green ÷ cycle length)** | ← |
| **The green ratio** | **g/C = 27 ÷ 90 = 0.30** ← |
| **Capacity** | **1,800 × 0.30 = 540 PCU/h** ← |

> **THE RELATION IS INTUITIVE ONCE STATED IN WORDS AND IT IS WORTH HOLDING THAT WAY: the approach discharges at the saturation flow rate, but only for the fraction of each cycle that it has green.**

> **So it achieves 30 per cent of what it would achieve with a permanent green.**

> **That makes the green ratio the single most important quantity in signal design — it is the share of the intersection's time that each approach receives.**

> **And since the green ratios of all the phases plus the lost time must sum to one, allocating green to one approach necessarily takes it from another, which is the constraint that makes signal timing a genuine optimisation.**

**SATURATION FLOW DESERVES DEFINITION SINCE IT IS THE OTHER TERM:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the maximum rate at which vehicles can cross the stop line** ← | **Once the queue is moving freely and the green is fully effective** ← |
| **Typically 1,800 to 2,000 PCU/h per lane under ideal conditions** ← | ← |
| **Reduced by narrow lanes, gradients, turning movements, parking and pedestrians** ← | ← |
| **It is a RATE, not a volume** ← | **Expressed per hour but sustained only for the green period** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A DISTINCTION THAT CAUSES REAL CONFUSION AND IT EXPLAINS THE ARITHMETIC: a saturation flow of 1,800 PCU/h does not mean 1,800 vehicles cross in an hour.**

> **It means that WHILE the queue is discharging, vehicles cross at a rate equivalent to 1,800 per hour — that is, one every two seconds.**

> **In 27 seconds of green, that is 27/2 = 13.5 vehicles per cycle.**

> **With 90-second cycles there are 40 cycles an hour, so 13.5 × 40 = 540 vehicles an hour — which recovers the answer by a completely different route and confirms it.**

**THE EFFECTIVE GREEN IS NOT THE DISPLAYED GREEN AND THAT IS THE SUBTLETY THE QUESTION SIDESTEPS BY SUPPLYING IT DIRECTLY:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Displayed green** ← | **What the signal shows** ← |
| **START-UP LOST TIME** ← | **The first few vehicles accelerate from rest, so the first seconds discharge below saturation — typically 2 s lost** ← |
| **END GAIN** ← | **Vehicles continue to cross during the amber, recovering some time — typically 2 to 3 s** ← |
| **EFFECTIVE green** | **Displayed green + amber − lost time** ← |
| **Total LOST TIME per cycle** ← | **The sum over all phases, typically 3 to 4 s per phase** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHY CYCLE LENGTH MATTERS AND IT DRIVES THE WHOLE OPTIMISATION: lost time is incurred once per PHASE per cycle, regardless of the cycle's length.**

> **So a short cycle incurs that lost time more often per hour and wastes a larger proportion of the intersection's capacity.**

> **A long cycle wastes less but produces longer waits for everyone, and longer queues.**

> **The optimum balances the two, and Webster's formula — C = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y), with L the total lost time and Y the sum of the critical flow ratios — is the classic expression of that balance, giving the cycle length that minimises total delay.**
tags: capacity = saturation flow times green ratio

examTip.trap: **Saturation flow is a RATE sustained only during green** — 1,800/h means one vehicle every 2 s, so 13.5 per cycle × 40 cycles = 540.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lost time is per PHASE per CYCLE** — so short cycles waste more capacity. Webster's C = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y) balances that against delay.

questions.stem: A BLACK SPOT in road safety analysis is:
options: A location where the road surface has deteriorated badly
A section of road with poor street lighting
A location with a CONCENTRATION of accidents significantly above what would be expected for that type of road and traffic volume
Any location where a fatal accident has occurred
questions.solution:
**A location with a CONCENTRATION of accidents significantly above what would be expected for that type of road and traffic volume** — identified from accident records and prioritised for investigation and treatment.

**How black spots are identified and treated:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Collect accident data with accurate LOCATION** ← | **Which is the step that fails most often — a record without a precise location is useless for this purpose** ← |
| **2. Plot accidents on a map or against chainage** ← | ← |
| **3. Identify locations exceeding a threshold** ← | **A number per km per year, or a rate per vehicle-kilometre** ← |
| **4. Investigate each site — a detailed study of the accident patterns and a site inspection** ← | ← |
| **5. Identify the common factors among the accidents** ← | **The key analytical step** ← |
| **6. Design a remedial treatment addressing those factors** ← | ← |
| **7. Implement, then MONITOR to confirm the treatment worked** ← | ← |

> **STEP 5 IS WHERE THE ANALYSIS SUCCEEDS OR FAILS AND IT IS OFTEN SKIPPED IN FAVOUR OF A GENERIC TREATMENT: a location with twelve accidents may have twelve unrelated ones, or twelve of the same kind.**

> **If ten of them are rear-end collisions in the wet, the problem is likely skid resistance or an unexpected queue.**

> **If ten are right-turning vehicles struck by oncoming traffic, the problem is the turning arrangement.**

> **If ten involve pedestrians, the problem is crossing provision.**

> **Each demands a different remedy, and installing a generic package of signs and markings at every black spot treats none of them — which is why the accident PATTERN, not merely the accident COUNT, is what the investigation must establish.**

**THE REGRESSION-TO-THE-MEAN PROBLEM IS THE MOST IMPORTANT STATISTICAL PITFALL AND IT MUST BE UNDERSTOOD:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Accidents are random events with a fluctuating count** ← | ← |
| **A site selected BECAUSE it had an unusually high count last year** ← | ← |
| **Is likely to have a lower count next year regardless of any treatment** ← | **Simply because the high count was partly bad luck** ← |
| **So the apparent benefit of a treatment is OVERSTATED** ← | ← |
| **Sometimes entirely — a treatment with no effect can appear highly successful** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS DESCRIBE A TRAP THAT HAS PRODUCED A GREAT DEAL OF MISLEADING EVIDENCE IN ROAD SAFETY AND IT IS NOT OBVIOUS: the very act of selecting the worst sites guarantees that most of them will improve.**

> **So a before-and-after comparison at treated black spots overstates the treatment's effect, and the overstatement can be large.**

> **The corrections are to use several years of BEFORE data, to use a comparison group of untreated similar sites, and formally to apply the empirical Bayes method, which combines the site's own record with the expected rate for its type.**

> **Without those corrections, an evaluation can conclude that a treatment works when it does nothing, and the resources then go on repeating an ineffective measure — which makes the statistical correction a practical matter of where money goes rather than an academic refinement.**

> **STEP 1 DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD BECAUSE IT IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IN PRACTICE: none of this analysis is possible without accident records that are complete, consistent and accurately located.**

> **Under-reporting, inconsistent classification and vague locations — 'near the bridge' — make the data unusable for black spot identification however sophisticated the analysis.**

> **So investment in the accident recording system, including GPS location at the scene, is the precondition for everything else in road safety engineering.**

> **It is unglamorous, it belongs to the police rather than to the roads authority, and it determines whether the roads authority can do its safety work at all — which is an institutional coordination problem of exactly the kind that recurs throughout infrastructure management.**
tags: accident data quality is the precondition

examTip.trick: **A concentration of accidents above the expected rate** for that road type and volume — not simply anywhere a fatality occurred.
examTip.trap: **Find the PATTERN, not just the count** — twelve rear-end wet-weather crashes and twelve assorted ones need entirely different remedies.
examTip.mnemonic: **Regression to the mean flatters every black spot treatment** — sites picked for a bad year improve anyway. Use multi-year data and a control group.

questions.stem: In road safety, the SAFE SYSTEM approach differs from traditional road safety thinking principally in that it:
options: Accepts that people WILL make mistakes
Focuses exclusively on enforcing traffic laws against drivers
Aims to eliminate all road accidents of every severity
Requires all vehicles to be fitted with speed limiters
questions.solution:
**It accepts that people WILL make mistakes, and therefore designs the road system so that those mistakes do not result in death or serious injury** — placing responsibility on system designers rather than solely on road users.

**The principles of the Safe System:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **People make MISTAKES — this is a given, not a failing to be eliminated** ← | ← |
| **The human body has a known and limited tolerance to physical force** ← | ← |
| **Responsibility is SHARED between road users and system designers** ← | ← |
| **All parts of the system must be strengthened, so that if one fails, others protect** ← | ← |
| **The goal is ZERO deaths and serious injuries, not zero collisions** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE SHIFT THAT DEFINES THE APPROACH AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: the objective is not to prevent crashes but to prevent crashes from KILLING people.**

> **Preventing all crashes is impossible, because it would require people never to err.**

> **Preventing crashes from being fatal is achievable, because it requires only that the energy involved stay below what a human body can tolerate.**

> **So the approach redirects effort from the unattainable goal to the attainable one, and that redirection is what makes it practically powerful rather than merely aspirational.**

**THE HUMAN TOLERANCE LIMITS ARE THE APPROACH'S QUANTITATIVE FOUNDATION AND THEY DRIVE THE DESIGN:**

| Crash type | Survivable impact speed |
|---|---|
| **Pedestrian struck by a vehicle** ← | **30 km/h** ← |
| **Side impact between vehicles** ← | **50 km/h** ← |
| **Head-on impact between vehicles** ← | **70 km/h** ← |
| **Vehicle striking a roadside object** ← | **40 km/h** ← |

> **THESE FOUR FIGURES GENERATE A COMPLETE DESIGN LOGIC AND THAT IS THEIR POWER: wherever the system cannot guarantee that impact speeds stay below the relevant threshold, either the speed must be reduced or the conflict must be removed.**

> **Where pedestrians mix with traffic, the speed must be 30 km/h — or the pedestrians must be separated.**

> **Where vehicles cross each other's paths, the speed must be below 50 km/h — or the crossing must be grade-separated or converted to a roundabout, which reduces impact angles and speeds.**

> **Where head-on collision is possible, the speed must be below 70 km/h — or the directions must be physically separated by a median barrier.**

> **So a high-speed road without median separation is, by this logic, a road whose design accepts fatal outcomes — and stating it that plainly is precisely what the Safe System framework is for.**

> **THE THIRD PRINCIPLE — SHARED RESPONSIBILITY — IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL INSTITUTIONALLY AND IT REDIRECTS BLAME PRODUCTIVELY: traditional analysis attributes most crashes to 'driver error' and concludes that drivers must be educated and enforced against.**

> **The Safe System asks instead why the system permitted that error to be fatal.**

> **A driver who drifts across a centre line has erred; a road that allows that error to produce a head-on collision at 90 km/h has been designed to permit a fatal outcome from a common and predictable mistake.**

> **So the question shifts from 'who was at fault' to 'what would have prevented death', and the answers to the second question — a barrier, a rumble strip, a lower speed — are within the engineer's control in a way that human fallibility is not.**

examTip.trick: **Accept human error; design so it is not fatal** — responsibility shared with system designers, not loaded onto road users.
examTip.trap: **The goal is zero DEATHS, not zero crashes** — preventing all collisions is impossible; keeping impact energy survivable is not.
examTip.mnemonic: **30 pedestrian, 50 side, 70 head-on, 40 roadside object** — four numbers that generate the whole design logic.

questions.stem: The LEVEL OF SERVICE (LOS) of a road section is a qualitative measure, graded A to F, that describes:
options: The structural condition of the pavement
The quality of the road's maintenance regime
The number of accidents per vehicle-kilometre
The OPERATING CONDITIONS experienced by drivers
questions.solution:
**The OPERATING CONDITIONS experienced by drivers — speed, freedom to manoeuvre, comfort and delay** — with A representing free flow and F representing breakdown and forced flow.

**The six levels:**

| Level | Condition |
|---|---|
| **A** ← | **FREE FLOW. Drivers unaffected by others; speed and manoeuvring entirely free** ← |
| **B** ← | **Reasonably free flow. Presence of others noticeable but not restricting** ← |
| **C** ← | **Stable flow. Manoeuvring requires vigilance; comfort declining** ← |
| **D** ← | **Approaching unstable flow. Speeds falling; little freedom to manoeuvre** ← |
| **E** ← | **At CAPACITY. Unstable; any disturbance causes breakdown** ← |
| **F** ← | **Forced or breakdown flow. Stop-and-go; demand exceeds capacity; queues form** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN E AND F IS THE ONE MOST WORTH UNDERSTANDING AND IT IS NOT MERELY A MATTER OF DEGREE: LOS E is the road operating AT capacity, carrying the maximum flow it can.**

> **LOS F is the road having BROKEN DOWN, and it carries LESS than capacity.**

> **That is the counter-intuitive part — a congested road moves fewer vehicles per hour than the same road at capacity, because stop-and-go operation is less efficient than steady flow.**

> **It follows directly from the fundamental diagram established earlier, where flow falls away beyond the critical density, and it is why preventing breakdown is so valuable: once a road tips into LOS F, it loses capacity precisely when it most needs it.**

**HOW LOS IS MEASURED DIFFERS BY FACILITY TYPE AND THAT IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Facility | LOS measured by |
|---|---|
| **Freeway or multilane highway** ← | **DENSITY, in passenger cars per km per lane** ← |
| **Two-lane rural highway** ← | **Percent time spent following, and average travel speed** ← |
| **Signalised intersection** ← | **Average control DELAY per vehicle, in seconds** ← |
| **Unsignalised intersection** ← | **Average delay for the minor movements** ← |
| **Urban street** ← | **Average travel speed as a proportion of free-flow speed** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST RELEVANT MEASURE FOR MOST OF NEPAL'S HIGHWAY NETWORK AND IT CAPTURES SOMETHING THE OTHERS DO NOT: on a two-lane road, the quality of service depends largely on how much time a driver spends trapped behind a slower vehicle unable to overtake.**

> **That is not a matter of speed alone — a driver travelling at 55 km/h freely has a much better experience than one travelling at 55 km/h in a queue of eight vehicles.**

> **So 'percent time spent following' measures the frustration and the overtaking pressure directly, and it is the measure that correlates with both service quality and with overtaking-related accident risk.**

> **A two-lane road with a high percent-time-following is a road where dangerous overtaking will occur, which connects the capacity analysis to the safety analysis in a direct and useful way.**

> **A CLOSING CAUTION ON APPLYING LOS IN SOUTH ASIAN CONDITIONS: the level of service framework was developed for homogeneous, lane-disciplined traffic.**

> **Where traffic is mixed and lane discipline is absent, the concepts of density per lane and freedom to manoeuvre translate poorly, and the tabulated thresholds do not apply.**

> **So LOS thresholds must be locally calibrated, and importing them directly produces assessments that do not match what a road is observably doing.**

> **The practical consequence is that a Nepali urban road may be assessed as LOS C by imported criteria while functioning, to any observer, as a congested street — and the discrepancy is a calibration failure rather than a measurement one.**
tags: level of service A to F
E is at capacity F is breakdown

examTip.trick: **Operating conditions experienced by drivers** — A free flow through F breakdown.
examTip.trap: **E is AT capacity; F carries LESS than capacity** — a broken-down road moves fewer vehicles than a road running at its maximum.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two-lane roads are measured by 'percent time spent following'** — which links service quality directly to dangerous-overtaking risk.

questions.stem: A RUMBLE STRIP placed across the carriageway on the approach to a hazard works by:
options: Physically preventing vehicles from exceeding a given speed
Producing an AUDIBLE and TACTILE warning
Improving the skid resistance of the approach
Draining water from the carriageway
questions.solution:
**Producing an AUDIBLE and TACTILE warning — noise and vibration transmitted to the driver** — that alerts an inattentive driver to an approaching hazard, and encourages a speed reduction.

**The two applications and how they differ:**

| Type | Location | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **TRANSVERSE rumble strips** ← | **Across the carriageway, in sets, on the approach to a hazard** ← | **Alert and slow the driver approaching a junction, a settlement or a sharp bend** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL rumble strips** ← | **Along the edge line or the centre line** ← | **Warn a driver who is DRIFTING out of lane — the run-off-road and head-on crash types** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE APPLICATION WITH THE BEST-DOCUMENTED SAFETY BENEFIT OF ALMOST ANY LOW-COST TREATMENT AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: edge-line and centre-line rumble strips address drowsy and distracted driving directly.**

> **A driver falling asleep or looking away does not brake, does not steer and does not slow — the vehicle simply drifts.**

> **No sign, no marking and no speed limit reaches such a driver, because all of them require attention that is absent.**

> **A rumble strip does reach them, because noise and vibration wake a sleeping driver and startle a distracted one — which makes it one of the very few interventions effective against the inattention crash types, and its cost is trivial relative to its benefit.**

**THE SAFE SYSTEM CONNECTION IS DIRECT AND WORTH DRAWING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Drifting out of lane is a predictable human error** ← | ← |
| **It cannot be eliminated by education or enforcement** ← | **The driver is not choosing to do it** ← |
| **So the system must be designed to tolerate it** ← | ← |
| **A rumble strip gives the driver a chance to recover** ← | ← |
| **And a barrier or a forgiving roadside limits the consequence if they do not** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE TWO LAYERS OF THE SAME DEFENCE AND THE SAFE SYSTEM'S PRINCIPLE OF REDUNDANCY IS VISIBLE IN THEM: the rumble strip prevents the departure, and the roadside treatment limits its consequence.**

> **Providing both means a single failure does not produce a death.**

> **Providing only one means the whole outcome rests on that one measure working every time.**

> **That layering is what the principle 'strengthen all parts of the system' means in practice, and it is why safety treatments are best considered as a package for a length of road rather than as individual items at individual points.**

**THE PRACTICAL LIMITATIONS DESERVE HONEST STATEMENT SINCE RUMBLE STRIPS ARE OFTEN OVERUSED:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **NOISE affects residents nearby** ← | **Which makes them unsuitable through settlements — precisely where speed reduction is often wanted** ← |
| **They are hazardous to MOTORCYCLES and cyclists** ← | **Particularly aggressive transverse strips, which can destabilise a two-wheeler** ← |
| **Drivers HABITUATE where they are overused** ← | **A strip on every approach ceases to signal anything** ← |
| **They deteriorate and need maintenance** ← | ← |
| **And they are a warning, not a physical restraint** ← | **A determined driver passes over them at any speed** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A SERIOUS CONSIDERATION IN NEPAL, WHERE MOTORCYCLES ARE A LARGE SHARE OF THE TRAFFIC: a strip designed to shake a car noticeably can unsettle a motorcycle dangerously, especially in the wet or on a curve.**

> **So the profile must be moderate, the strips must not be placed where a two-wheeler would be braking or turning, and a gap should be left at the edge of the carriageway where cyclists and motorcycles travel.**

> **The third row is the design discipline that keeps them effective: a warning that appears everywhere warns of nothing.**

> **So transverse rumble strips should be reserved for genuinely significant hazards — the approach to a serious bend, a settlement, a junction with a poor record — and not applied routinely, which is the practice that renders them invisible to the drivers they were meant to alert.**

examTip.trick: **Noise and vibration alerting an inattentive driver** — a warning, not a physical restraint.
examTip.trap: **Longitudinal (edge and centre line) strips have the strongest evidence** — they reach drowsy and distracted drivers that no sign can.
examTip.mnemonic: **Overuse destroys them** — a warning on every approach warns of nothing. And keep the profile moderate for motorcycles.

questions.stem: The design hourly volume (DHV) used for geometric design of a highway is conventionally taken as the:
options: Highest hourly volume recorded in the year
Average hourly volume over the whole year
30TH HIGHEST HOURLY VOLUME of the year
Hourly volume during the busiest day of the festival season
questions.solution:
**30TH HIGHEST HOURLY VOLUME of the year** — a compromise that accommodates all but about 29 hours of the year, beyond which providing capacity becomes uneconomic.

**Why the highest hour is not used:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hourly volumes through the year vary enormously** ← | ← |
| **The very highest hours are festival or holiday peaks** ← | **Dashain and Tihar travel in Nepal's case** ← |
| **They occur on only a handful of days** ← | ← |
| **Designing for them means large capacity idle for 8,700 hours a year** ← | ← |
| **So a design volume somewhat below the peak is the economic choice** ← | ← |
| **The 30th highest hour is the conventional point** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ECONOMIC ARGUMENT AND IT IS THE SAME 'THIN SLICE' REASONING THAT APPEARED IN HYDROPOWER SIZING: the last increment of capacity serves only the rarest hours, so it earns very little for its cost.**

> **The relationship between the hour ranking and the volume is a steeply falling curve — the highest hours are much busier than the hundredth highest, and by the two hundredth the curve has flattened.**

> **The 30th highest hour sits at the KNEE of that curve, where the volume stops falling steeply and begins to level.**

> **Designing to the knee gives most of the benefit for much less than the cost of designing to the peak, which is why the convention lands where it does rather than at some rounder number.**

**THE CONSEQUENCE OF THE CHOICE IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The road will be over capacity for about 29 hours a year** ← | ← |
| **That is accepted deliberately** ← | ← |
| **On those hours there will be congestion and delay** ← | ← |
| **And on the other 8,731 hours the capacity is adequate** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PART THAT MUST BE COMMUNICATED RATHER THAN BURIED: the design accepts congestion on the busiest days.**

> **When those days arrive and the highway is congested, that is the design working as intended, not failing.**

> **Explaining this in advance is far better than explaining it afterwards, because a public that has been told the road is designed for normal conditions and not for Dashain will judge it differently from one that believed it was designed for everything.**

> **So the design volume's basis belongs in the project's public communication as much as in its technical report — a point that applies to any design accepting a stated level of service shortfall.**

**AND THE RELATIONSHIP TO THE AADT IS THE PRACTICAL ROUTE TO THE NUMBER SINCE THE HOURLY RANKING IS RARELY AVAILABLE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **DHV = AADT × K** ← | **K being the ratio of the design hour volume to the AADT** ← |
| **K is typically 0.08 to 0.12 for rural roads** ← | **8 to 12 per cent of the day's traffic in the design hour** ← |
| **Lower — around 0.08 to 0.10 — for urban roads** ← | **Urban traffic is spread more evenly through the day** ← |
| **And the DIRECTIONAL split D must also be applied** ← | **DDHV = AADT × K × D, with D commonly 0.55 to 0.70** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN OMITTED AND IT MATTERS FOR A DIVIDED ROAD OR ONE WHERE THE LANES SERVE DIRECTIONS SEPARATELY: traffic in the peak hour is rarely balanced.**

> **A commuter corridor may run 70:30 in the morning and reverse in the evening, so the busier direction carries far more than half the design hour volume.**

> **Designing each direction for half the total under-provides the busy direction by a substantial margin.**

> **So the directional design hour volume, not the total, is what sizes the carriageway in each direction — and on a two-lane two-way road the total governs, while on any divided facility the directional figure does.**
tags: knee of the ranked hour curve

examTip.trick: **The 30th highest hour of the year** — at the knee of the ranked-hour curve, where volume stops falling steeply.
examTip.trap: **It deliberately accepts congestion on about 29 hours a year** — when Dashain traffic queues, the design is working as intended.
examTip.mnemonic: **DDHV = AADT × K × D** — and the directional split D (0.55-0.70) is the step most often forgotten on a divided road.

questions.stem: Traffic signs are classified into three groups. These are:
options: REGULATORY (mandatory), WARNING (cautionary) and INFORMATORY signs
Permanent, temporary and emergency signs
Urban, rural and highway signs
Illuminated, reflective and plain signs
questions.solution:
**REGULATORY (mandatory), WARNING (cautionary) and INFORMATORY signs** — distinguished by whether they impose a legal requirement, alert to a hazard, or provide guidance.

**The three classes and their conventional shapes and colours:**

| Class | Shape and colour | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **REGULATORY** ← | **CIRCULAR. Red border with white background for prohibitions; blue for mandatory instructions** ← | **Speed limit, no entry, no overtaking, compulsory turn** ← |
| **Special regulatory** ← | **OCTAGONAL red for STOP; inverted TRIANGLE for GIVE WAY** ← | **Unique shapes so they are recognisable even when obscured or from behind** ← |
| **WARNING** ← | **TRIANGULAR, red border, white or yellow background** ← | **Sharp bend, steep gradient, pedestrian crossing ahead, falling rocks** ← |
| **INFORMATORY** ← | **RECTANGULAR. Blue or green background** ← | **Direction, distance, place names, facilities, route numbers** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW EXPLAINS A DESIGN DECISION THAT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED AND IS RATHER ELEGANT: STOP and GIVE WAY have unique shapes that no other sign uses.**

> **A driver can recognise an octagon or an inverted triangle from its outline alone — in fog, at night, when the face is dirty, when it is partly obscured by vegetation, or even from behind.**

> **That redundancy is deliberate, because these two signs govern the most safety-critical instruction in the system: whether to give way at a conflict point.**

> **So the shape carries the message independently of the colour and the legend, and that principle of encoding critical information in more than one way is worth recognising wherever safety-critical signage is designed.**

**THE PRINCIPLES OF GOOD SIGNING ARE FEW AND ARE ROUTINELY VIOLATED:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **A sign must fulfil a NEED** ← | **Signs that serve no purpose dilute those that do** ← |
| **It must command ATTENTION** ← | **Size, position, retroreflectivity, contrast with its background** ← |
| **It must convey a CLEAR, SIMPLE meaning** ← | ← |
| **It must command RESPECT** ← | **Which depends on its being credible — see below** ← |
| **It must give ADEQUATE TIME for response** ← | **Placed far enough in advance for perception, decision and action** ← |

> **THE FOURTH PRINCIPLE IS THE ONE THAT DECAYS FASTEST IN PRACTICE AND IT IS SELF-INFLICTED: a sign commands respect only if drivers find it credible.**

> **A 'sharp bend' warning before a gentle curve, a 30 km/h limit on an open stretch, or a 'road works' sign left in place for months after the works finished all teach drivers that signs need not be believed.**

> **Having learned that, they apply the same discount to the sign that genuinely matters.**

> **So over-signing and stale signing are not merely untidy — they actively degrade the effectiveness of the whole signing system, and removing unnecessary signs is a genuine safety measure rather than a cost saving.**

> **THE FIFTH PRINCIPLE GIVES THE PLACEMENT RULE AND IT IS CALCULABLE RATHER THAN A MATTER OF JUDGEMENT: the sign must be visible and legible far enough ahead for the driver to perceive it, read it, decide and act.**

> **At 60 km/h a vehicle covers about 17 m a second, so a sign requiring three seconds of reading and a further three of response must be legible more than 100 m before the point of action.**

> **For a complex direction sign at a junction, the requirement is considerably greater — which is why advance direction signs are placed several hundred metres ahead and repeated.**

> **A sign placed at the hazard itself, which is the intuitive location, gives no time at all and is therefore of almost no use for anything requiring a manoeuvre.**
tags: unique shapes for STOP and GIVE WAY

examTip.trick: **Regulatory (circular), warning (triangular), informatory (rectangular)** — legal requirement, hazard alert, guidance.
examTip.trap: **STOP and GIVE WAY have UNIQUE shapes** — recognisable by outline alone, even obscured or from behind. Deliberate redundancy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Over-signing destroys credibility** — an unbelievable sign teaches drivers to discount the one that matters. Removing signs can be a safety measure.

questions.stem: A PARKING STUDY that measures PARKING ACCUMULATION determines:
options: The total number of vehicles that parked during the whole day
The NUMBER of vehicles parked in a given area at successive points in TIME
The average time each vehicle remains parked
The revenue collected from parking charges
questions.solution:
**The NUMBER of vehicles parked in a given area at successive points in TIME** — from which the peak demand and its timing are found.

**The parking study measures and what each answers:**

| Measure | Definition | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **ACCUMULATION** ← | **Vehicles parked at a given instant, plotted against time** ← | **How much space is needed, and when** ← |
| **PARKING VOLUME** ← | **Total vehicles parking in the period** ← | **How many users are served** ← |
| **PARKING LOAD** ← | **Vehicle-hours — the area under the accumulation curve** ← | **The total demand, for charging and economics** ← |
| **PARKING DURATION** ← | **How long each vehicle stays** ← | **Whether the users are short-stay shoppers or all-day commuters** ← |
| **TURNOVER** ← | **Vehicles served per space per period** ← | **How productively each space is used** ← |
| **PARKING INDEX** ← | **Occupancy as a percentage of capacity** ← | **How full the facility is** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN ACCUMULATION AND VOLUME IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE ONE THE QUESTION TURNS ON AND IT IS THE SAME DISTINCTION AS BETWEEN DENSITY AND FLOW IN TRAFFIC: accumulation is a stock at an instant, and volume is a count over a period.**

> **A car park with 50 spaces might serve 400 vehicles in a day while never holding more than 50 at once.**

> **So the volume is 400 and the peak accumulation is 50, and only the second determines how many spaces are required.**

> **Confusing the two leads to sizing a car park for the day's total users, which would be absurdly large — and the analogous confusion between flow and density in traffic analysis produces equally wrong conclusions.**

**THE DURATION AND TURNOVER MEASURES TOGETHER REVEAL THE POLICY PROBLEM AND THAT IS THEIR VALUE:**

| Situation | Interpretation | Policy response |
|---|---|---|
| **Long durations, low turnover** ← | **All-day parkers — commuters and shop staff — occupying prime spaces** ← | **Time limits or graduated charges to displace them** ← |
| **Short durations, high turnover** ← | **Shoppers and short-stay visitors — the intended users of central spaces** ← | **Working as intended** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW DESCRIBES THE COMMONEST URBAN PARKING PROBLEM AND IT IS A MANAGEMENT FAILURE RATHER THAN A CAPACITY ONE: a central area's kerbside spaces are the most valuable parking resource it has.**

> **If they are occupied from eight in the morning by people who will not move until evening, they serve perhaps one user each per day.**

> **The same spaces with a two-hour limit serve five or six, so the effective capacity multiplies without a single new space being built.**

> **So the first response to a parking shortage should be to examine the duration data, and building new capacity before doing so frequently adds supply while leaving the underlying misallocation untouched.**

**THE PARKING LAYOUT DECISION IS WORTH A CLOSING NOTE SINCE IT FOLLOWS FROM SIMPLE GEOMETRY:**

| Angle | Space per vehicle along the kerb | Depth required |
|---|---|---|
| **PARALLEL (0°)** ← | **Most kerb length per vehicle — about 6 m** ← | **Least depth — about 2.5 m** ← |
| **30°** ← | **Less kerb per vehicle** ← | **More depth** ← |
| **45°** ← | ← | ← |
| **60°** ← | ← | ← |
| **90° (right angle)** ← | **LEAST kerb per vehicle — about 2.5 m** ← | **MOST depth — about 5 m plus aisle** ← |

> **The trade is entirely geometric and it decides the choice: angle parking fits more vehicles per metre of kerb and takes more width from the carriageway.**

> **So a wide street can use angle parking and a narrow one cannot.**

> **Parallel parking is also safer for the traffic stream, because a vehicle leaving a parallel space moves forward into the flow with good visibility, while one reversing out of a right-angle space emerges blind into the carriageway.**

> **That safety difference is substantial where traffic speeds are moderate, which is why angle parking is generally restricted to low-speed streets and off-street facilities rather than used wherever the width happens to allow it.**
tags: accumulation is a stock volume is a count

examTip.trick: **Vehicles parked at successive instants** — giving the peak demand and when it occurs. That is what sizes the facility.
examTip.trap: **Accumulation is a stock; volume is a count over time** — 50 spaces can serve 400 vehicles a day. Same distinction as density versus flow.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check DURATION before building capacity** — a two-hour limit can multiply effective capacity five-fold with no new spaces.

questions.stem: In a signalised intersection, the AMBER (yellow) interval is provided to:
options: Allow pedestrians to complete their crossing
Give drivers time to accelerate before the green begins
Allow vehicles that are too close to the stop line to stop safely to CLEAR the intersection
Indicate that the signal is about to fail
questions.solution:
**To allow vehicles that are too close to the stop line to stop safely to CLEAR the intersection** — resolving the dilemma zone in which a driver can neither stop comfortably nor cross before the red.

**The dilemma zone explained:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **When the green ends, a driver must decide to stop or to proceed** ← | ← |
| **A driver far away can stop comfortably** ← | ← |
| **A driver very close can cross before the conflicting green begins** ← | ← |
| **A driver at an intermediate distance can do NEITHER** ← | **That region is the DILEMMA ZONE** ← |
| **The amber interval must be long enough that the dilemma zone does not exist** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PROBLEM THE AMBER SOLVES AND IT IS A GEOMETRIC ONE RATHER THAN A BEHAVIOURAL ONE: at any given moment there is a distance beyond which a driver can stop and a distance within which they can clear.**

> **If the second distance is greater than the first, every driver can do one or the other and there is no dilemma.**

> **If the first is greater, there is a band of positions from which neither is possible, and a driver in that band must either brake hard or enter on red.**

> **So the amber's length determines whether the dilemma zone exists, and a too-short amber creates it — which is why red-light violations and rear-end collisions at a junction are frequently a signal timing fault rather than a driver behaviour problem.**

**THE AMBER DURATION IS CALCULABLE:**

| Element | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Amber time** | **τ = t + v/(2a) + (W + L)/v** ← |
| **With** | **t the reaction time (about 1 s), a the deceleration rate, v the approach speed** ← |
| ** ** | **W the intersection width, L the vehicle length** ← |
| **Typical values** | **3 to 5 seconds, longer for higher approach speeds and wider intersections** ← |

> **THE THREE TERMS CORRESPOND TO THE THREE THINGS THE DRIVER MUST DO AND SEEING THAT MAKES THE FORMULA MEMORABLE: react, stop, and — for one who chooses to continue — clear the junction.**

> **The third term is why a WIDE intersection needs a longer amber: the vehicle has further to travel before it is clear of conflicting traffic.**

> **Where that term would make the amber uncomfortably long, the practice is to keep the amber at a conventional 3 to 4 seconds and add an ALL-RED interval afterwards, during which every approach shows red.**

> **That separates the two functions cleanly — the amber warns and permits the stopping decision, and the all-red gives the clearing time — and it avoids an excessively long amber, which drivers learn to treat as an extension of green.**

> **THE LAST POINT IS A REAL BEHAVIOURAL RISK AND IT BOUNDS THE SOLUTION FROM ABOVE: an amber that is too long is not merely wasteful of capacity but actively harmful.**

> **Drivers learn its duration and begin to enter on amber knowing they will clear, so the interval that was meant as a warning becomes additional green in practice.**

> **The conflicting traffic then starts against a junction that is not yet clear.**

> **So the amber has both a minimum and a maximum — long enough to eliminate the dilemma zone, short enough not to be treated as green — which is another instance of the two-sided criterion that has recurred throughout this material, and the all-red interval exists precisely because one interval cannot satisfy both bounds at a wide junction.**
tags: too long an amber becomes green

examTip.trick: **To clear the dilemma zone** — the band where a driver can neither stop comfortably nor cross before the conflicting green.
examTip.trap: **A short amber CREATES the dilemma zone** — so red-light running and rear-end crashes are often a timing fault, not a behaviour problem.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep amber conventional and add ALL-RED for clearance** — a long amber is learned and treated as extra green.

questions.stem: A road section carries 900 vehicles per hour at an average space mean speed of 45 km/h. The traffic density is:
options: 40,500 veh/km
20 veh/km
45 veh/km
0.05 veh/km
questions.solution:
**20 vehicles per km.**

**From q = k v, rearranged:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **k = q / v** | ← |
| **Substituting** | **k = 900 ÷ 45** ← |
| ** ** | **= 20 veh/km** ← |

> **THE UNITS CONFIRM THE REARRANGEMENT IMMEDIATELY: (veh/h) ÷ (km/h) = veh/km, which is density.**

> **So the division is the right operation and the answer is in the right units.**

> **The distractor at 40,500 is the PRODUCT 900 × 45, which gives veh·km/h² — a quantity with no meaning, and the error of multiplying when the relation required division.**

> **Since q = kv, only one of the three quantities is obtained by multiplication, and the other two by division — so identifying which is being asked for before touching the numbers prevents the error entirely.**

**WHAT A DENSITY OF 20 VEH/KM MEANS PHYSICALLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **20 vehicles spread over one kilometre** ← | ← |
| **So the average SPACING is 1000/20 = 50 m between vehicle fronts** ← | ← |
| **At 45 km/h, or 12.5 m/s, that is a HEADWAY of 50/12.5 = 4 seconds** ← | ← |
| **Which is comfortable, uncongested flow** ← | **A following gap of about 4 s is more than most drivers keep** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW INTRODUCES HEADWAY, WHICH IS THE RECIPROCAL OF FLOW AND IS OFTEN THE MORE INTUITIVE QUANTITY: a flow of 900 veh/h is one vehicle every 3600/900 = 4 seconds.**

> **So the time headway falls directly out of the flow, without needing the speed at all.**

> **And the SPACE headway — the 50 m spacing — is the reciprocal of density.**

> **The three pairs are: flow and time headway, density and space headway, and the speed links them — which is the whole of the fundamental relation expressed in a different vocabulary, and it is worth being fluent in both because different sources use different ones.**

**AND THE RESULT SHOULD BE PLACED AGAINST THE CAPACITY CONDITION, WHICH GIVES IT MEANING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Jam density for a lane is typically around 120 to 150 veh/km** ← | **Vehicles bumper to bumper at about 7 m spacing** ← |
| **Critical density, at capacity, is roughly half of that — 60 to 75 veh/km** ← | ← |
| **So 20 veh/km is well below the critical density** ← | ← |
| **The road is operating in the free-flow region** ← | **Consistent with a speed near free-flow** ← |

> **The fourth row closes the check by confirming internal consistency: a low density and a high speed belong together, and a low density with a low speed would indicate something wrong — an incident, a bottleneck downstream, or a measurement error.**

> **That cross-check is worth making on any traffic data, because the three quantities are not independent and an inconsistent set of three indicates a problem in the data rather than an unusual traffic state.**

> **So a detector reporting 900 veh/h at 15 km/h implies a density of 60 veh/km, which is the congested branch of the fundamental diagram — the same flow, a very different situation, and exactly the ambiguity noted earlier that speed resolves.**
tags: consistency check against the fundamental diagram

examTip.trick: **k = q/v = 900/45 = 20 veh/km.** Units: (veh/h)/(km/h) = veh/km.
examTip.trap: **40,500 is the product** — only one of the three quantities is found by multiplying. Identify which is asked before touching the numbers.
examTip.mnemonic: **Time headway = 3600/q; space headway = 1000/k** — reciprocals of flow and density, and often the more intuitive pair.

questions.stem: A ROAD SAFETY AUDIT is best described as:
options: An investigation carried out after a serious accident to determine its cause
A financial audit of a road project's safety expenditure
An inspection of vehicles to check their roadworthiness
A formal, INDEPENDENT examination of a road scheme
questions.solution:
**A formal, INDEPENDENT examination of a road scheme — at design, pre-opening or in-service stage — by auditors who did not design it**, to identify potential safety hazards BEFORE they cause accidents.

**The defining features:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **PROACTIVE — it precedes accidents rather than following them** ← | **Distinguishing it from black spot investigation** ← |
| **INDEPENDENT — the auditor did not design the scheme** ← | **The essential requirement** ← |
| **FORMAL — a defined procedure, a written report, and a documented response** ← | ← |
| **Focused on SAFETY ONLY** ← | **Not a general design review or a check of compliance with standards** ← |
| **Carried out at defined STAGES** ← | **Feasibility, preliminary design, detailed design, pre-opening, and early operation** ← |

> **THE INDEPENDENCE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE FEATURE THAT MAKES THE PROCESS WORK AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN COMPROMISED: a designer cannot audit their own work effectively.**

> **Not through any dishonesty, but because they see what they intended rather than what they drew, and because the assumptions that produced a hazard are invisible to the person who made them.**

> **A fresh examiner asks 'why is this here' about features the designer has stopped seeing.**

> **So an audit conducted by the design team, or by a colleague in the same office under the same pressures, provides documentation without providing the scrutiny — and where the independence is compromised, the process becomes a formality that consumes effort and finds nothing.**

**THE STAGES AND WHAT EACH CAN STILL CHANGE:**

| Stage | What can be changed | Cost of change |
|---|---|---|
| **FEASIBILITY** ← | **Route, standard, junction strategy — everything** ← | **Negligible** ← |
| **PRELIMINARY design** ← | **Alignment, cross-section, junction layouts** ← | **Low** ← |
| **DETAILED design** ← | **Details, signing, markings, roadside features** ← | **Moderate** ← |
| **PRE-OPENING** ← | **Signs, markings, minor works** ← | **High for anything structural** ← |
| **IN-SERVICE** ← | **Retrofits only** ← | **Highest** ← |

> **THE COST COLUMN IS THE ARGUMENT FOR AUDITING EARLY AND IT IS OVERWHELMING: a junction strategy changed at feasibility stage costs a meeting, and changed after construction costs a reconstruction.**

> **Yet audits are most commonly done at the pre-opening stage, because that is when the scheme is visible and the process is easy to schedule.**

> **An audit at that stage can recommend signs and markings and little else, so it addresses the least significant layer of the safety problem.**

> **The audits that matter most are the early ones, which examine the decisions that determine the scheme's safety, and they are the ones most often omitted because at that stage there is little to look at and the pressure to proceed is greatest.**

**THE RESPONSE PROCEDURE IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE AUDIT AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The auditor reports findings and recommendations** ← | **The auditor does not redesign the scheme** ← |
| **The design team responds formally to each finding** ← | **Accepting it, or stating why it is not accepted** ← |
| **The client decides where the two disagree** ← | ← |
| **Every finding and its resolution is RECORDED** ← | ← |
| **And the record is retained** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE WHAT GIVE THE PROCESS ITS FORCE AND THEY DO SO IN A PARTICULAR WAY: a finding may legitimately be rejected, because the auditor sees only safety and the designer must balance safety against cost, environment and function.**

> **What may not happen is for a finding to be ignored without a reason being recorded.**

> **So the process does not give the auditor authority; it gives the finding visibility, and requires a decision to be taken and owned by someone.**

> **That is a modest-sounding mechanism and it is remarkably effective, because a hazard that someone has had to decide in writing to accept is treated very differently from one nobody has considered.**
tags: recorded decisions give the process force

examTip.trick: **A formal independent examination, BEFORE accidents happen** — by someone who did not design the scheme.
examTip.trap: **Independence is the essential feature** — a designer sees what they intended, not what they drew. A self-audit documents without scrutinising.
examTip.mnemonic: **Audit early — that is where decisions can still change cheaply** — yet most audits happen pre-opening, when only signs remain adjustable.

questions.stem: Road markings are an essential part of traffic control. A CONTINUOUS (solid) white centre line indicates that:
options: Overtaking is PROHIBITED
The road is a one-way street
Parking is permitted on both sides
The road ahead narrows
questions.solution:
**Overtaking is PROHIBITED — drivers must not cross the line**, because the available sight distance is insufficient for a safe overtaking manoeuvre.

**The centre line markings and their meanings:**

| Marking | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **BROKEN line, short marks with long gaps** ← | **Centre line — crossing permitted with care** ← |
| **BROKEN line, long marks with short gaps** ← | **Warning line — a hazard ahead; crossing permitted but discouraged** ← |
| **CONTINUOUS single line** ← | **No crossing — overtaking prohibited** ← |
| **DOUBLE continuous lines** ← | **No crossing from either direction** ← |
| **One continuous and one broken** ← | **Crossing permitted from the BROKEN side only** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS AN ELEGANT AND USEFUL ARRANGEMENT THAT IS FREQUENTLY MISREAD: where the sight distance is adequate in one direction and not in the other — which happens constantly on a crest or a bend — the marking can permit overtaking one way and forbid it the other.**

> **The rule is simple: a driver may cross if the line NEARER to them is broken.**

> **So the same length of road allows overtaking for uphill traffic, say, and forbids it for downhill traffic, which reflects the asymmetric sight lines exactly.**

> **Using a double continuous line where a combination would serve imposes an unnecessary restriction, and drivers who can see the road is clear will ignore it — which returns to the credibility problem noted with signs.**

**THE SECOND ROW'S WARNING LINE DESERVES ATTENTION BECAUSE IT IS SO OFTEN OMITTED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A warning line precedes a continuous line** ← | ← |
| **It tells the driver that the no-overtaking section is approaching** ← | ← |
| **So a driver already overtaking can complete or abandon the manoeuvre in time** ← | ← |
| **Without it, the continuous line begins abruptly** ← | ← |
| **And a driver mid-overtake is committed with no warning** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE HAZARD THAT THE WARNING LINE EXISTS TO PREVENT AND IT IS A REAL ONE: overtaking takes several seconds, and a driver who begins one just before an unmarked transition arrives in the no-overtaking section mid-manoeuvre.**

> **The warning line gives them the information in advance, so the decision to start is an informed one.**

> **Its omission is common because it appears to be merely a lead-in to the real marking, and it is in fact the marking that influences the decision — the continuous line only records a decision that was effectively made earlier.**

**AND THE OTHER CATEGORIES OF MARKING ARE WORTH LISTING FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| **LONGITUDINAL** ← | **Centre lines, lane lines, edge lines, no-overtaking lines** ← |
| **TRANSVERSE** ← | **Stop lines, give-way lines, pedestrian crossings, rumble markings** ← |
| **HAZARD markings** ← | **Obstruction approach markings, chevrons, diagonal hatching** ← |
| **WORD and SYMBOL markings** ← | **STOP, SLOW, arrows, cycle symbols, speed roundels** ← |
| **OBJECT and KERB markings** ← | **On islands, bridge piers, culvert headwalls** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S EDGE LINE, GROUPED UNDER LONGITUDINAL ABOVE, DESERVES A SPECIFIC MENTION BECAUSE ITS SAFETY VALUE IS OUT OF PROPORTION TO ITS COST: an edge line defines the carriageway's boundary, which matters most at night, in rain and in fog when the road's edge is otherwise invisible.**

> **On an unlit rural road with no kerb, the edge line is the only thing telling the driver where the road stops.**

> **Studies consistently show edge lining reducing run-off-road crashes substantially, and it is among the cheapest treatments available.**

> **On Nepal's hill roads, where the road's edge is frequently the top of a steep drop, its value is greater still — and combining it with an edge-line rumble strip addresses the same crash type with two layers, which is the redundancy principle applied at very low cost.**

Drivers must not cross the line, because the available sight distance is insufficient for a safe overtaking manoeuvre.
tags: combination line permits from the broken side

examTip.trick: **No crossing — overtaking prohibited** because sight distance is inadequate.
examTip.trap: **With one continuous and one broken line, cross only if the NEARER line is broken** — allowing overtaking one way and forbidding it the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **The WARNING line does the real work** — it informs the decision to start overtaking; the continuous line only records it.

questions.stem: TRAFFIC CALMING measures in a residential or settlement area work primarily by:
options: Increasing the width of the carriageway so vehicles can pass freely
Installing more traffic signals
Prohibiting all vehicular access
Physically and visually altering the street so that LOWER SPEEDS feel natural and appropriate to the driver
questions.solution:
**Physically and visually altering the street so that LOWER SPEEDS feel natural and appropriate to the driver** — through vertical and horizontal deflection, narrowing, surface changes and visual enclosure — rather than relying on signs and enforcement alone.

**The main measures, grouped by mechanism:**

| Mechanism | Measures |
|---|---|
| **VERTICAL deflection** ← | **Speed humps, speed tables, raised junctions, raised crossings, rumble areas** ← |
| **HORIZONTAL deflection** ← | **Chicanes, build-outs, central islands, mini-roundabouts** ← |
| **NARROWING** ← | **Kerb extensions, reduced lane width, pinch points, gateways at the settlement entry** ← |
| **SURFACE and VISUAL change** ← | **Different paving texture and colour, planting, street furniture, visual enclosure** ← |
| **NETWORK measures** ← | **Road closures, one-way loops, restricting through movement entirely** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE GROUP THAT IS MOST UNDERUSED AND IT WORKS THROUGH PERCEPTION RATHER THAN PHYSICS: drivers choose speed largely from what the street LOOKS like.**

> **A wide, straight, open carriageway reads as a road for driving, and drivers drive.**

> **The same width enclosed by trees, narrowed visually by planting and parking, with a change of surface and buildings close to the edge, reads as a place where people are — and speeds fall without any physical obstacle at all.**

> **So visual treatment achieves what signs cannot, because it operates on the driver's automatic speed choice rather than on their conscious compliance, and a self-enforcing street needs no enforcement.**

**THE GATEWAY TREATMENT DESERVES SPECIFIC MENTION FOR NEPAL'S HIGHWAY SETTLEMENTS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A highway passing through a settlement is the classic conflict** ← | **Mobility function and access function in the same space** ← |
| **Drivers arrive at highway speed and do not perceive the change** ← | ← |
| **A GATEWAY at each end marks the transition emphatically** ← | **Narrowing, a change of surface, signing, planting, a physical island** ← |
| **It tells the driver they have ENTERED somewhere different** ← | ← |
| **And speeds through the settlement fall accordingly** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PSYCHOLOGICAL MECHANISM AND IT IS WHY A GATEWAY WORKS BETTER THAN A SPEED LIMIT SIGN ALONE: a sign informs, and a gateway changes the driver's mental model of where they are.**

> **A driver who believes they are still on the highway drives at highway speed whatever the sign says.**

> **One who perceives they have entered a village drives accordingly, because that is what people do in villages.**

> **Given how many of Nepal's road deaths occur where highways pass through settlements, gateway treatment is one of the highest-value safety investments available — and it is inexpensive relative to almost any other engineering measure.**

**THE OBJECTIONS TO TRAFFIC CALMING ARE REAL AND DESERVE HONEST TREATMENT:**

| Objection | Response |
|---|---|
| **Delays EMERGENCY vehicles** ← | **Genuine. Speed tables and cushions delay them far less than humps; routes should be agreed with the services** ← |
| **Damages vehicles and is uncomfortable** ← | **Only if badly designed or badly built — profile and height must follow the standard** ← |
| **Increases noise and emissions from braking and accelerating** ← | **Real for humps; much less for measures producing a steady lower speed** ← |
| **Displaces traffic to other streets** ← | **A network effect that must be anticipated, not a reason not to act** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST SERIOUS OBJECTION AND IT HAS A GOOD TECHNICAL ANSWER: a speed CUSHION is narrower than the lane, so a wide-track vehicle — a fire appliance or an ambulance — straddles it while a car must ride over it.**

> **So the measure slows cars and barely affects emergency vehicles, which resolves the conflict rather than trading it off.**

> **Speed TABLES, being long and flat-topped, are also far gentler for a large vehicle than a short round hump.**

> **So the objection argues for choosing the right measure rather than against calming as such — and designing the scheme with the emergency services at the table, rather than presenting it to them afterwards, is what turns a likely objection into a workable agreement.**

examTip.trick: **Make lower speeds feel natural** — deflection, narrowing, surface change and visual enclosure, not signs and enforcement.
examTip.trap: **Visual treatment works on automatic speed choice** — a street that looks like a place, not a road, is self-enforcing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Speed CUSHIONS let emergency vehicles straddle them** — slowing cars while barely delaying a fire appliance. Resolves the objection rather than trading it.

questions.stem: In accident analysis, the ACCIDENT RATE expressed per 100 million vehicle-kilometres is preferred to the simple accident COUNT because it:
options: Is easier to calculate from available records
Always produces a smaller and more acceptable number
Normalises for EXPOSURE
Is required by international convention for reporting purposes only
questions.solution:
**It normalises for EXPOSURE** — allowing roads carrying very different traffic volumes and of different lengths to be compared fairly, since a busy road will have more accidents than a quiet one simply by carrying more traffic.

**The measures and what each is for:**

| Measure | Formula | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Accident COUNT** ← | **Number of accidents** ← | **Total burden; resource planning** ← |
| **Accident RATE per vehicle-km** ← | **A × 10⁸ / (365 × AADT × L × years)** ← | **Comparing road SECTIONS of different volume and length** ← |
| **Accident rate per million entering vehicles** ← | **A × 10⁶ / (365 × entering vehicles × years)** ← | **Comparing JUNCTIONS** ← |
| **Accidents per km per year** ← | **A / (L × years)** ← | **Identifying concentrations along a route** ← |
| **Deaths per 100,000 population** ← | ← | **Comparing COUNTRIES and national performance** ← |

> **CHOOSING THE RIGHT MEASURE FOR THE QUESTION BEING ASKED IS THE SKILL HERE AND USING THE WRONG ONE PRODUCES CONFIDENT NONSENSE: a rate per vehicle-kilometre compares how dangerous a road is PER UNIT OF TRAVEL, and a count tells you how many people are being hurt.**

> **A rural road with a very high rate and very little traffic may injure fewer people than an urban road with a low rate and enormous traffic.**

> **So the rate identifies where the road is deficient and the count identifies where the harm is.**

> **Both matter and they point to different places, which is why a safety programme uses the rate to find defective sites and the count to allocate the budget between them.**

**THE FORMULA'S STRUCTURE IS WORTH SETTING OUT SINCE THE ARITHMETIC IS EASY TO GET WRONG:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vehicle-kilometres per year = AADT × 365 × length in km** ← | ← |
| **Over n years, multiply by n** ← | ← |
| **Accident rate = accidents × 10⁸ ÷ that total** ← | **The 10⁸ scales it to a readable number** ← |
| **A worked case: 12 accidents in 3 years on 5 km with AADT 4,000** ← | ← |
| **Vehicle-km = 4,000 × 365 × 5 × 3 = 21.9 million** ← | ← |
| **Rate = 12 × 10⁸ ÷ 21.9 × 10⁶ = 54.8 per 100 million veh-km** ← | ← |

> **THE 10⁸ MULTIPLIER EXISTS ONLY TO MAKE THE NUMBER CONVENIENT AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING AS SUCH: the raw rate would be 0.000000548 accidents per vehicle-kilometre, which is unreadable and invites arithmetic slips.**

> **Scaling by 100 million produces a figure in the tens, which can be held in mind and compared.**

> **So the unit is chosen for human convenience rather than for any physical reason, and one must be careful when comparing figures from different sources that both use the same scaling — per 100 million and per million vehicle-kilometres differ by a factor of a hundred, and both are in use.**

> **THE LAST ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE POINTS TO THE MEASURE USED FOR NATIONAL COMPARISON AND IT DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE NEPAL'S POSITION IS SOBERING: deaths per 100,000 population is the standard international measure, and low- and middle-income countries carry a share of global road deaths far exceeding their share of vehicles.**

> **The reasons are structural — mixed traffic, vulnerable road users sharing space with fast vehicles, older vehicles, limited trauma care, and roads built for mobility running through places where people live.**

> **Each of those is addressable, and the engineering measures in this subchapter address several of them directly.**

> **So the gap between countries is not a fact about their populations but about their road systems, which is an encouraging conclusion because road systems can be changed.**
tags: rate finds defects count finds harm

examTip.trick: **It normalises for exposure** — a busy road has more accidents simply by carrying more traffic.
examTip.trap: **Rate finds the defective site; COUNT finds where the harm is** — they point to different places, and a programme needs both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Veh-km = AADT × 365 × L × years, then × 10⁸/that** — and check whether a quoted rate is per million or per hundred million.

questions.stem: The fundamental difference between a FLEXIBLE and a RIGID pavement is that:
options: A flexible pavement transmits the wheel load to the subgrade through GRAIN-TO-GRAIN contact
A flexible pavement is thinner than a rigid one in every case
A rigid pavement contains no reinforcement
A flexible pavement can only be used on a strong subgrade
questions.solution:
**A flexible pavement transmits the wheel load to the subgrade through GRAIN-TO-GRAIN contact, spreading it progressively over a widening area with depth** — whereas a rigid pavement's slab acts in BENDING and distributes the load over a wide area by its own flexural rigidity.

**The two load-spreading mechanisms:**

| Aspect | FLEXIBLE | RIGID |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transfer** | **Grain to grain, layer by layer** ← | **Slab bending — the concrete carries it in flexure** ← |
| **Load spread** | **A cone widening with depth; high stress at the surface, low at the subgrade** ← | **Spread very widely by the slab itself** ← |
| **Strength comes from** | **The COMBINED thickness and quality of all the layers** ← | **Mostly the SLAB's flexural strength** ← |
| **Subgrade role** | **Critical — it carries the spread load and its strength governs the design** ← | **Less critical — a poor subgrade increases slab stresses but the slab dominates** ← |
| **Deflection** | **Deforms with the subgrade — a settlement shows through to the surface** ← | **Bridges over local weak spots** ← |
| **Design criterion** | **Subgrade strain and bituminous layer strain** ← | **Flexural stress in the slab** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN A PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE THAT IS OFTEN DECISIVE: a rigid pavement can bridge a local soft spot and a flexible one cannot.**

> **A flexible pavement is a stack of granular and bituminous layers that follows whatever the subgrade does beneath it, so a soft patch produces a depression at the surface.**

> **A concrete slab spans across it, and the only consequence is a higher bending stress in the slab at that point.**

> **So rigid pavements tolerate variable subgrades better, which is one argument for using them over made ground, over old fill, or where the subgrade is known to be inconsistent — though the slab must be designed for the increased stress rather than merely relied upon.**

**THE ECONOMIC AND PRACTICAL COMPARISON:**

| Factor | FLEXIBLE | RIGID |
|---|---|---|
| **Initial cost** | **Lower** ← | **Higher** ← |
| **Design life** | **10 to 20 years to overlay** ← | **30 to 40 years** ← |
| **Maintenance** | **Frequent — patching, sealing, overlays** ← | **Infrequent but specialised — joint sealing, slab replacement** ← |
| **Staged construction** | **EASY — layers can be added later** ← | **Not practical** ← |
| **Utility openings** | **Easy to cut and reinstate** ← | **Difficult and the reinstatement is never as good** ← |
| **Opening to traffic** | **Immediate** ← | **After curing — days to weeks** ← |
| **Suits** | **Most roads; staged development; areas needing frequent access** ← | **Heavy slow traffic, junctions, bus stops, toll plazas, flood-prone sections** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW'S LIST FOR RIGID PAVEMENTS SHARES A COMMON THREAD WORTH NAMING: all are places where flexible pavements fail early.**

> **Heavy slow-moving or stationary traffic ruts a bituminous surface, because the load is applied for longer and bitumen is viscous — which is why bus stops and toll plazas deform.**

> **Junctions suffer the same from braking and turning shear.**

> **And flood-prone sections destroy bituminous pavements through saturation and stripping, while concrete tolerates inundation well.**

> **So the rigid pavement is used selectively at these locations even on a road that is otherwise flexible, which is a sensible hybrid strategy and is common practice on Nepal's highways where they pass through towns and bus stopping places.**

> **A THIRD CATEGORY DESERVES MENTION SINCE IT IS INCREASINGLY USED: the SEMI-RIGID pavement, in which a cement-stabilised or cement-bound base lies beneath a bituminous surfacing.**

> **It behaves between the two — the bound base spreads load far better than a granular one, allowing a thinner total pavement, while the bituminous surface gives a good riding quality and easy maintenance.**

> **Its characteristic weakness is REFLECTION CRACKING: the bound base cracks from shrinkage and thermal movement, and those cracks propagate up through the bituminous layer.**

> **So it requires either a crack-relief interlayer, a sufficiently thick bituminous cover, or deliberate pre-cracking of the base at controlled spacings — and a semi-rigid pavement built without addressing reflection cracking will show a regular pattern of transverse cracks within a few years, which is diagnostic of exactly this omission.**
tags: grain to grain versus slab bending
selective rigid use at junctions and bus stops

examTip.trick: **Flexible spreads grain to grain in a widening cone; rigid carries load in slab BENDING.**
examTip.trap: **A rigid slab bridges a local soft spot; a flexible pavement follows the subgrade down** — which is why rigid suits variable ground.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use rigid selectively at bus stops, junctions, toll plazas and flood reaches** — all places where slow, stationary or wet conditions destroy bitumen.

questions.stem: The EQUIVALENT SINGLE AXLE LOAD (ESAL) concept converts a mixed axle load spectrum into a number of standard axles using the FOURTH POWER LAW, which states that the damage caused by an axle is proportional to:
options: The axle load itself, in direct proportion
The SQUARE of the ratio of the axle load to the standard axle load
The FOURTH POWER of the ratio of the axle load to the standard axle load
The number of tyres on the axle
questions.solution:
**The FOURTH POWER of the ratio of the axle load to the standard axle load** — so an axle twice the standard load does sixteen times the damage.

**The relation and what it implies:**

| Element | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Damage factor** | **F = (L / L_std)⁴** ← |
| **Standard axle** | **80 kN (8.16 tonnes) in most systems; 8,170 kg in the Indian and Nepali convention** ← |
| **An axle at 1.5 × standard** | **1.5⁴ = 5.06 — five times the damage** ← |
| **An axle at 2 × standard** | **2⁴ = 16 — sixteen times** ← |
| **An axle at 3 × standard** | **3⁴ = 81 — eighty-one times** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE WHERE THE LAW'S PRACTICAL FORCE LIES AND THE NUMBERS DESERVE TO BE FELT RATHER THAN MERELY READ: overloading is catastrophically damaging, not merely proportionally so.**

> **A truck carrying 50 per cent more than its legal axle load does five times the pavement damage of a legally loaded one, not 1.5 times.**

> **So a small proportion of overloaded vehicles can account for most of a pavement's damage.**

> **If 10 per cent of trucks are loaded to twice the legal axle limit, those 10 per cent do more damage than the other 90 per cent combined — which reframes axle load enforcement from a regulatory nicety into the single most effective pavement preservation measure available.**

**THE CONSEQUENCES FOR DESIGN AND POLICY ARE WORTH SETTING OUT:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **CARS are irrelevant to pavement design** ← | **A car axle at 10 kN gives (10/80)⁴ = 0.00024 — effectively zero** ← |
| **The design traffic is essentially the COMMERCIAL vehicle traffic** ← | ← |
| **An accurate axle load survey matters more than an accurate vehicle count** ← | ← |
| **Enforcement of axle limits protects the pavement more than extra thickness does** ← | ← |
| **And a weighbridge is a cheaper pavement investment than an overlay** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IT IS EXACTLY RIGHT: a passenger car does about one ten-thousandth of the damage of a standard axle, so a million cars do less damage than a hundred trucks.**

> **This is why pavement design considers only commercial vehicles and ignores cars entirely.**

> **It also means that traffic growth in cars, however dramatic, has almost no effect on pavement life — while a modest growth in heavy vehicles has a large one.**

> **So a pavement design's sensitivity lies entirely in the commercial vehicle forecast and the axle load assumption, and effort spent refining the total traffic count while guessing the axle loads has been misallocated.**

> **THE FOURTH POWER LAW'S ORIGIN AND LIMITS DESERVE AN HONEST NOTE: it derives from the AASHO Road Test of the late 1950s, an empirical study on particular pavements in a particular climate.**

> **The exponent is not a physical constant — it varies with the pavement type, the failure mode and the layer considered, and values from about 2 to 6 are reported in different studies.**

> **Rigid pavements, where the failure is flexural fatigue of the slab, show a considerably higher exponent than four.**

> **So the fourth power is a useful and widely adopted convention rather than a law of nature, and where the axle spectrum is extreme, the sensitivity of the result to the exponent chosen should be checked — because at high load ratios, the difference between an exponent of 4 and one of 5 changes the answer by a very large factor.**
tags: cars are irrelevant to pavement design

examTip.trick: **F = (L/L_std)⁴** — twice the load, sixteen times the damage. Standard axle 80 kN.
examTip.trap: **A car does about 0.0002 standard axles** — pavement design ignores cars entirely and depends only on commercial vehicles.
examTip.mnemonic: **A weighbridge is cheaper than an overlay** — 10% of trucks at double the limit out-damage the other 90% combined.

questions.stem: In a rigid pavement, CONTRACTION JOINTS are provided to:
options: Allow the slab to be constructed in convenient widths
Provide drainage paths through the slab
Allow the slab to expand in hot weather
Control the location of the CRACKS that shrinkage and thermal contraction will inevitably produce
questions.solution:
**To control the location of the CRACKS that shrinkage and thermal contraction will inevitably produce** — by creating a plane of weakness at which the slab cracks in a straight, sealed, load-transferring line rather than randomly.

**The joint types in a concrete pavement:**

| Joint | Purpose | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTRACTION (transverse)** ← | **Control shrinkage and thermal contraction cracking** ← | **A sawn or formed groove, typically a quarter to a third of the slab depth; DOWEL bars for load transfer** ← |
| **EXPANSION** ← | **Accommodate thermal expansion** ← | **A full-depth gap with a compressible filler; dowels with one end free to slide in a cap** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL** ← | **Control cracking along the pavement; separate construction lanes** ← | **TIE bars, which hold the slabs together rather than allowing movement** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION** ← | **Where a day's work ends** ← | **Located at a planned joint position wherever possible** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN DOWEL BARS AND TIE BARS IN THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS IS A COMMON EXAMINATION POINT AND THEIR PURPOSES ARE OPPOSITE: a DOWEL transfers load across a joint while ALLOWING the slabs to move apart.**

> **So it is smooth, it is coated or greased over half its length, and it slides.**

> **A TIE BAR HOLDS two slabs together and PREVENTS them separating.**

> **So it is deformed, it is fully bonded, and it does not slide — and confusing the two produces either a contraction joint that cannot open, which cracks elsewhere, or a longitudinal joint that opens progressively, which is how a lane separates from its neighbour.**

**THE CONTRACTION JOINT'S OPERATING PRINCIPLE IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY BECAUSE IT IS SLIGHTLY COUNTER-INTUITIVE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concrete WILL crack from shrinkage and thermal contraction** ← | **This cannot be prevented** ← |
| **An uncontrolled crack is ragged, unsealed and has no load transfer** ← | ← |
| **Water enters it, the subgrade below is eroded, and the slab edges spall and rock** ← | ← |
| **A contraction joint concentrates the crack at a chosen place** ← | **By reducing the section so the tension is relieved there first** ← |
| **Where it can be sealed, dowelled and maintained** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MECHANISM AND THE TIMING OF THE SAW CUT IS CRITICAL TO IT: the groove must be cut before the concrete develops enough tensile strength to crack on its own.**

> **Cut too early and the saw ravels the green concrete; too late and the slab has already cracked somewhere else, and the joint is then pointless.**

> **The window is typically 4 to 12 hours after placing, depending on the temperature, and it narrows in hot weather.**

> **So concrete paving requires the sawing crew to work through the night behind the paver, and a sawing operation that falls behind produces random cracking that no subsequent work can undo — which is why saw timing is one of the most carefully managed operations on a concrete paving job.**

> **THE EXPANSION JOINT IN THE SECOND ROW DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE PRACTICE HAS CHANGED: expansion joints were once provided routinely at regular intervals, and modern practice largely omits them in plain jointed concrete pavements.**

> **The reason is that the contraction joints, once open, provide ample room to accommodate expansion — a pavement that has contracted has joints that can close again.**

> **Expansion joints are also weak points: they are wide, their filler deteriorates, they accumulate incompressible material, and they suffer more faulting than contraction joints.**

> **So they are now used only where genuinely needed — at structures, at junctions with existing pavements, and at sharp changes in alignment — and omitting them elsewhere gives a better pavement rather than a compromised one.**

examTip.trick: **Control WHERE the inevitable shrinkage crack forms** — a sealed, dowelled, straight crack instead of a random ragged one.
examTip.trap: **DOWELS are smooth and slide (transfer load, allow movement); TIE bars are deformed and bonded (prevent separation)** — opposite purposes.
examTip.mnemonic: **The saw cut window is 4-12 hours and narrows in heat** — too late and the slab has cracked elsewhere, making the joint pointless.

questions.stem: The BENKELMAN BEAM is used on flexible pavements to:
options: Measure the rebound DEFLECTION of the pavement surface under a standard wheel load
Measure the thickness of each pavement layer
Measure the roughness of the riding surface
Determine the bitumen content of the surfacing
questions.solution:
**Measure the rebound DEFLECTION of the pavement surface under a standard wheel load** — from which the pavement's structural adequacy is assessed and the thickness of any required overlay is determined.

**How the test works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A loaded truck with a standard rear axle load is positioned over the test point** ← | **8.17 tonnes on dual wheels at a specified tyre pressure** ← |
| **The beam's probe is inserted between the dual tyres, resting on the pavement** ← | ← |
| **The initial dial reading is taken** ← | ← |
| **The truck is driven slowly forward** ← | ← |
| **The pavement REBOUNDS as the load moves away, and the final reading is taken** ← | ← |
| **The difference, corrected for temperature and seasonal moisture, is the rebound deflection** ← | ← |

> **THE CORRECTIONS IN THE LAST ROW ARE ESSENTIAL AND OMITTING THEM MAKES THE RESULT MEANINGLESS: a bituminous pavement is far more flexible when hot, so a deflection measured at midday in May is much larger than the same pavement's deflection in January.**

> **And the subgrade is weaker when wet, so the deflection after the monsoon exceeds that in the dry season.**

> **The design deflection is the one representing the pavement's WEAKEST condition, so measurements are corrected to a standard temperature of 35 °C and to the most critical moisture condition.**

> **A survey conducted in the dry season and used uncorrected will judge a marginal pavement adequate, and the overlay designed from it will be too thin.**

**WHAT THE DEFLECTION MEANS:**

| Point | Note |
