|---|---|
| **A LARGE deflection means a WEAK pavement** ← | **It bends more under the same load** ← |
| **Deflection reflects the whole pavement-subgrade system, not any one layer** ← | ← |
| **The characteristic deflection is computed statistically from many points** ← | **Mean plus one or two standard deviations, depending on the road's importance** ← |
| **Overlay thickness is read from design curves relating deflection to the required overlay** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS BOTH THE METHOD'S STRENGTH AND ITS LIMITATION AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT: a single deflection number summarises the entire structure's response.**

> **That is convenient — one measurement characterises the pavement — and it is uninformative about WHERE the weakness lies.**

> **A high deflection might mean a weak subgrade, a thin base, a deteriorated bituminous layer, or all three, and the overlay design treats them identically by adding material on top.**

> **Where the weakness is in the subgrade, an overlay is the right response; where it is a debonded or cracked bituminous layer, adding more material over the fault treats the symptom and the fault propagates upward through the new work.**

> **THE FALLING WEIGHT DEFLECTOMETER SUPERSEDES THE BEAM PRECISELY ON THIS POINT AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING WHY: an FWD drops a weight onto a plate and measures the deflection at SEVERAL radial distances, producing a deflection BOWL rather than a single value.**

> **The bowl's shape carries information the single value cannot: deflections far from the load reflect the deep layers and the subgrade, and those close to the load reflect the upper layers.**

> **So an FWD survey can BACK-CALCULATE the stiffness of each layer separately, identifying which one is deficient.**

> **That turns a pavement evaluation from 'this section is weak' into 'this section has a sound base and a failed subgrade' — a diagnosis rather than a measurement, and the difference determines whether the treatment chosen will work.**
tags: single value cannot locate the weakness

examTip.trick: **Rebound deflection under a standard wheel load** — from which overlay thickness is read off design curves.
examTip.trap: **Correct for temperature and season** — an uncorrected dry-season measurement judges a marginal pavement adequate and gives too thin an overlay.
examTip.mnemonic: **The beam gives one number; the FWD gives a deflection BOWL** — and the bowl's shape back-calculates each layer's stiffness separately.

questions.stem: A road carries 300 commercial vehicles per day in the design lane, with a vehicle damage factor of 2.5 standard axles per vehicle, growing at 6 per cent per year over a 15-year design life. The cumulative standard axles (CSA) is approximately:
options: 1.64 million
4.11 million
6.37 million
0.41 million
questions.solution:
**About 6.37 million standard axles.**

**Using the standard cumulative traffic formula:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **N = 365 × A × D × F × [(1+r)ⁿ − 1] / r** | **With A the initial CVPD, F the vehicle damage factor** ← |
| **Growth factor** | **[(1.06)¹⁵ − 1] / 0.06** ← |
| ** ** | **1.06¹⁵ = 2.3966** ← |
| ** ** | **(2.3966 − 1) / 0.06 = 1.3966 / 0.06 = 23.28** ← |
| **Substituting** | **N = 365 × 300 × 2.5 × 23.28** ← |
| ** ** | **365 × 300 = 109,500** ← |
| ** ** | **109,500 × 2.5 = 273,750** ← |
| ** ** | **273,750 × 23.28 = 6,373,000** ← |
| **So** | **CSA ≈ 6.37 million** ← |

> **THE GROWTH FACTOR OF 23.28 IS THE HEART OF THE CALCULATION AND IT IS WORTH INTERPRETING: it is the number of 'first-year equivalents' of traffic accumulated over the fifteen years.**

> **Without growth it would be simply 15.**

> **With 6 per cent growth it is 23.28, so the growth adds more than half again to the total.**

> **That is the compounding at work over the design life, and it is why the growth rate assumption matters so much — at 8 per cent the factor would be 27.2, and at 4 per cent it would be 20.0, a spread of a third around the middle value.**

**THE DISTRACTORS EACH CORRESPOND TO A SPECIFIC OMISSION AND NAMING THEM IS INSTRUCTIVE:**

| Option | The error |
|---|---|
| **4.11 million** | **Using n = 15 directly instead of the growth factor 23.28 — that is, ignoring growth** ← |
| **1.64 million** | **Omitting the vehicle damage factor as well** ← |
| **0.41 million** | **A further order-of-magnitude slip** ← |
| **6.37 million** | **Correct** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE COMMONEST OMISSION AND IT UNDERSTATES THE DESIGN TRAFFIC BY A THIRD, which on a pavement design translates directly into an under-thickness.**

> **Since pavement thickness responds to CSA roughly logarithmically, a 35 per cent understatement of traffic does not produce a 35 per cent thickness error — but it produces enough to shorten the pavement's life materially.**

> **The check is to notice that the growth factor must EXCEED the number of years whenever growth is positive, so any factor of 15 or less for a 15-year life with growth is wrong on inspection.**

> **That single observation catches the error without any recomputation.**

**THE LANE DISTRIBUTION FACTOR D DESERVES A NOTE SINCE THE QUESTION FOLDED IT AWAY:**

| Road type | Lane distribution factor |
|---|---|
| **Single lane** ← | **1.0 — all traffic in the one lane** ← |
| **Two-lane single carriageway** ← | **0.75 of the two-way commercial traffic in the design lane** ← |
| **Four-lane single carriageway** ← | **0.40** ← |
| **Dual two-lane carriageway** ← | **0.75 of the traffic in each direction** ← |

> **The second row is the case most commonly encountered and it is worth being careful with: the factor applies to the TWO-WAY commercial vehicle count.**

> **So a two-lane road carrying 400 commercial vehicles per day in both directions has 400 × 0.75 = 300 in the design lane, which is the figure this question supplied directly.**

> **Applying the factor to a one-way count, or applying it twice, are both common errors and both change the answer substantially.**

> **So the first step in any CSA calculation should be to establish exactly what the quoted traffic figure represents — two-way or directional, total or commercial, and whether any factor has already been applied — because the arithmetic afterwards is trivial and the interpretation is where the mistakes live.**
tags: growth factor must exceed the years

examTip.trap: **4.11 million uses n = 15 instead of the growth factor** — and the growth factor must always EXCEED the number of years when growth is positive.
examTip.mnemonic: **Establish what the traffic figure MEANS first** — two-way or directional, total or commercial, factor applied or not. The arithmetic is the easy part.

questions.stem: RUTTING in a flexible pavement appears as longitudinal depressions in the wheel paths. When the rutting occurs WITHIN the bituminous layer rather than in the subgrade, the likely cause is:
options: An inadequately thick subgrade
Excessive traffic volume of light vehicles
Poor drainage of the shoulders only
An unstable MIX
questions.solution:
**An unstable MIX — too much bitumen, too soft a binder for the climate, excessive rounded fine aggregate, or inadequate compaction** — allowing the mix to deform plastically under repeated loading, particularly in hot weather and at slow-moving locations.

**Distinguishing the two rutting mechanisms is the diagnostic task:**

| Feature | STRUCTURAL rutting (subgrade or base) | MIX rutting (bituminous layer) |
|---|---|---|
| **Shape** | **A broad, shallow depression across the whole pavement width** ← | **A narrow rut in the wheel path with HEAVING at its edges** ← |
| **The heave** | **Absent — the material has consolidated** ← | **PRESENT — the mix has flowed sideways, so what left the rut appears beside it** ← |
| **Cause** | **Inadequate pavement thickness for the traffic and subgrade** ← | **Unstable mix** ← |
| **Depth of deformation** | **Deep — in the subgrade or lower layers** ← | **Confined to the upper bituminous layers** ← |
| **Remedy** | **Strengthening — an overlay or reconstruction** ← | **Remove and replace the deficient layer; an overlay will simply rut too** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE FIELD DIAGNOSTIC AND IT REQUIRES ONLY A STRAIGHTEDGE: if the material displaced from the rut has appeared as ridges alongside it, the mix has flowed and the problem is in the bituminous layer.**

> **If the surface has simply sunk with no heave, the material beneath has consolidated or the subgrade has deformed.**

> **That distinction is visible on site and it determines the entire treatment.**

> **The fifth row states why it matters so much: overlaying a mix-rutting problem places new material over an unstable layer that will continue to flow, so the rut reappears through the overlay within a season or two — and the money is wasted entirely.**

**THE CAUSES OF MIX RUTTING AND THEIR REMEDIES:**

| Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **Excess BITUMEN** ← | **Reduce the binder content; check the mix design and the plant's calibration** ← |
| **Binder too SOFT for the climate** ← | **Use a harder penetration grade, or a modified binder** ← |
| **Too much rounded natural sand in the fine fraction** ← | **Use crushed fines, which interlock** ← |
| **Inadequate compaction at construction** ← | **The mix densifies under traffic instead, which appears as rutting** ← |
| **Insufficient coarse aggregate skeleton** ← | **Redesign the grading, or use a stone mastic asphalt** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN IMPORTANT AND UNDER-RECOGNISED CAUSE AND IT IS PURELY A CONSTRUCTION FAULT: a mix laid at 92 per cent of its achievable density will be compacted by traffic to perhaps 96 per cent over the following year.**

> **That densification appears at the surface as a rut in the wheel paths, and it is often mistaken for a mix instability problem.**

> **The mix may be entirely sound; it was simply not compacted.**

> **So a rut appearing within the first year, in the wheel paths, without edge heaving, is characteristically a compaction deficiency rather than a mix design fault — and distinguishing it matters because the remedy is to enforce compaction on future work rather than to redesign a mix that was correct.**

> **THE THIRD ROW DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS A COMMON PROBLEM WHERE RIVER SAND IS PLENTIFUL: rounded natural sand particles roll over one another under load, giving the mix very little internal friction.**

> **Crushed fines, being angular, interlock and resist shear.**

> **A mix with a high proportion of rounded sand can meet its grading specification exactly and still be unstable, because the grading curve says nothing about particle shape.**

> **So a specification limiting the proportion of natural sand, or requiring a minimum proportion of crushed fines, is doing work that the grading requirement cannot do — and its omission is a plausible cause whenever a mix that appears correct on paper ruts in service.**

examTip.trick: **An unstable mix flowing plastically** — excess binder, too soft a grade, rounded fines, or poor compaction.
examTip.trap: **HEAVE beside the rut means the mix flowed; no heave means the structure sank** — a straightedge on site settles the diagnosis.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never overlay a mix-rutting problem** — the unstable layer keeps flowing and the rut reappears through the new work.

questions.stem: ALLIGATOR (fatigue) CRACKING in a flexible pavement is characterised by interconnected cracks forming a pattern of small polygons in the wheel paths. Its fundamental cause is:
options: Shrinkage of the bituminous binder in cold weather
Repeated flexing under traffic causing FATIGUE failure of the bituminous layer
Chemical attack on the bitumen by de-icing salts
Excessive camber causing the surface to spread
questions.solution:
**Repeated flexing under traffic causing FATIGUE failure of the bituminous layer, which begins as tensile cracking at the BOTTOM of the layer and propagates upward** — indicating that the pavement is structurally inadequate for the traffic it carries.

**The mechanism, step by step:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Each wheel passage bends the bituminous layer** ← | ← |
| **The BOTTOM of the layer goes into TENSION as it bends over the softer layers below** ← | ← |
| **Bitumen-bound material has limited fatigue resistance in tension** ← | ← |
| **After enough repetitions, a crack initiates at the bottom** ← | ← |
| **It propagates UPWARD, eventually reaching the surface** ← | ← |
| **Adjacent cracks interconnect, forming the characteristic polygon pattern** ← | ← |
| **Ultimately the pieces become loose and potholes form** ← | ← |

> **THE BOTTOM-UP PROPAGATION IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE CRITICAL FACT AND IT HAS A SEVERE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: by the time alligator cracking is VISIBLE at the surface, the crack has already traversed the full thickness of the bituminous layer.**

> **So the distress is far more advanced than its appearance suggests.**

> **A surface treatment applied at that point seals a layer that has already failed structurally, and the cracking continues beneath it.**

> **That is why alligator cracking calls for structural strengthening — an overlay designed from a deflection survey, or reconstruction — rather than for a surface seal, and why treating it as a surfacing problem wastes the treatment.**

**THE CLASSIFICATION OF CRACKING TYPES IS WORTH HAVING SINCE THE DIAGNOSIS FOLLOWS FROM THE PATTERN:**

| Pattern | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| **ALLIGATOR / crocodile, in the wheel paths** ← | **Structural fatigue — as above** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL, along the wheel path** ← | **Early-stage fatigue, or a construction joint** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL, at the pavement EDGE** ← | **Inadequate edge support, shoulder erosion, or subgrade moisture at the edge** ← |
| **TRANSVERSE, at regular spacing** ← | **Reflection cracking from a cement-bound layer beneath, or thermal cracking** ← |
| **BLOCK cracking over the whole area, not just wheel paths** ← | **Binder AGEING and shrinkage — not traffic-related** ← |
| **CRESCENT-shaped, at braking or turning areas** ← | **Slippage — a failed bond between layers** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS WORTH DISTINGUISHING FROM THE FIRST BECAUSE THEY LOOK SIMILAR AND MEAN OPPOSITE THINGS: block cracking covers the WHOLE surface, including areas no wheel ever touches.**

> **Fatigue cracking is confined to the WHEEL PATHS.**

> **So the location of the cracking distinguishes a traffic-loading problem from a binder-ageing problem, and the remedies differ completely — strengthening for one, resurfacing for the other.**

> **A pavement with block cracking may be structurally sound and merely old at the surface, and reconstructing it would be a considerable waste.**

> **THE SIXTH ROW CONNECTS BACK TO THE TACK COAT DISCUSSION AND IT IS WORTH CLOSING ON: crescent-shaped cracks at braking areas indicate that the surfacing has SLIPPED over the layer beneath.**

> **The cause is a missing, contaminated or inadequate tack coat, so the two layers were never bonded.**

> **Braking traffic applies a horizontal shear that the unbonded interface cannot carry, and the surface layer moves and wrinkles.**

> **The diagnosis is distinctive and the lesson is retrospective — the fault was committed at construction and shows up years later in a specific and recognisable pattern, which is a good argument for the interlayer bond being inspected and recorded at the time rather than taken on trust.**
tags: block cracking is ageing not traffic
slippage cracking from a failed tack coat

examTip.trick: **Fatigue from repeated flexing, cracking from the BOTTOM upward** — a structural inadequacy, not a surface defect.
examTip.trap: **When it is visible, the crack has already gone through the full layer** — so it needs strengthening, not a seal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wheel paths = fatigue; whole surface = binder ageing** — location distinguishes a structural problem from a surfacing one.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of a SUB-BASE layer in a flexible pavement is to:
options: Provide the riding surface for traffic
Act as the main structural layer resisting bending
Waterproof the subgrade completely
Spread the load further
questions.solution:
**Spread the load further, provide a DRAINAGE path, act as a separator preventing subgrade intrusion into the base, and give a working platform for constructing the layers above.**

**The four functions, each of which can govern:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **STRUCTURAL — further load spreading before the subgrade** ← | **Its nominal purpose** ← |
| **DRAINAGE — carrying water that enters the pavement out to the side drains** ← | **Often the most valuable function** ← |
| **SEPARATION — preventing the subgrade pumping up into the base** ← | **The geotextile's role, performed by grading** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION PLATFORM — allowing plant to work over a soft subgrade** ← | **Frequently the reason its thickness is what it is** ← |
| **FROST protection, where relevant** ← | **Not generally an issue in Nepal except at high altitude** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A PRACTICAL DRIVER THAT OFTEN GOVERNS THE THICKNESS IN A WAY THE STRUCTURAL CALCULATION DOES NOT: a soft subgrade cannot support a paver, a roller and a loaded tipper.**

> **So the first granular layer must be thick enough to carry construction plant before any structural requirement is considered.**

> **On a very soft subgrade that construction-platform thickness may exceed the structural requirement considerably, and the sub-base is then sized by buildability rather than by the design method.**

> **That is a legitimate reason for a thicker layer and it should be stated as such in the design, rather than being disguised as a structural requirement — because a reviewer who cannot see why the layer is thick may reduce it, and the works then become unbuildable.**

**THE DRAINAGE FUNCTION DESERVES SPECIAL EMPHASIS IN A MONSOON CLIMATE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water enters a pavement through cracks, joints, the shoulders and the verges** ← | **No surface is perfectly impermeable** ← |
| **Once in, it must get OUT** ← | ← |
| **A permeable sub-base conducts it laterally to the side drain** ← | ← |
| **If it cannot escape, it saturates the layers and softens the subgrade** ← | ← |
| **And repeated loading then PUMPS the saturated fines upward** ← | ← |
| **Which destroys the base's strength and the sub-base's drainage together** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS DESCRIBE THE FAILURE SPIRAL THAT DESTROYS MOST PAVEMENTS IN WET CLIMATES AND IT IS SELF-ACCELERATING: trapped water plus traffic equals pumping, pumping contaminates the drainage layer, the contaminated layer traps more water, and the process accelerates.**

> **So the drainage path must be continuous all the way to a free outlet, and the commonest defect is a sub-base that is permeable across the carriageway and is sealed at its edge by the shoulder material or by a raised verge.**

> **That arrangement creates a bathtub — water enters and cannot leave — and it is worse than having no drainage layer at all.**

> **So the sub-base must DAYLIGHT at the side drain, or be connected to it by a drain, and confirming that on site is one of the most valuable inspections available during construction.**

> **THE THIRD ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE IS ACHIEVED BY GRADING RATHER THAN BY A SEPARATE ELEMENT AND THAT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: a sub-base that satisfies the filter criteria against the subgrade will not allow the subgrade's particles to pass into it.**

> **So the separation function is designed in through the grading specification, and it is why sub-base grading limits include a fines requirement as well as a coarse one.**

> **Where the subgrade is very fine and the sub-base necessarily coarse, no single grading satisfies both the filter criterion and the drainage requirement — and that is precisely the case in which a geotextile separator is the correct addition, doing the job that the grading cannot.**

examTip.trick: **Load spreading, drainage, separation and a construction platform** — four functions, any of which can govern the thickness.
examTip.trap: **The construction platform requirement often exceeds the structural one** on soft ground — state that reason explicitly so nobody value-engineers it away.
examTip.mnemonic: **A sub-base sealed at its edge is a bathtub** — worse than none. It must daylight at the side drain.

questions.stem: A SURFACE DRESSING (chip seal) applied to an existing road:
options: Adds significant structural strength to the pavement
Is a thin SURFACING treatment
Replaces the need for any future maintenance for at least 20 years
Can only be applied to concrete pavements
questions.solution:
**It is a thin SURFACING treatment — a film of binder sprayed on the existing surface and covered with chippings — that restores skid resistance, seals the surface against water and arrests ravelling, but adds essentially NO structural capacity.**

**What a surface dressing does and does not do:**

| Does | Does NOT |
|---|---|
| **SEALS the surface against water ingress** ← | **Add structural strength** ← |
| **Restores SKID RESISTANCE with fresh angular chippings** ← | **Correct rutting or profile defects** ← |
| **Arrests RAVELLING and fretting** ← | **Repair structural cracking, which reflects through** ← |
| **Seals fine cracks** ← | **Improve the riding quality — it may worsen it slightly** ← |
| **Is very CHEAP per square metre** ← | ← |
| **Extends the pavement's life considerably when applied in time** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONTAINS THE PHRASE THAT MATTERS AND IT IS THE WHOLE OF PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE POLICY: 'when applied in time'.**

> **A surface dressing applied to a sound but ageing pavement seals it, keeps water out, and can add many years of life for a very small cost.**

> **The same treatment applied to a pavement that has already begun to fail structurally accomplishes nothing, because the failure is beneath it and continues regardless.**

> **So the treatment's value depends almost entirely on TIMING, and the window is while the pavement still looks acceptable — which is precisely when it is hardest to justify spending money on it.**

**THAT TIMING PROBLEM IS WORTH SETTING OUT EXPLICITLY BECAUSE IT DRIVES SO MUCH POOR PRACTICE:**

| Pavement condition | Appropriate treatment | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Good, slightly aged** ← | **Surface dressing** ← | **Very low** ← |
| **Fair, surface defects, no structural distress** ← | **Thin overlay or surface dressing** ← | **Low** ← |
| **Poor, structural cracking beginning** ← | **Structural overlay, designed from deflection** ← | **High** ← |
| **Failed** ← | **Reconstruction** ← | **Very high** ← |

> **THE COST COLUMN RISES BY ROUGHLY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE FROM TOP TO BOTTOM AND THE PROGRESSION IS INEXORABLE IF NOTHING IS DONE: a pavement left untreated moves down the table on its own.**

> **So the cheapest possible strategy is to keep pavements in the top two rows, treating them before they deteriorate into the expensive ones.**

> **The obstacle is political and budgetary rather than technical — spending on a road that looks fine, while another road is visibly failing, is a difficult case to make.**

> **But the arithmetic is decisive: the money spent keeping ten good roads good preserves more network than the same money spent reconstructing one failed road, and a maintenance regime that only responds to visible failure will always be short of funds because it is always paying the highest price available.**

**THE PRACTICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR A SUCCESSFUL SURFACE DRESSING DESERVE A CLOSING NOTE, SINCE IT FAILS EASILY WHEN DONE BADLY:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **A CLEAN, dry, sound existing surface** ← | **Sweeping is essential; binder will not bond to dust** ← |
| **Correct binder SPRAY RATE for the chipping size and the surface's texture** ← | **Too little and the chippings are lost; too much and it bleeds** ← |
| **Chippings applied IMMEDIATELY after the binder, before it cools or breaks** ← | ← |
| **Prompt ROLLING with a pneumatic-tyred roller to bed the chippings** ← | ← |
| **Traffic speed RESTRICTED until the chippings are held** ← | **Commonly 30 km/h for a day or two** ← |
| **Surplus chippings SWEPT UP afterwards** ← | **Loose chippings break windscreens and are a genuine hazard** ← |

> **The second row is where most failures originate and the reason is that the correct rate is not a single number: a smooth, non-porous existing surface needs less binder than a rough, hungry one, because the rough surface absorbs part of what is sprayed.**

> **So the rate must be assessed for the actual surface, usually by a standard procedure relating it to the surface texture depth and the chipping size.**

> **Applying a standard rate everywhere gives chipping loss on the rough sections and bleeding on the smooth ones, both on the same job — which is a recognisable signature of a rate that was assumed rather than assessed.**
tags: spray rate depends on surface texture

examTip.trick: **A thin seal restoring skid resistance and waterproofing** — with essentially no structural contribution.
examTip.trap: **Its value depends entirely on TIMING** — applied to a sound ageing pavement it adds years; applied to a failing one it achieves nothing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Spray rate depends on the EXISTING surface's texture** — a hungry rough surface absorbs binder. A single assumed rate bleeds and sheds on the same job.

questions.stem: The MODULUS OF SUBGRADE REACTION (k), used in rigid pavement design, is determined by:
options: The CBR test on a soaked sample
A triaxial compression test on an undisturbed sample
A sieve analysis combined with the Atterberg limits
A PLATE LOAD TEST
questions.solution:
**A PLATE LOAD TEST — a rigid plate of standard diameter is loaded on the subgrade and k is the pressure divided by the resulting deflection**, conventionally at 1.25 mm settlement.

**The test and the definition:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A rigid plate, standard diameter 750 mm, is placed on the prepared subgrade** ← | **Smaller plates are used with a correction** ← |
| **Load is applied in increments and the settlement measured** ← | ← |
| **k = pressure ÷ settlement, taken at 1.25 mm settlement** ← | ← |
| **Units are kg/cm³ or MPa/m** ← | **A pressure divided by a length, which is an unusual-looking unit** ← |
| **Typical values: 2 to 4 kg/cm³ for a weak subgrade, 8 or more for a strong one** ← | ← |

> **THE UNITS IN THE FOURTH ROW ARE WORTH A MOMENT BECAUSE THEY REVEAL WHAT THE QUANTITY IS: pressure per unit of settlement is a SPRING STIFFNESS per unit area.**

> **So k treats the subgrade as a bed of independent springs — the Winkler foundation — each deflecting in proportion to the pressure on it and independently of its neighbours.**

> **That is the model underlying Westergaard's rigid pavement analysis, and it is why k and not a modulus is the parameter used.**

> **The Winkler assumption is a considerable simplification, since real soil does interact between adjacent points, but it makes the slab analysis tractable and it gives results that have served well in practice.**

**THE 750 mm PLATE SIZE IS NOT ARBITRARY AND THE REASON IS INSTRUCTIVE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A larger plate stresses the soil to a greater DEPTH** ← | ← |
| **So the measured k depends on the plate size** ← | ← |
| **A small plate samples only the near-surface material** ← | ← |
| **A 750 mm plate approximates the stressed depth beneath a real slab and wheel load** ← | ← |
| **Where a smaller plate is used, a correction factor must be applied** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A GENUINELY IMPORTANT POINT ABOUT ALL PLATE AND BEARING TESTS AND IT GENERALISES: the result depends on the size of the loaded area, because the zone of influence scales with it.**

> **So a bearing capacity or a stiffness measured on a small plate does not transfer directly to a large foundation, and the same principle appears in shallow foundation design as the scale effect.**

> **A subgrade with a strong crust over soft material will give a high k on a small plate and a low one on a large plate, because only the large plate reaches the soft layer.**

> **That is exactly the situation in which an uncorrected small-plate test is dangerously misleading, and it is why the correction factors are specified rather than left to judgement.**

**THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN k AND CBR IS WORTH KNOWING SINCE CBR DATA IS FAR MORE COMMONLY AVAILABLE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Correlations exist between CBR and k, and they are published in design guides** ← | ← |
| **They are approximate and scatter considerably** ← | ← |
| **A direct plate load test is preferable where the pavement is important** ← | ← |
| **And the k value is increased by a granular or cement-treated SUB-BASE beneath the slab** ← | **The 'effective k' at the top of the sub-base, which is what the slab actually bears on** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A DESIGN POINT THAT IS EASY TO MISS AND IT MATTERS FOR THE SLAB THICKNESS: the k value used in design is not the subgrade's own k but the EFFECTIVE k at the top of whatever lies directly beneath the slab.**

> **A 150 mm granular sub-base over a subgrade with k = 3 might give an effective k of 4.5 or so at its top.**

> **A cement-treated sub-base raises it considerably more.**

> **So improving the layer beneath the slab raises k and reduces the required slab thickness — though the relationship is weak, because rigid pavement thickness is relatively insensitive to k, which is the same point as the slab's ability to bridge soft spots seen from the design side.**
tags: effective k at the top of the sub-base

examTip.trick: **Plate load test — pressure ÷ settlement at 1.25 mm**, using a 750 mm plate.
examTip.trap: **The result depends on PLATE SIZE** — a small plate samples only the near surface, so a crust over soft soil reads misleadingly high.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use the EFFECTIVE k at the top of the sub-base**, not the subgrade's own — though slab thickness is fairly insensitive to it.

questions.stem: WARPING STRESSES in a concrete pavement slab arise because:
options: The slab shrinks uniformly as the concrete cures
A TEMPERATURE DIFFERENTIAL between the top and bottom of the slab makes it tend to curl
Traffic loads are applied off the centre of the slab
The subgrade settles unevenly beneath the slab
questions.solution:
**A TEMPERATURE DIFFERENTIAL between the top and bottom of the slab makes it tend to curl, and the slab's own weight and its restraint at the joints prevent it from doing so freely** — inducing bending stresses.

**The mechanism by day and by night:**

| Time | Temperature | Slab tends to | Restrained by | Stress |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DAY** ← | **Top HOTTER than bottom** ← | **Curl DOWNWARD at the edges — the top expands more** ← | **The edges are held down by the slab's weight** ← | **TENSION at the bottom, mid-slab** ← |
| **NIGHT** ← | **Top COOLER than bottom** ← | **Curl UPWARD at the edges** ← | **The centre is held down by the weight of the lifted portions** ← | **TENSION at the TOP, mid-slab** ← |

> **THE NIGHT CASE IS THE MORE DANGEROUS AND IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT: at night the slab's edges and corners lift off the sub-base.**

> **A wheel load arriving at an unsupported corner is then carried by a cantilever rather than by a supported slab.**

> **So the night-time warping stress and the load stress at a corner ADD, and the combination is the critical design case for corner cracking.**

> **By day the edges are pressed down and the support is good, so the load stresses are lower even though the warping stress itself may be larger — which is why the critical combination is not simply the largest warping stress.**

**THE THREE CRITICAL LOAD POSITIONS IN WESTERGAARD'S ANALYSIS:**

| Position | Note |
|---|---|
| **INTERIOR loading** ← | **Load well away from any edge; the slab is supported all round** ← |
| **EDGE loading** ← | **Load at the edge of the slab, away from a corner — generally the CRITICAL case for flexural stress** ← |
| **CORNER loading** ← | **Load at a corner; the slab acts as a cantilever — critical when combined with night-time curling** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE GOVERNING CASE FOR MOST DESIGNS AND THE REASON IS GEOMETRIC: at an interior point the slab is supported in all directions and the load spreads radially.**

> **At an edge, support is available from only one side, so the effective spread is roughly halved and the stress is correspondingly higher.**

> **At a corner, support is available from even less, but the stress distribution differs and the failure mode is a diagonal crack rather than a flexural one.**

> **So all three must be checked, with the appropriate warping stress combined with each — and the combinations, rather than any single stress, are what the design must satisfy.**

**THE PRACTICAL MEASURES THAT REDUCE WARPING STRESS ARE WORTH LISTING:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHORTER slabs, achieved by closer joint spacing** ← | **The warping stress rises with slab length, so this is the direct remedy** ← |
| **A thinner slab has less temperature differential** ← | **Though it is weaker — the two effects oppose** ← |
| **A lighter-coloured surface reflects heat** ← | **Reducing the differential** ← |
| **Curing and construction in cooler conditions** ← | **Setting the zero-stress temperature favourably** ← |
| **Reinforcement does NOT prevent warping** ← | **It holds cracks tight once they form; it does not stop them forming** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WHY CONCRETE PAVEMENT SLABS ARE AS SHORT AS THEY ARE AND IT IS THE PRIMARY CONTROL: a plain jointed concrete pavement typically uses slabs of 4.5 m and the joint spacing is not a construction convenience but a stress-control decision.**

> **Longer slabs warp more, so the stresses rise, so the slab must be thicker.**

> **The last row deserves emphasis because it is widely misunderstood: reinforcement in a concrete pavement is not there to carry load.**

> **Its purpose is to hold shrinkage and thermal cracks TIGHT, so that aggregate interlock across them is maintained and water cannot enter — which allows longer slabs to be used in a jointed reinforced pavement, at the cost of the steel, and is an entirely different function from the flexural reinforcement in a beam.**
tags: reinforcement holds cracks tight not load

examTip.trick: **A temperature differential makes the slab curl, and weight plus restraint prevent it** — inducing bending stress.
examTip.trap: **Night is worse: edges and corners LIFT, so a corner load is carried by a cantilever** — warping and load stresses then add.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pavement reinforcement holds cracks TIGHT; it does not carry load** — an entirely different function from beam reinforcement.

questions.stem: In pavement design, the PERIOD after which a flexible pavement is expected to require a structural overlay rather than routine maintenance is the:
options: Service period, which is fixed by statute at 20 years for all roads
Design life — commonly 10 to 15 years for a flexible pavement
Warranty period offered by the contractor
Period between successive surface dressings
questions.solution:
**Design life — commonly 10 to 15 years for a flexible pavement**, chosen as an economic optimum balancing initial thickness against the timing and cost of the future strengthening.

**Why the design life is an economic choice rather than a technical constant:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A thicker pavement lasts longer before needing strengthening** ← | ← |
| **But it costs more NOW** ← | ← |
| **A thinner one costs less now and needs an overlay sooner** ← | ← |
| **Discounting makes a future cost worth less than a present one** ← | ← |
| **So there is an optimum initial thickness, and it corresponds to a particular design life** ← | ← |
| **Which for flexible pavements typically falls at 10 to 15 years** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHY SHORTER DESIGN LIVES ARE ECONOMIC FOR FLEXIBLE PAVEMENTS AND IT IS A GENUINE RESULT RATHER THAN A CONVENIENCE: an overlay in fifteen years, discounted, costs a fraction of its nominal amount in present-value terms.**

> **So deferring expenditure by building thinner now and strengthening later is often cheaper in present value than building thick at the outset.**

> **That reasoning holds provided the overlay ACTUALLY HAPPENS when it is due.**

> **Where maintenance funding is unreliable — which describes much of Nepal's network — the staged strategy fails, the overlay is not built, the pavement deteriorates past the point where an overlay suffices, and reconstruction becomes necessary at many times the cost.**

**THAT CONDITIONALITY IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT AND IT DESERVES TO GOVERN THE CHOICE:**

| Situation | Appropriate strategy |
|---|---|
| **Reliable maintenance funding and organisation** ← | **A shorter design life with planned strengthening — economically optimal** ← |
| **Unreliable maintenance funding** ← | **A LONGER design life and a thicker initial pavement — less optimal on paper, far more robust in practice** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A LEGITIMATE ENGINEERING RESPONSE TO AN INSTITUTIONAL REALITY AND IT SHOULD BE STATED AS SUCH RATHER THAN APPLIED QUIETLY: designing for a longer life where maintenance cannot be relied upon is not over-design, it is designing for the actual conditions the asset will experience.**

> **The conditions include the maintenance regime, which is as real a design input as the traffic and the subgrade.**

> **So the design life should be selected with the client's maintenance capacity explicitly considered, and the reasoning recorded.**

> **A design that assumes an overlay in year twelve, in an organisation that has never overlaid anything, has made an assumption that is demonstrably false and has built a pavement that will fail on schedule.**

**TYPICAL DESIGN LIVES BY PAVEMENT TYPE ARE WORTH KNOWING:**

| Pavement | Design life |
|---|---|
| **Flexible, to first structural overlay** ← | **10 to 15 years** ← |
| **Flexible, 'long-life' or perpetual design** ← | **40 years or more, with only surface renewal** ← |
| **RIGID concrete** ← | **30 to 40 years** ← |
| **Semi-rigid** ← | **20 years or so** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A CONCEPT WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT CHANGES THE TERMS OF THE TRADE: a PERPETUAL pavement is built thick enough that the tensile strain at the bottom of the bituminous layer never exceeds the fatigue endurance limit.**

> **Below that strain, the material does not accumulate fatigue damage at all, however many load repetitions occur.**

> **So the pavement never fails structurally, and only the surface course wears out and is periodically replaced.**

> **The initial cost is high and the whole-life cost can be lower, and it suits exactly the situation described above — a heavily trafficked route where future closures for reconstruction would be very disruptive and where the maintenance that IS reliable is surface renewal rather than structural work.**
tags: perpetual pavements and the endurance limit

examTip.trick: **Design life — 10 to 15 years for flexible** — an economic optimum, not a technical constant.
examTip.trap: **The staged strategy only works if the overlay actually happens** — where maintenance is unreliable, design thicker for longer, and record why.
examTip.mnemonic: **A perpetual pavement keeps strain below the fatigue ENDURANCE LIMIT** — so no damage accumulates and only the surface is renewed.

questions.stem: A POTHOLE forms in a bituminous pavement principally by the following sequence:
options: Water enters through a CRACK
The subgrade swells and pushes material out of the surface
Bitumen evaporates from the surface leaving a cavity
The aggregate dissolves in rainwater over time
questions.solution:
**Water enters through a CRACK, weakens the material beneath, traffic loading then pumps the saturated material out and breaks up the weakened surfacing, and the hole enlarges rapidly once formed.**

**The sequence in detail:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. A crack forms — from fatigue, ageing, reflection or a joint** ← | ← |
| **2. WATER enters through it** ← | ← |
| **3. The base and subgrade beneath soften and lose strength** ← | ← |
| **4. Traffic loading PUMPS the saturated fines up through the crack** ← | **Visible as a fan of fines on the surface after rain** ← |
| **5. A void forms beneath the surfacing, which is now unsupported** ← | ← |
| **6. The unsupported surfacing cracks further and pieces break out** ← | ← |
| **7. The hole's edges are then exposed and impacted by every wheel** ← | ← |
| **8. It enlarges rapidly, and faster in wet weather** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO STAGES ARE WHERE THE CHEAP INTERVENTION LIES AND THAT IS THE PRACTICAL LESSON: a crack sealed before water enters does not become a pothole.**

> **Crack sealing costs a tiny fraction of pothole repair, which itself costs a fraction of the reconstruction that widespread potholing eventually requires.**

> **So the maintenance hierarchy is clear — seal cracks, and the potholes largely do not form.**

> **The obstacle is again one of visibility: a crack is easy to ignore and a pothole is not, so resources flow to the expensive late intervention rather than the cheap early one.**

**THE REPAIR ITSELF HAS REQUIREMENTS THAT ARE ROUTINELY IGNORED AND THE IGNORING IS WHY REPAIRS FAIL:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **CUT BACK to sound material, with VERTICAL faces** ← | **A square or rectangular hole, not the ragged original shape** ← |
| **Remove ALL loose and wet material** ← | ← |
| **DRY the hole** ← | **Patching into water guarantees failure** ← |
| **Apply a TACK COAT to the faces and the base** ← | **So the patch bonds to the surrounding pavement** ← |
| **Fill in LAYERS and compact each properly** ← | **A deep hole filled in one lift cannot be compacted** ← |
| **Finish slightly PROUD and compact to level** ← | ← |
| **And FIND AND FIX the reason water was entering** ← | **Otherwise the patch fails and the adjacent pavement continues to deteriorate** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST FREQUENTLY OMITTED AND ITS OMISSION GUARANTEES A SHORT-LIVED REPAIR: a pothole's natural edges are ragged, undercut and cracked.**

> **Material placed against them bears on cracked, loose pavement that is itself about to fail.**

> **A vertical-faced rectangular cut, extending into sound material, gives the patch a solid abutment on every side and a definite thickness at its edges.**

> **So the repair that lasts takes a few extra minutes with a saw or a cutter, and the repair that fails is the one shovelled into the hole as found — which is why a road showing rings of failed patches around former potholes has a repair-practice problem rather than a materials problem.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE POINT THAT DISTINGUISHES MAINTENANCE FROM REPAIR AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING EMPHASIS: a pothole is a SYMPTOM.**

> **Water got in somewhere, and if it still can, the patched area and its surroundings will continue to deteriorate.**

> **So a pothole repair should include an inspection of why water was present — a blocked side drain, a failed seal, a low spot holding water, an adjacent crack — and the correction of that cause.**

> **A programme that counts potholes filled as its output measure will fill the same potholes repeatedly, and a programme that counts water-entry points eliminated will run out of potholes.**
tags: crack sealing is the cheap intervention
treat the cause not the symptom

examTip.trick: **Crack → water → softening → pumping → void → break-up → rapid enlargement.**
examTip.trap: **Cut back to SOUND material with VERTICAL faces** — a patch shovelled into the ragged hole bears on cracked pavement and fails quickly.
examTip.mnemonic: **A pothole is a symptom; find where the water entered** — otherwise the same hole is filled every year.

questions.stem: A flexible pavement is designed for a subgrade CBR of 5 per cent and 10 million standard axles. If the actual subgrade CBR turns out to be 3 per cent, the required pavement thickness will be:
options: GREATER
Unchanged, since thickness depends only on traffic
Smaller, since a softer subgrade absorbs more of the load
Halved, in proportion to the reduction in CBR
questions.solution:
**GREATER, since a weaker subgrade must be protected by a greater depth of pavement to reduce the vertical stress and strain reaching it to a tolerable level.**

**Why a weaker subgrade demands more thickness:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A wheel load spreads through the pavement in a widening cone** ← | ← |
| **The vertical stress at any depth falls as the depth increases** ← | ← |
| **A weak subgrade can tolerate only a small vertical stress or strain** ← | ← |
| **So the pavement must be thick enough to reduce the stress to that level before it arrives** ← | ← |
| **Hence a weaker subgrade requires a GREATER total thickness** ← | ← |

> **THE RELATIONSHIP IS NOT PROPORTIONAL, WHICH IS WHY OPTION (d) IS WRONG AS WELL AS OPTION (c): halving the CBR does not double the thickness.**

> **The design charts show thickness rising steeply at low CBR and flattening at higher values — going from CBR 2 to CBR 5 saves a great deal of thickness, and from CBR 10 to CBR 15 saves relatively little.**

> **So subgrade improvement is highly worthwhile on very weak ground and barely worthwhile on already-adequate ground.**

> **That non-linearity is what makes the decision to improve or replace a weak subgrade an economic calculation rather than an automatic one, and it explains why standards often set a minimum subgrade CBR — commonly 2 or 3 per cent — below which improvement is required rather than being traded against thickness.**

**THE DESIGN RESPONSE TO DISCOVERING A WEAKER SUBGRADE THAN ASSUMED:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Increase the pavement thickness** ← | **The direct response; read the new thickness from the design chart** ← |
| **IMPROVE the subgrade** ← | **Lime or cement stabilisation of the top 300 mm, raising its effective CBR** ← |
| **REPLACE the top of the subgrade with better material** ← | **A capping layer** ← |
| **Improve the DRAINAGE so the subgrade is not saturated when tested** ← | **Sometimes the CBR is low because the drainage is poor, not because the soil is bad** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WORTH CHECKING BEFORE THE OTHERS AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED: the soaked CBR represents the subgrade at its worst.**

> **If the drainage design ensures the subgrade never reaches that condition, a less pessimistic value may be justified — though this argument must be made carefully and only where the drainage is genuinely reliable and maintainable.**

> **Conversely, a subgrade whose measured CBR is low because groundwater is high may be improved more cheaply by lowering the water table than by any amount of added pavement.**

> **So the question 'why is this CBR low' is worth asking before the question 'how much more pavement does it need', and the answer sometimes makes the second question unnecessary.**

**THE PRACTICAL IMPLICATION FOR SITE INVESTIGATION DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Subgrade CBR varies along a road, often considerably** ← | ← |
| **Designing the whole road for the worst value is wasteful** ← | ← |
| **Designing for the average leaves the weak sections under-designed** ← | ← |
| **The practice is to divide the road into HOMOGENEOUS SECTIONS** ← | **Each with a similar subgrade, designed separately** ← |
| **Using a design value at a stated percentile within each section** ← | **Commonly the 90th percentile of the weakest values, or the mean minus a margin** ← |

> **The fourth row is the technique that resolves the dilemma and it is standard practice: the road is not one design problem but several.**

> **Sections of a kilometre or more with consistent subgrade are identified from the CBR profile, and each is designed for its own conditions.**

> **That produces a pavement whose thickness varies along the road, which is slightly more complex to construct and considerably cheaper overall.**

> **And it avoids the two failure modes of a single design — the waste of designing everything for the worst point, and the early failure of the weak sections if the average is used.**
tags: ask why the CBR is low

examTip.trick: **Greater thickness** — the pavement must reduce the stress reaching a weaker subgrade to what it can tolerate.
examTip.trap: **The relationship is NOT proportional** — thickness rises steeply at low CBR and flattens at high. Improvement pays on weak ground, not on adequate ground.
examTip.mnemonic: **Divide the road into HOMOGENEOUS SECTIONS** — one design for the worst point wastes money; one for the average fails the weak sections.

questions.stem: The IRI (International Roughness Index) of a road is expressed in m/km and measures:
options: The number of potholes per kilometre
The percentage of the surface area that is cracked
The ACCUMULATED SUSPENSION MOVEMENT of a standard quarter-car travelling at 80 km/h
The depth of rutting in the wheel paths
questions.solution:
**The ACCUMULATED SUSPENSION MOVEMENT of a standard quarter-car travelling at 80 km/h, per unit distance** — a measure of RIDING QUALITY that correlates with user comfort and vehicle operating cost.

**What IRI is and what the scale means:**

| IRI (m/km) | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Below 2** ← | **New airport runway or superhighway quality** ← |
| **2 to 4** ← | **New pavement; comfortable at high speed** ← |
| **4 to 6** ← | **Older pavement; acceptable; some discomfort above 100 km/h** ← |
| **6 to 8** ← | **Maintained unpaved road, or a damaged paved one** ← |
| **8 to 12** ← | **Rough unpaved road; speeds limited by roughness** ← |
| **Above 16** ← | **Severely damaged; passable only at low speed** ← |

> **THE DEFINITION AS A SIMULATED QUARTER-CAR RESPONSE IS THE PART THAT MAKES IRI USEFUL AND TRANSFERABLE: the index is computed from a measured longitudinal profile by running it through a standard mathematical vehicle model.**

> **So the result does not depend on the measuring device — a rod and level, a profilometer, a laser vehicle or a smartphone accelerometer all produce the same IRI from the same road, provided they capture the profile accurately.**

> **That device-independence is why IRI became the international standard, replacing earlier indices tied to particular measuring machines whose results could not be compared.**

> **And the 80 km/h in the definition is part of the model, not a requirement on the survey vehicle — the profile can be measured at any speed and the index computed as though a standard car had driven it at 80.**

**WHY RIDING QUALITY MATTERS AS MUCH AS STRUCTURAL CONDITION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **IRI is what road USERS actually experience** ← | **Nobody perceives a pavement's fatigue life** ← |
| **It drives VEHICLE OPERATING COSTS directly** ← | **As established earlier — tyres, suspension, fuel, time** ← |
| **It affects safety, since a rough surface reduces tyre contact and control** ← | ← |
| **It is the measure against which the public judges the road authority** ← | ← |
| **And it can be measured cheaply and rapidly over a whole network** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHAT MAKES IRI THE BACKBONE OF NETWORK-LEVEL PAVEMENT MANAGEMENT AND IT IS A PRACTICAL RATHER THAN A THEORETICAL ADVANTAGE: a vehicle-mounted profilometer can survey hundreds of kilometres a day.**

> **Structural condition, by contrast, requires deflection testing at intervals, which is far slower.**

> **So a pavement management system typically uses IRI as its primary network-level indicator, screening the network annually, and applies structural testing only to the sections that the roughness survey has flagged.**

> **That two-tier approach — cheap and universal screening, expensive and targeted investigation — is the same pattern as the road location survey sequence and the black spot process, and it recurs because it is the efficient way to allocate investigative effort.**

> **A CAUTION ABOUT WHAT IRI DOES NOT TELL YOU DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD: a pavement can have a good IRI and be structurally near failure.**

> **Fatigue cracking, for instance, may cover a wheel path without yet producing significant roughness.**

> **So a network managed on IRI alone will discover structural problems only when they have progressed far enough to affect the ride, by which point the cheap remedies have passed.**

> **Which is why the screening must include a visual condition survey for cracking alongside the roughness measurement — the two together give a reasonable picture, and either alone misses a whole class of deterioration.**

examTip.trick: **Simulated quarter-car suspension movement per km at 80 km/h** — a riding quality measure, in m/km.
examTip.trap: **The 80 km/h is in the MODEL, not the survey** — the profile can be measured at any speed and the index computed identically.
examTip.mnemonic: **Good IRI can hide near-failure** — fatigue cracking barely affects roughness. Pair the roughness survey with a visual crack survey.

questions.stem: A pavement's total thickness above the subgrade is 550 mm, comprising 40 mm wearing course, 60 mm binder course, 250 mm granular base and 200 mm sub-base. If the wearing course is later milled off and replaced with a 90 mm overlay, the net increase in total pavement thickness is:
options: 90 mm
130 mm
50 mm
40 mm
questions.solution:
**50 mm.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Thickness removed by milling** | **40 mm (the wearing course)** ← |
| **Thickness added** | **90 mm** ← |
| **Net increase** | **90 − 40 = 50 mm** ← |
| **New total** | **550 − 40 + 90 = 600 mm** ← |

> **THE DISTRACTOR AT 90 mm IS THE OVERLAY THICKNESS WITH THE MILLING IGNORED, and it is the error the question tests: milling removes material before the overlay is placed, so the net gain is the difference.**

> **The one at 130 mm adds the two rather than subtracting, and 40 mm is simply the milled thickness.**

> **The arithmetic is trivial and the comprehension is the point — the question is whether the candidate registers that two operations are occurring, one removing and one adding.**

> **Reading the question completely before calculating is the entire technique, and it is the one most often abandoned under time pressure.**

**WHY MILLING BEFORE OVERLAYING IS DONE AT ALL IS THE ENGINEERING CONTENT:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Maintaining the existing LEVELS** ← | **At kerbs, at bridge parapets, at property accesses, under overbridges** ← |
| **Removing the deteriorated, oxidised or cracked upper material** ← | **Which would otherwise remain as a weak layer within the pavement** ← |
| **Removing a RUTTED profile so the overlay has a uniform thickness** ← | ← |
| **Providing a rough, clean surface for the overlay to bond to** ← | ← |
| **The milled material can be RECYCLED** ← | **Reclaimed asphalt pavement, a valuable material** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS USUALLY THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IN URBAN WORK AND IT IS ABSOLUTE RATHER THAN A PREFERENCE: a road cannot simply keep rising with each overlay.**

> **Each 50 mm added reduces the kerb upstand, raises the road relative to the properties draining onto it, reduces the headroom under structures, and eventually leaves the kerb flush and the drainage inverted.**

> **Many urban roads that flood have been overlaid repeatedly until the carriageway sits above the adjoining ground.**

> **So milling is what makes repeated resurfacing sustainable, and a maintenance regime that overlays without milling is storing up a drainage problem that eventually requires the whole road to be reconstructed to its original level.**

**THE SECOND ROW DESERVES ELABORATION SINCE IT IS A STRUCTURAL ARGUMENT RATHER THAN A GEOMETRIC ONE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The top of an old bituminous layer is the most oxidised and most cracked** ← | ← |
| **Overlaying it leaves that weak, cracked material buried in the pavement** ← | ← |
| **Its cracks then REFLECT upward through the new overlay** ← | ← |
| **Milling it off removes the crack source** ← | ← |
| **Which is a far more effective anti-reflection measure than any interlayer** ← | ← |

> **The fifth row is worth stating plainly because reflection cracking is otherwise difficult to prevent: an interlayer, a geogrid or a stress-absorbing membrane all DELAY reflection, and removing the cracked layer PREVENTS it.**

> **So where the cracking is confined to the upper part of the bituminous layers, milling to below the cracks is the definitive remedy.**

> **Where the cracking extends through the full depth, milling the surface achieves less and the problem is structural rather than superficial.**

> **Establishing which case applies — by coring, which is cheap — before deciding the treatment is therefore worth doing, and it is the difference between an overlay that lasts its design life and one that cracks through within two years.**

examTip.trick: **90 mm added − 40 mm milled = 50 mm net.** Two operations, one removing and one adding.
examTip.trap: **90 mm ignores the milling** — the question describes a removal as well as an addition.
examTip.mnemonic: **Milling is what makes repeated overlaying sustainable** — otherwise the road rises above its kerbs and its drainage inverts.

questions.stem: In a PAVEMENT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM, the essential function is to:
options: Record the contractual details of each construction project
Store the design calculations for each pavement section
Schedule the daily work of the maintenance gangs
Hold an INVENTORY and CONDITION record of the network
questions.solution:
**Hold an INVENTORY and CONDITION record of the network, PREDICT how each section will deteriorate under alternative maintenance strategies, and identify the programme that maximises network condition or minimises whole-life cost within the available budget.**

**The components of a pavement management system:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **INVENTORY — what exists: location, length, width, construction, age** ← | **The foundation; without it nothing else is possible** ← |
| **CONDITION data — roughness, cracking, rutting, deflection, updated periodically** ← | ← |
| **TRAFFIC data — volumes, composition, axle loads** ← | ← |
| **DETERIORATION models — predicting future condition under each strategy** ← | **The analytical core** ← |
| **TREATMENT options with unit costs and expected effects** ← | ← |
| **OPTIMISATION — selecting the programme that best meets the objective within the budget** ← | ← |
| **Reporting, to inform decisions and to justify budgets** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHAT DISTINGUISHES A MANAGEMENT SYSTEM FROM A DATABASE AND IT IS THE COMPONENT MOST OFTEN MISSING: a record of current condition tells you what the network is like today.**

> **A deterioration model tells you what it will be like in five years under each of the strategies you might adopt.**

> **Only the second supports a decision, because the decision is about the future.**

> **So a system that records condition beautifully and predicts nothing is an inventory rather than a management system, and it can answer 'what is bad now' but not the far more important question of 'what will it cost us if we do nothing'.**

**THE OPTIMISATION IN THE SIXTH ROW IS WHERE THE VALUE IS REALISED AND IT PRODUCES COUNTER-INTUITIVE ANSWERS:**

| Intuitive policy | Optimal policy |
|---|---|
| **Fix the WORST roads first** ← | **Often wrong — the worst roads are the most expensive to fix per km** ← |
| ← | **Preserving GOOD roads before they deteriorate protects more network per rupee** ← |
| **Spread the budget evenly across districts** ← | **Concentrate it where the deterioration curve is steepest** ← |
| **Respond to complaints** ← | **Act on predicted condition, not on reported condition** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE MOST POLITICALLY DIFFICULT FINDING THAT EVERY SUCH SYSTEM PRODUCES: 'worst first' is an intuitive, defensible-sounding and generally wrong policy.**

> **A road that has failed requires reconstruction at perhaps ten times the cost per kilometre of the preventive treatment that would keep a good road good.**

> **So a budget spent on worst-first restores a few kilometres while the rest of the network slides toward the same condition.**

> **A budget spent on preservation holds a large part of the network in good condition and allows the failed sections to be addressed progressively as funds permit — which produces a better network overall, and looks like neglect to anyone driving the worst road.**

> **THAT COMMUNICATION PROBLEM IS REAL AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD: the optimal policy is hard to explain and easy to attack.**

> **A resident on a failed road, told that the budget is being spent on roads that are still good, has a grievance that is understandable and that no amount of optimisation theory will satisfy.**

> **So a pavement management system's outputs need to be accompanied by an explanation of the reasoning, and usually by a compromise — some proportion of the budget reserved for the worst sections, accepting a less than optimal allocation in exchange for a sustainable one.**

> **Recognising that the optimum must be politically deliverable to be delivered at all is not a failure of the analysis but a condition on its use, and a recommendation that ignores it will be overridden and will have achieved nothing.**

examTip.trick: **Inventory, condition, deterioration prediction and optimisation** — deciding the programme, not merely recording the network.
examTip.trap: **Without DETERIORATION MODELS it is a database, not a management system** — decisions are about the future, not the present.
examTip.mnemonic: **'Worst first' is intuitive and usually wrong** — preserving good roads protects far more network per rupee than reconstructing failed ones.

questions.stem: In road earthwork, the MASS HAUL DIAGRAM is used to:
options: Plot the CUMULATIVE volume of cut minus fill against chainage
Show the weight of materials delivered to site each day
Record the number of haulage vehicles on site
Show the mass of each pavement layer per square metre
questions.solution:
**Plot the CUMULATIVE volume of cut minus fill against chainage** — from which the balance of earthwork, the direction and distance of haul, and the economic limit of hauling against borrowing or wasting are all determined.

**How the diagram is read:**

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **The curve RISING** ← | **Cut exceeds fill over that stretch — material is being generated** ← |
| **The curve FALLING** ← | **Fill exceeds cut — material is required** ← |
| **A MAXIMUM (peak)** ← | **A change from cut to fill; material is hauled FORWARD from here** ← |
| **A MINIMUM (trough)** ← | **A change from fill to cut** ← |
| **A horizontal BALANCING LINE** ← | **Cuts the curve at points between which cut and fill balance exactly** ← |
| **The AREA between the curve and the balancing line** ← | **The HAUL — volume times distance** ← |
| **The LENGTH of the balancing line** ← | **The maximum haul distance within that balance** ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE DIAGRAM'S MOST USEFUL PROPERTY AND IT IS NOT OBVIOUS FROM THE CONSTRUCTION: the AREA enclosed between the curve and a balancing line has units of volume × distance, which is exactly the quantity haulage is paid for.**

> **So the diagram does not merely show where material balances; it measures the transport effort directly.**

> **Comparing two possible balancing arrangements is then a matter of comparing areas, which can be done by eye for a rough answer and by planimeter or calculation for a precise one.**

> **That makes the diagram a genuine optimisation tool rather than a presentational device, and it is why it survived long after most graphical methods were superseded by computation.**

**THE FREE HAUL AND OVERHAUL CONCEPT IS THE COMMERCIAL PURPOSE OF THE DIAGRAM:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FREE HAUL distance** ← | **The distance within which haulage is included in the excavation rate and not paid separately** ← |
| **OVERHAUL** ← | **Haulage beyond the free haul distance, paid as an extra** ← |
| **LIMIT OF ECONOMIC HAUL** ← | **The distance beyond which it is cheaper to BORROW new material and WASTE the surplus than to haul** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE DECISION THE DIAGRAM EXISTS TO INFORM AND IT HAS A SIMPLE BREAK-EVEN: hauling material a long way costs more per cubic metre than digging fresh material from a borrow pit nearby and tipping the surplus in a spoil area nearby.**

> **The limit of economic haul is where those two costs are equal, and it is computed as the free haul distance plus the cost of borrow-and-waste divided by the cost of overhaul per unit distance.**

> **Beyond that distance the diagram's balancing lines should not be extended, and borrow and waste should be planned instead.**

> **In hill terrain the limit is short, because haulage on a narrow winding road under construction is slow and expensive — so hill road earthwork is balanced over short lengths and uses local borrow and local tipping far more than a plains project would.**

> **A CAUTION SPECIFIC TO HILL ROADS DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD AND IT CONNECTS TO THE GREEN ROAD PRINCIPLE: the 'waste' in a mass haul analysis has to GO somewhere, and on a hillside that somewhere matters enormously.**

> **A plains project can tip surplus in a designated area with modest consequence.**

> **A hill project that treats spoil as a quantity to be disposed of at least cost will side-tip it, with the slope failures described earlier.**

> **So the mass haul optimisation on a hill road must be constrained by the availability of ACCEPTABLE tipping sites, identified and secured in advance — and where they are scarce, the correct answer may be to haul further than the economic limit suggests, because the true cost of the cheap disposal is not in the haulage rate.**

examTip.trick: **Cumulative cut minus fill against chainage** — rising means surplus, falling means deficit, and a horizontal line balances the two.
examTip.trap: **The AREA between the curve and the balancing line is the HAUL** — volume × distance, which is what haulage is paid for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Beyond the economic haul limit, borrow and waste instead** — but on a hillside, acceptable tipping sites constrain the answer more than cost does.

questions.stem: The BULKING and SHRINKAGE factors applied to earthwork volumes account for the fact that:
options: Soil BULKS when excavated
Material is lost during transport and handling
The surveyed cross-sections are always inaccurate
The material absorbs water during the monsoon
questions.solution:
**Soil BULKS when excavated because it becomes loose, and then SHRINKS when compacted in the fill, often to a volume less than it occupied in situ** — so bank, loose and compacted volumes of the same material all differ.

**The three volume states:**

| State | Description | Relative volume |
|---|---|---|
| **BANK (in situ) measure** ← | **As it lies undisturbed in the ground** ← | **1.00, the reference** ← |
| **LOOSE measure** ← | **After excavation, in the truck** ← | **1.10 to 1.40 — BULKING** ← |
| **COMPACTED measure** ← | **After placing and compacting in the fill** ← | **0.85 to 1.00 — SHRINKAGE relative to bank** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE UNTIL EXPLAINED: compacted fill can occupy LESS volume than the material did in the ground.**

> **That happens because modern compaction plant achieves a higher density than the material had naturally, particularly for a soil that was loosely deposited or weathered in place.**

> **So 100 m³ excavated from a cutting might yield 130 m³ in trucks and produce only 90 m³ of compacted embankment.**

> **A calculation that ignores this will under-supply the fill by 10 per cent, and the shortfall appears near the end of the earthwork when the borrow sources have been closed — which is a familiar and avoidable problem.**

**THE FACTORS VARY WITH THE MATERIAL AND THE VALUES ARE WORTH KNOWING APPROXIMATELY:**

| Material | Bulking | Shrinkage |
|---|---|---|
| **Sand and gravel** ← | **10 to 15 per cent** ← | **Small — it was already fairly dense** ← |
| **Common earth and clay** ← | **20 to 30 per cent** ← | **10 to 15 per cent** ← |
| **ROCK, blasted** ← | **40 to 60 per cent** ← | **NEGATIVE — rock fill occupies MORE than the rock did in situ** ← |

> **THE ROCK ROW IS THE IMPORTANT EXCEPTION AND IT REVERSES THE USUAL RELATIONSHIP: blasted rock cannot be compacted back to the density of intact rock.**

> **The fragments interlock with voids between them that no compaction can close.**

> **So a cubic metre of rock excavated produces perhaps 1.3 cubic metres of rock fill, and a project balancing rock cut against fill has a SURPLUS rather than a deficit.**

> **On a hill road through rock, that surplus is substantial and it must be disposed of — which returns directly to the spoil disposal problem, and means that a rocky alignment generates a spoil management problem even when the cut and fill quantities appear balanced on a simple volume calculation.**

**THE PRACTICAL RULE FOR APPLYING THE FACTORS DESERVES STATING BECAUSE ERRORS ARE COMMON:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cut quantities are measured and paid in BANK measure** ← | **What was removed from the ground** ← |
| **Fill quantities are measured and paid in COMPACTED measure** ← | **What is in the embankment** ← |
| **Haulage is often priced in LOOSE measure** ← | **What the truck carries** ← |
| **So the same material has three different quantities in the same bill** ← | ← |
| **And the conversion factors must be stated in the contract** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS A CONTRACTUAL NECESSITY AND ITS OMISSION IS A RELIABLE SOURCE OF DISPUTE: if the contract does not state the conversion factors, the contractor and the engineer will each adopt the interpretation favourable to them.**

> **The factors also depend on the actual material, which is not fully known until excavation begins.**

> **So the better contractual arrangement specifies how the factors will be DETERMINED — by measurement on site during the early works, using an agreed procedure — rather than fixing values in advance that may prove wrong.**

> **That converts a likely dispute into an agreed measurement exercise, which is generally the right way to handle a quantity that cannot be known accurately at tender.**
tags: compacted can be less than bank

examTip.trick: **Bank, loose and compacted are three different volumes of the same material** — it bulks on excavation and shrinks on compaction.
examTip.trap: **ROCK reverses it** — blasted rock fill occupies MORE than the intact rock did, so a rock cutting generates a surplus to dispose of.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cut is paid in bank, fill in compacted, haul in loose** — three quantities in one bill, and the contract must say how the factors are determined.

questions.stem: In a hill road, a BREAST WALL and a RETAINING WALL differ in that the breast wall:
options: Is always constructed of reinforced concrete while a retaining wall is of masonry
Is built on the VALLEY side to support the fill, whereas a retaining wall is built on the hill side
Is built on the HILL side to support the cut slope and prevent material falling onto the road, whereas a retaining wall is built on the VALLEY side to retain the fill that carries the road
Is a temporary structure removed after construction
questions.solution:
**It is built on the HILL side to support the cut slope and prevent material falling onto the road, whereas a retaining wall is built on the VALLEY side to retain the fill that carries the road.**

**The two walls and what each does:**

| Wall | Position | Retains | Loading |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BREAST wall** ← | **HILL side, at the toe of the cut slope** ← | **The cut face — natural ground** ← | **Generally LIGHTER; it supports a slope that is largely self-supporting** ← |
| **RETAINING wall** ← | **VALLEY side, below the road** ← | **The fill that the carriageway sits on** ← | **HEAVIER; it carries the fill and the traffic load above it** ← |

> **THE LOADING DIFFERENCE IN THE LAST COLUMN IS WHY THE TWO ARE DISTINGUISHED RATHER THAN BOTH BEING CALLED RETAINING WALLS: a breast wall supports material that would mostly stand on its own.**

> **Its function is to hold the toe of the cut, prevent gradual ravelling and erosion, and allow a steeper cut face than the material would otherwise sustain — so it reduces the width of excavation needed.**

> **A retaining wall on the valley side carries the full weight of the fill plus the traffic on it, and its failure takes the road with it.**

> **So the retaining wall is the more critical structure and is designed accordingly, while a breast wall is often a lighter dry-stone or masonry construction — and the terminology reflects a real difference in consequence rather than merely in position.**

**BOTH REQUIRE DRAINAGE AND IT IS THE MOST COMMON CAUSE OF FAILURE IN BOTH:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **WEEP HOLES through the wall at regular spacing** ← | **Commonly 75 to 100 mm diameter at 1 to 1.5 m centres, both ways** ← |
| **A granular FILTER or drainage layer behind the wall** ← | **So the weep holes do not clog and the fines are not washed out** ← |
| **A longitudinal drain at the back of the wall base** ← | ← |
| **Surface drainage above the wall, so water does not run in from the top** ← | ← |

> **THE REASON DRAINAGE IS SO CRITICAL IS WORTH STATING QUANTITATIVELY: water behind a wall generates HYDROSTATIC pressure, and that pressure can easily exceed the earth pressure the wall was designed for.**

> **Saturated backfill roughly doubles the lateral thrust — the effective earth pressure plus the full water pressure — so a wall designed for drained conditions and subjected to undrained ones is loaded far beyond its capacity.**

> **Since drainage is cheap and additional wall thickness is expensive, every retaining structure is designed on the assumption that it drains, and that assumption is only as good as the weep holes and the filter behind them.**

> **A wall whose weep holes have clogged is therefore carrying a load it was never designed for, silently — which is the same category of invisible degradation seen with dam drains and pressure tunnel drainage, and it is the reason weep holes should be checked and cleared as a routine maintenance item.**

**THE ALTERNATIVES TO MASONRY WALLS DESERVE MENTION SINCE THEY SUIT HILL CONDITIONS WELL:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **GABION walls** ← | **Rock-filled wire baskets — FLEXIBLE, free-draining, tolerant of settlement, built by hand from local stone** ← |
| **Dry stone masonry** ← | **Traditional, labour-based, free-draining; limited in height** ← |
| **Mortared stone masonry** ← | **Stronger, but must be deliberately drained since it is not permeable** ← |
| **Reinforced concrete** ← | **Highest capacity, requires cement, steel, formwork and plant** ← |
| **REINFORCED SOIL** ← | **Geogrid-reinforced fill with a facing — very tolerant of settlement and economical at height** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW SUITS NEPAL'S HILL ROADS PARTICULARLY WELL AND THE REASONS ARE WORTH NAMING: a gabion wall is free-draining by construction, so the hydrostatic problem does not arise.**

> **It is flexible, so it deforms with ground movement rather than cracking — which matters greatly on slopes that are still settling.**

> **It uses local stone and local labour and needs no cement, formwork or plant.**

> **And it can be repaired and extended incrementally, which suits the multi-season green road approach exactly — its weakness being the wire, which corrodes and is vulnerable to damage, so the mesh coating specification and periodic inspection are what determine its life.**

examTip.trick: **Breast wall on the HILL side supporting the cut; retaining wall on the VALLEY side carrying the fill and the road.**
examTip.trap: **Saturated backfill roughly doubles the lateral thrust** — every wall is designed assuming it drains, so clogged weep holes overload it silently.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gabions are free-draining, flexible, local stone and local labour** — which is why they suit Himalayan hill roads so well.

questions.stem: The purpose of a CATCH DRAIN (or catchwater drain) above a hill road cutting is to:
options: Collect water from the road surface and carry it away
Supply water for construction purposes
INTERCEPT surface runoff from the hillside ABOVE the cutting and carry it away to a safe outfall
Collect groundwater from within the cut slope
questions.solution:
**INTERCEPT surface runoff from the hillside ABOVE the cutting and carry it away to a safe outfall**, before it can reach and erode the cut face.

**The drainage elements of a hill road and what each handles:**

| Element | Handles |
|---|---|
| **CATCH (catchwater) drain, above the cutting** ← | **Runoff from the hillside above, intercepted before it reaches the cut face** ← |
| **SIDE drain, at the toe of the cut** ← | **Runoff from the cut face and from the carriageway** ← |
| **CROSS drainage — culverts and causeways** ← | **Natural watercourses crossing the alignment** ← |
| **Chutes and cascades** ← | **Carrying collected water DOWN the slope to a safe outfall** ← |
| **Subsurface drains** ← | **Groundwater within the slope, which the catch drain does not address** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS AND IT IS THE POINT OPTION (d) TESTS: a catch drain intercepts SURFACE water only.**

> **Water already within the slope, moving as groundwater, passes beneath the catch drain entirely.**

> **That requires a different measure — counterfort drains, horizontal drains drilled into the slope, or a drainage blanket.**

> **So a slope failing from groundwater will continue to fail however well it is caught at the surface, and correctly diagnosing which water is causing the problem is the first step — a distinction exactly parallel to the surface-versus-groundwater diagnosis in the drainage congestion question.**

**THE CATCH DRAIN'S OWN DESIGN REQUIREMENTS ARE WHERE IT MOST OFTEN FAILS:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Located far enough BACK from the crest of the cut** ← | **Typically several metres, so that leakage does not saturate the cut face** ← |
| **LINED, or at least well compacted** ← | **An unlined drain on a slope erodes into a gully** ← |
| **Adequate longitudinal GRADIENT** ← | **Enough to be self-cleansing, not so much as to erode** ← |
| **Discharging at a SAFE outfall** ← | **A natural watercourse, via a lined chute with energy dissipation** ← |
| **MAINTAINED — cleared of debris and slips** ← | **A blocked catch drain overtops and concentrates water onto the slope it was protecting** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DESCRIBES A FAILURE MODE THAT IS WORSE THAN HAVING NO DRAIN AT ALL AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: an unmaintained catch drain collects water along its length and then discharges it all at the point where it is blocked.**

> **So instead of runoff arriving at the cut face diffusely, spread along the whole length, it arrives concentrated at one point.**

> **A concentrated flow erodes where a diffuse one would not, and the resulting gully can initiate a slope failure.**

> **So the drain converts a diffuse problem into a concentrated one whenever it is blocked, and a catch drain that will not be maintained is genuinely better omitted — which is an uncomfortable conclusion and a true one, and it argues for designing drainage that can realistically be maintained rather than drainage that would be ideal if it were.**
